title: Annotated Diamond Sutra
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: All that has marks is false and illusory; not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.

inline.s: All that has marks is false and illusory; not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.
Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.
It dissolves the inverted thoughts of my millions of kalpas; without passing through asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I attain the Dharma body.

For a thousand years and more, why has the Diamond Sutra been so widely savored, known in every household, discussed in countless lectures, and annotated without number? The reason is not only that the merit and virtue of upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra are beyond compare, but also that people sense in it the revelation of an inconceivably powerful yet profoundly mysterious truth—a wish-fulfilling jewel sovereign for escaping suffering, transcending birth and death, and accomplishing the Buddha Way. And so they untiringly explore and awaken to it: What does the Diamond Sutra teach? What is it truly teaching?
The Diamond Sutra—its full title is the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra. In the
years during which the World-Honored One taught the Dharma, he expounded the Prajñāpāramitā scriptures for

of them, in seven hundred and fifty-one fascicles in all. The largest of these is the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (in full, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra), six hundred fascicles in total, completed over the course of sixteen assemblies. The Diamond Sutra is what was spoken at the ninth of those assemblies, the “Able to Cut Off the Vajra” section (fascicle five hundred and seventy-seven), amounting to a little over five thousand characters. Prajñā is the essence of Mahāyāna Buddhadharma, and the Diamond Sutra in turn is the essence of the six-hundred-fascicle Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra.
The essential purport of this sutra: compassion and emptiness working together, leaving illusion behind and waking from the dream.

All dharmas are matters within the dream of ignorance. While dreaming, the myriad phenomena appear in profusion; when the dream ends, nothing whatsoever remains. Hence the characteristic of all dharmas is this: they have marks but no substance. Therefore, with respect to all dharmas, one must neither deludedly cling to their existence (taking them to be real) nor deludedly cling to their non-existence (denying even their phenomenal marks). One should walk the middle way that abides in neither of the two extremes, joining compassion and emptiness, using illusion to leave illusion, until all illusions are gone and the dream of ignorance ends. Throughout this sutra, the World-Honored One reveals this essential purport again and again.

[Substance, marks] Substance means the reality of all dharmas, that is, the true characteristic of all dharmas. Marks means the manifold forms and appearances of all dharmas. We live within the dream of ignorance, and all dharmas are matters within that dream; hence they have their marks but not their substance (marks exist while substance does not). [Marks exist while substance does not] While within the dream of ignorance, all dharmas appear in myriad profusion; when the dream of ignorance ends, nothing whatsoever remains. The Song of Realizing the Way says:
“In the dream there clearly are the six destinies
(the six paths)
, but after awakening all is empty—there is no great trichiliocosm
(the great trichiliocosm)
For a detailed discussion of the true characteristic of all dharmas and the dream of ignorance, see
The True Characteristic of All Dharmas

Yet when innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings have thus been delivered to extinction, in truth there is no sentient being who attains extinction.”

Sentences such as these—breaking existence, breaking non-existence, abiding in neither extreme—are found everywhere in the Diamond Sutra, too many to enumerate. Practitioners should take up the middle way that abides in neither extreme. If one has fallen to one side, one should take the medicine suited to the illness: those clinging to existence should cultivate the contemplation of emptiness and non-existence; those clinging to non-existence should cultivate compassion.
The Diamond Sutra has five great features:
(1) The Diamond Sutra is the most widely circulated and known in every household

For more than a thousand years, those who study Buddhism—whatever their school, whatever Dharma-gate they practice—have made a point of reciting the Diamond Sutra; and even scholars who do not study Buddhism have made a point of reading it. According to the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra Oral Instructions of Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, in his time (the age of Empress Wu Zetian) those who composed commentaries and annotations on the Diamond Sutra numbered more than eight hundred. The preface to the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra Oral Instructions says:
“Of this sutra
(the Diamond Sutra)
there are countless who read and recite it, boundless who praise it, and those who composed commentaries and annotations number over eight hundred.”
(2) The Diamond Sutra is the mother of all Buddhas, the most perfect, the most sudden, the most real
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom
volume seventy-four says:
“Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas; abiding in this prajñā, one can fulfill all Buddhadharmas.”

Thus we know that prajñā is the guiding principle of all Buddhadharma, and the Diamond Sutra in turn is the guiding principle of the six-hundred-fascicle Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra. In this sutra the World-Honored One says:
“All Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra.”

This shows that the Diamond Sutra is the mind-dharma of the Tathāgata, the most perfect, most sudden, most real dharma for accomplishing Buddhahood. Hence the influence of the Diamond Sutra is exceedingly vast and far-reaching; those who study it, annotate it, uphold it, and recite it are countless, and those who thereby awaken to the Way and realize the fruit are countless as well. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records:
“The Master
(Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan)
constantly urged monks and laypeople alike simply to uphold the Diamond Sutra, and thereby see their own nature and immediately accomplish Buddhahood.”

The Sixth Patriarch himself was inspired by the Diamond Sutra to journey to the Eastern Mountain in search of the Way; through the Diamond Sutra he awakened and realized the fruit. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is itself the great practice of the Diamond Sutra.
(3) The merit and virtue of upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra are boundless

The merit and virtue of upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra are exceedingly great, and their karmic reward is inconceivable; the World-Honored One says so repeatedly in the sutra. For example:

In future ages, if good men and good women are able to uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by his Buddha-wisdom, will know such people and see such people, and they will all accomplish measureless, boundless merit and virtue.”

Subhūti! If good men and good women in the first watch of the day give in charity their bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in the middle watch of the day again give in charity their bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and in the last watch of the day also give in charity their bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—thus for measureless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas giving their bodies in charity; and if another person hears this scripture and his faith is not reversed, his merit surpasses that of the former, how much more so if he writes it out, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others.”

(Translation: Subhūti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the morning, again give in charity their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges at noon, and again give in charity their bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the evening—thus for measureless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, giving their bodies and lives in charity three times each day; and if another person hears this scripture and believes without doubt, the merit he gains surpasses that of the former. How much more so if he also writes it out, upholds, reads, and recites the Diamond Sutra, and explains it for others—the merit he gains is then beyond all reckoning!)

“If someone is able to uphold, read, and recite it and to expound it widely for others, the Tathāgata will know such a person and see such a person, and he will accomplish merit that is immeasurable, ineffable, boundless, and inconceivable. Such a person is one who bears on his shoulders the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of the Tathāgata.”
“If in a future age, in the last five hundred years, there be a sentient being who hears this sutra and believes, understands, and upholds it, such a person is foremost and most rare.”

“I recall that in the past, throughout measureless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, before I met Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty million nayutas of Buddhas, and I honored and served them all without ever passing one by in vain. But if someone in a later age of decline can uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he gains—compared with the merit I gained by honoring all those Buddhas—my merit does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand myriad billionth of his, nor indeed to any fraction of his that reckoning or simile could describe.”

(Translation: I recall that throughout countless kalpas in the past, before I met Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty million times ten million nayutas of Buddhas, and I honored and served them all without ever passing one by in vain. If someone in a later age of decline can uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he gains—compared with the merit I gained by honoring all those Buddhas—my merit does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand myriad billionth of his, nor indeed to any fraction of his that even reckoning or simile cannot describe.)

“If good men and good women in a later age of decline uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and if I were to set forth in full the merit they gain, some who heard it would have their minds become frenzied and would doubt and disbelieve. Subhūti! You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is likewise inconceivable.”
Therefore, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra is the dual cultivation of merit and wisdom. The Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra
its preface says:

“If good people and worthy scholars can truly cultivate diligently and sincerely, reverently uphold and recite, seek the Dharma through the sutra, and awaken through the Dharma, they will at once extinguish measureless transgressions and at once obtain the most excellent field of merit.”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“By reciting the Diamond Prajñā Sutra, one at once sees one’s nature. You should know that the merit of this sutra is measureless and boundless; it is plainly praised in the sutra itself, and cannot be fully set forth.”
(4) Upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra eradicates karmic obstruction
In the Diamond Sutra the Buddha says:

“If good men and good women uphold and recite this sutra and are despised by others, it is because of evil karma from former lives that they should have fallen into the evil paths. But because in this present life they are despised by others, the evil karma of former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

(Translation: If good men and good women uphold and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because of evil karma created in the past (including this present life before upholding and reciting this sutra, and all lives before it); by that karma they should have fallen into the evil paths immediately after death. Now, because they uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra, although in this present life they are despised by others, the evil karma created in the past is thereby extinguished, and they shall certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.) This teaches: those who uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra have grave offenses lightly requited—the grave offense being to fall into the evil paths after death, the light requital being to be despised by others in this present life—and the merit and virtue they gain are exceedingly great: they shall certainly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
(5) Upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra requires faith, understanding, and practice

In upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra, faith, understanding, and practice stand as three legs of a tripod, and not one may be missing. Yet the link of “understanding” is all too often neglected. If one does not understand the sutra’s meaning, “faith” has nothing to rest on—one does not know what it is one believes—and “practice” likewise does not know how to proceed, and may even proceed in reverse. Therefore, in upholding the Diamond Sutra, one must expend great effort on “understanding,” giving rise to faith in accord with principle, and setting out in practice in reliance on principle, so that faith, understanding, and practice correspond.

In reading the scriptures, the essential thing is to see the words, grasp the meaning, and clarify the mind—that is, to understand through hearing, to awaken through reflection, and to realize through practice. The point where it all comes to rest is: practice in accordance with the teaching. The Diamond Sutra is a dialogue of Socratic questioning between the World-Honored One and his great disciple Subhūti, penetrating layer upon layer, leading Subhūti and the assembly to awaken to the truth of human life and the universe, and teaching them how to wake from this nightmare of manifold suffering, birth-and-death transmigration, and endless affliction, to realize the great freedom whose spiritual powers and wondrous functions are inexhaustible, and to move through all things with great wisdom.
[Clarifying the mind] Extinguishing the deluded mind.
Question: How should one uphold the Diamond Sutra?

Answer: By prajñā contemplation. Prajñā contemplation has two links: clarifying principle (the middle-way principle of neither existence nor non-existence) and putting it into practice (the mark-detached practice of joining compassion and emptiness). Clarifying principle is understanding; putting it into practice is practice.
If prajñā contemplation is to have real effect, understanding and practice must correspond: understand in accord with principle, and set out in practice in reliance on understanding.
Mr. Jiang Weinong
Lectures on the Diamond Sutra
says:
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, the essential thing is to be deeply self-watchful
(fearful of transgression)
, taking what the Buddha has spoken as a mirror, and at all times and in all places using it to reflect upon oneself
(to check whether one’s body, speech, and mind accord with what the Buddha has spoken—accord is awakening, non-accord is delusion)

. If one does not observe and does not reflect, by what means shall delusion awaken? This is what is meant by relying on the words to give rise to contemplation. When the work of contemplation has long been established, then, in a vast and solemn manner, the mind of watchfulness arises of itself—this is initial enlightenment, the first opening of the intrinsic right wisdom of the principle-essence. If one does not retreat and does not slacken, the work of contemplation grows deeper and more mellow day by day. Then this initial enlightenment is at first like the new moon, gradually increasing in light and decreasing in dark
(same as “darkness”)

, until the moon’s disk is full and its radiance resplendent, and the nature-essence appears. This is initial enlightenment merging with original enlightenment, and then there is no division of initial and original. You should know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing other than the perfect clarity of the enlightened nature. And the opening of the enlightened nature has no other way than by relying on the power of the prajñā of words. Therefore it is said: all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”
[Contemplation] Observing matters and the principles of all dharmas with wisdom, and illuminating them clearly.
[Vast and solemn] Grand and magnificent in appearance.
Old Master Xuyun said:

“Bodhidharma said: ‘To understand the Buddha-mind school and to have practice and understanding correspond—this is what is called a patriarch.’ Practice and understanding corresponding means: what you can speak, you can also do. … Do not be turned by circumstances.
It is like herding an ox: keep a firm grip on the rope, and when the ox will not obey, give it a few lashes
If one can constantly subdue the mind in this way
, then as days pass and the work deepens, there will be news of arriving home.” “When you meet with circumstances, what you cannot let go of you must still let go; if your eyebrows so much as move
(the slightest thought arises)

, you have already broken the patriarchs’ rule. Having heard the good teacher explain it, do not lose your awareness and reflection. In all things, meet them in terms of the Way; the Way is principle. Principle is the mind. What is the mind? The mind is the Buddha. The Buddha neither increases nor decreases, is neither blue nor yellow, neither long nor short. As the Diamond Sutra says: ‘If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathāgata.’ Penetrate these paths of principle and you are the same as the Buddha. Govern affairs by principle—what matter can you not let go of? Shine the light of this principle upon it, and you let it go—‘all that has marks is false and illusory.’ From where would affliction and right and wrong come? If you want to cultivate, then what you cannot get past you must still get past, and you will grasp that the nature of all dharmas is thusness.”
(The Venerable Xuyun’s Informal Instructions)
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:

“This intrinsically pure mind of original source is always of itself perfectly clear and universally illumining. Worldly people do not awaken to it; they recognize only seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as the mind, and are covered over by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and so they do not perceive the luminous essence itself. But if one simply becomes mindless on the spot, the essence appears of itself, like the great sun’s disk rising in empty space and illumining the ten directions with nothing to obstruct it. Hence students of the Way recognize only seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and their actions and movements; but if they empty out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the paths of mind are cut off and there is no place to enter—one should simply recognize the original mind at the very place of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, nor is it apart from them. Simply do not give rise to views upon seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, do not stir thoughts upon them, do not seek the mind apart from them, and do not abandon them to grasp at dharmas; neither close nor apart, neither abiding nor attaching, free in every direction—there is nowhere that is not the bodhimaṇḍa.”
Six translations of the Diamond Sutra are extant:
1. The Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Kumārajīva of
Yao Qin) (“Yao Qin” is the Qin state of the Five Barbarians and Sixteen Kingdoms period.)
2. The Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Bodhiruci of
Yuan Wei) (“Yuan Wei” is the Northern Wei, one of the Northern Dynasties of the Northern and Southern Dynasties period.)
3. The Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Paramārtha of
Chen) (“Chen” is the Chen dynasty, one of the Southern Dynasties of the Northern and Southern Dynasties period.)
4. The Vajra Able to Cut Off Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Dharmagupta of
Sui)
5. The Able to Cut Off the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Xuanzang of
Tang), that is, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, fascicle five hundred and seventy-seven, the ninth “Able to Cut Off the Vajra” section.
6. The Buddha-Spoken Able to Cut Off the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra (translated by Yijing of
Tang)
Among these, the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra translated by Great Master Kumārajīva is the most widely current, and this book likewise adopts his translation.

Profound meaning” means that, before annotating the sutra text, one first clarifies the profound and wondrous principle that this sutra expounds. This is the outline of a sutra: it lets the reader first grasp the whole and afterward study the text—once the main cord is lifted, the net opens—so that it is easy to grasp and comprehend.
The principal theme of the Diamond Sutra is:
the middle-way principle of neither existence nor non-existence, and the mark-detached practice of joining compassion and emptiness.
[Detached from marks] Awakening to the fact that all marks are illusory (the sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”
), and so being free of love and hate, grasping and rejecting (the sutra says:
“Not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.”

). [Attached to marks] Taking marks to be real, and so giving rise to love and hate, grasping and rejecting. (And thereby creating karma and receiving its retribution, with birth and death continuing without end.)
Question: How does one become detached from marks?

Answer: One becomes detached from marks through contemplation. The cycle of continuous birth and death is: giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution. Therefore, to end birth and death, one must cut off the link of giving rise to delusion, and the method is to become detached from marks through contemplation. In his book
Lectures on the Diamond Sutra
, Mr. Jiang Weinong gives a profound and detailed exposition of this Dharma-gate of contemplation. For example:
“In reading the sutras and hearing the Dharma, the essential thing is to be deeply self-watchful
(fearful of transgression)
, taking what the Buddha has spoken as a mirror, and at all times and in all places using it to reflect upon oneself
(to check whether one’s body, speech, and mind accord with what the Buddha has spoken—accord is awakening, non-accord is delusion)

. If one does not observe and does not reflect, by what means shall delusion awaken? This is what is meant by relying on the words to give rise to contemplation. When the work of contemplation has long been established, then, in a vast and solemn manner, the mind of watchfulness arises of itself—this is initial enlightenment, the first opening of the intrinsic right wisdom of the principle-essence. If one does not retreat and does not slacken, the work of contemplation grows deeper and more mellow day by day. Then this initial enlightenment is at first like the new moon, gradually increasing in light and decreasing in dark
(same as “darkness”)

, until the moon’s disk is full and its radiance resplendent, and the nature-essence appears. This is initial enlightenment merging with original enlightenment, and then there is no division of initial and original. You should know that what is called becoming a Buddha is nothing other than the perfect clarity of the enlightened nature. And the opening of the enlightened nature has no other way than by relying on the power of the prajñā of words. Therefore it is said: all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”
[Vajra Prajñāpāramitā Sutra]
this is
the title of this sutra.
“Vajra”
is the vajra jewel, whose jewel-light streams in all directions, utterly hard and utterly sharp. The Buddhist scriptures say:
“Śakra has a jewel named vajra.”
The translator of this sutra, Great Master Kumārajīva, said:
“The vajra jewel, an inch square, has a radiance that can illumine several tens of miles.”

Here the vajra jewel is used to describe prajñā: its jewel-light streams in all directions, nothing is too hard for it to shatter, it drives out darkness, cuts off affliction, breaks delusion, and removes attachment.
Prajñā”

is a transliteration of Sanskrit, meaning wisdom; but this wisdom is not worldly cleverness or talent—it is the wondrous wisdom that fathoms human life and the universe and knows all and can do all, the right wisdom of one’s own nature. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
“Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas; abiding in this prajñā, one can fulfill all Buddhadharmas.”
Pāramitā”

is a transliteration of Sanskrit, also rendered as pāramitā, meaning: gone to the other shore. We ordinary beings, since beginningless time, have drifted on the sea of karma, rising and sinking. To cross this bitter sea of birth and death—where the winds of circumstance howl and the waves of consciousness surge—and reach the shore of ultimate nirvāṇa, one cannot do without a boat; and the vajra prajñā is the great treasure Dharma-ship that sails straight for the other shore, breasting the wind and breaking the waves.
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
“The prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas. All Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. That Dharma is precisely the prajñāpāramitā.”
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra says:
“The mahāprajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas; it can give birth to all Buddhas and embraces and upholds the bodhisattvas.”
Sutra”

is the teaching spoken by the Buddha. In Sanskrit it is called sūtra, meaning: to thread the meaning of the Dharma together so that it is not scattered or lost, above according with the wondrous principle of all Buddhas, below according with the capacities of sentient beings. It is meant to lead sentient beings to rely on the words, give rise to contemplation, and realize the true characteristic.
The fourteenth section of this sutra says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
This is the meaning contained in the sutra title, “Vajra Prajñāpāramitā”:
with the wondrous wisdom of the vajra, breaking delusion and removing attachment, becoming a Buddha by detaching from all marks.

In upholding this sutra, one must hold fast to this title, awaken to how the World-Honored One teaches us to use vajra prajñā to break delusion and remove attachment and so become Buddhas by detaching from marks, and then put it into practice, practicing in accordance with the teaching.

The so-called sutra body is the main substance of a sutra, that is, the principle that the sutra clarifies—the guiding purport, the core, the essential point of a sutra. The sutra body of this sutra is: clearly penetrating the true characteristic, breaking delusion and removing attachment, in order to end birth and death (fragmented birth-and-death and transformation birth-and-death).
Clearly penetrating the true characteristic:

thoroughly awakening to the true characteristic of all dharmas. The so-called “true characteristic” is the real situation; the “true characteristic of all dharmas” is the real situation of all dharmas. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury
the second chapter, “Buddha-Recollection,” the Buddha says:
“What is called the true characteristic of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and nothing whatsoever.”
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”
For a detailed discussion of the true characteristic of all dharmas, see
The True Characteristic of All Dharmas
Breaking delusion:

clearly seeing the true characteristic of all dharmas, awakening to and breaking through illusion—“all that has marks is false and illusory”—no longer deluded and inverted so as to create karma and receive retribution. Breaking delusion and returning to the real is the bodhi path. Great Master Hanshan says:

“The intrinsic nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally undefiled, and without any marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of initial non-awakening, they are confused about their original nature, and this is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, they give rise to all manner of deluded thoughts and various inversions, create all manner of karma, and deludedly grasp at the suffering of birth and death within the three realms. All of this is ignorance
(all of this ignorance)

, not understanding one’s own mind, turning with deluded thoughts, like a person fast asleep dreaming all manner of evil dreams. All manner of circumstances, all manner of terror, manifold suffering beyond endurance; and when he wakes, he seeks the things of the dream and cannot obtain them at all. Therefore sentient beings fall within the dream of ignorance, turning with deluded thoughts, creating all manner of karma, and bringing suffering upon themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could any of those inverted states be obtained?”
(Dream Roaming Collection
the instruction to Dong Zhiguang)
Removing attachment:
removing self-attachment and dharma-attachment. This sutra says:

“These sentient beings no longer have the marks of a self, the marks of a person, the marks of a sentient being, or the marks of a lifespan; they have no marks of dharma, nor any marks of non-dharma.”

[Self-attachment] Also called person-attachment: deludedly clinging to the body and mind falsely compounded of the five aggregates as a self. Because of self-attachment, the affliction-obstruction arises. [Deludedly clinging to the body and mind falsely compounded of the five aggregates as a self] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions—like a confused person who mistakes his directions in all four quarters, deludedly taking the four great elements as the marks of his own body and the shadowy impressions of the six sense objects as the marks of his own mind. It is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. The sky truly has no flowers; the diseased one deludedly grasps them, and because of that deluded grasping, he is not only confused about the nature of this empty space but is further deluded about the place where those real flowers arise. From this false existence, he revolves through birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

(Translation: All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had their intrinsic nature confounded, giving rise to all manner of inversions, taking the false as real—this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he deludedly takes the physical body formed of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as the marks of his own body, and the deliberating mind of the six faculties that take the six sense objects as their objects (the shadowy impressions of the six sense objects) as the marks of his own mind. This is like eyes blurred by disease that deludedly see flowers in the sky and a second moon. In reality the sky has no flowers at all; this is an illusion deludedly grasped by the diseased eyes, and because of that deluded grasping he not only deludedly grasps empty space as truly existing but further supposes that flowers truly arise from there. Because sentient beings are inverted and deluded, they deludedly take the illusorily appearing body and mind as truly existing and cling to them as a self, and so birth and death revolve without cease; therefore this is called ignorance.)

[Dharma-attachment] Deludedly clinging to the Dharma of the Way as real, thinking that there is a dharma to be attained, a Way to be cultivated, birth and death to be ended, nirvāṇa to be realized—clinging to the causal cultivation and the realized fruit. Because of dharma-attachment, the obstruction of the knowable arises. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
“Though the followers of the two vehicles have broken person-attachment
(that is, self-attachment)
, they still have dharma-attachment.”
The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says:
“From attachment to self and dharmas
(because self-attachment and dharma-attachment exist)
, the two obstructions both arise.”

[The two obstructions] The affliction-obstruction and the obstruction of the knowable. [The affliction-obstruction] The obstructive afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion that arise from deludedly clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as a self; because of the affliction-obstruction one revolves through birth and death. [The obstruction of the knowable] Giving rise to all manner of wrong views about the Dharma of the Way; such knowing obstructs perfect enlightenment.
The Heart Sutra says:

“Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or objects of mind; no realm of the eye, and so forth up to no realm of mental consciousness; no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so forth up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, its accumulation, its cessation, or the path; no wisdom; and no attainment.”
In this passage of sutra text,

“in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or objects of mind; no realm of the eye, and so forth up to no realm of mental consciousness” says that there are no five aggregates and no eighteen elements, and this breaks the self-attachment of ordinary beings; “no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so forth up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death” says that there are no dharmas of the twelve-fold chain of dependent origination, and this breaks the dharma-attachment of the pratyekabuddhas; “no suffering, its accumulation, its cessation, or the path”
says that there are no dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, and this breaks the dharma-attachment of the śrāvakas;
“no wisdom”
says that there are no dharmas of the six perfections, and this breaks the dharma-attachment of the bodhisattvas. (For detailed annotation see
A Precise Explanation of the Heart Sutra
In order to end birth and death:
to put an end to the two kinds of birth-and-death—fragmented birth-and-death and transformation birth-and-death.

[Fragmented birth-and-death] For sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil they have generated, their lifespans all have limits and their bodies all have divisions; hence their birth and death is called “fragmented birth-and-death.” One who ends fragmented birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformation birth-and-death] For the sages of the three vehicles, who have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended fragmented birth-and-death, in the course of cultivating the Way deluded thoughts gradually cease and realized awakening gradually increases; each stage of this shift from delusion to awakening is different, and the passage from the preceding stage into the succeeding one is just like passing through one birth and death. These transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable; hence they are called “transformation birth-and-death.” One who ends transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
The true characteristic of all dharmas is this: all dharmas are illusory, originally not a single thing exists. In the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra in a Smaller Compass
volume ten, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a mirage.”

In the Sutra of Sustaining the World, the Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like an illusion without reality, without any root.” In the Sutra in Which the Buddha Speaks to King Prasenajit on the Kingly Dharma, the Buddha says:

“All dharmas are empty in essence and are impermanent and subject to destruction. Suppose a person in a night dream sees fine gardens, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful. When he awakes from sleep
(waking from sleep; here the “jue” of “shuijiao” means to wake)
, he sees not one of them.”
(For a detailed discussion of the true characteristic of all dharmas, see
The True Characteristic of All Dharmas
[Dream-awakening] Waking from the dream. Great Master Taixu says:
“The mind within the dream is the ordinary being’s mind; the mind that knows, within the dream, that it is dreaming is the bodhisattva’s mind; the mind awakened from the dream is the Buddha’s mind.”
(An Outline of Consciousness-Only Contemplation)
The true characteristic of all dharmas is the ultimate truth. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false; where they cease—that is called the real, is called the true characteristic, is called the dharma realm, is called ultimate wisdom, is called the ultimate truth, is called ultimate emptiness.”
(Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra
volume forty)
The true characteristic of all dharmas is the dharma-seal of the Mahāyāna scriptures—the seal of the true characteristic. Great Master Zhiyi’s Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra
volume eight says:

“If a Hīnayāna sutra bears the seal of the three seals—impermanence, no-self, and nirvāṇa—then it is spoken by the Buddha, and cultivating it one attains the Way! Without the three dharma-seals, it is the teaching of Māra. A Mahāyāna sutra has only one dharma-seal, namely the true characteristic of all dharmas, and is called a sutra of definitive meaning, able to bring one to the great Way! Without the seal of the true characteristic, it is the teaching of Māra.”
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”

This says that all marks are illusions. This includes mountains and rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, birth and death and nirvāṇa, sentient beings and all Buddhas—all are illusions. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Within it, the Buddha-worlds of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas, ineffable as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, rising and vanishing in confusion.” “Originally there is no bodhi and no nirvāṇa, nor is there becoming a Buddha or not becoming a Buddha, no deluded transmigration and no non-transmigration.” “Birth and death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike the marks of flowers in the sky.”

[Asaṃkhyeya] Rendered into Chinese as “countless,” it means so many that no number can reckon them. [Flowers in the sky] In Buddhadharma this is often used as a metaphor for illusion. “Flowers in the sky” are flowers in empty space. One with diseased eyes sees flowers in the sky, though empty space originally has no flowers—it is merely the deluded perception of the diseased eye. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Deludedly taking the four great elements as one’s own body and the shadowy impressions of the six sense objects as the marks of one’s own mind, it is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon.”
The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp says:
“With a single film over the eye, flowers in the sky fall in confusion.”

is constantly used to establish that all dharmas are illusions. “

“Adorning the Buddha-lands

The Tathāgata says the thirty-two marks

(substance does not exist)
, and so called the thirty-two marks

Within the illusory realm of “all that has marks is false and illusory,” there are two utterly different roads: one is to use illusion to leave illusion, until illusions are exhausted and the dream ends—this is the bodhi path; the other is to use illusion to enter illusion, revolving in birth and death—this is the road of transmigration that sentient beings have walked since beginningless kalpas. The Diamond Sutra arms us with vajra prajñā, to awaken to and break through illusion, to be deluded and inverted no more, and to walk the great bodhi road of “using illusion to leave illusion, until illusions are exhausted and the dream ends.” This sutra says:

“All that has marks is false and illusory.” “No marks of self, no marks of a person, no marks of a sentient being, no marks of a lifespan.” “No marks of dharma, nor any marks of non-dharma.” “Not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.” “Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
The Sutra of the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata of the Great and Vast says:
“All Tathāgatas rely on this samādhi to accomplish measureless great awesome spiritual powers, and even to realize and enter the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are illusions)

, and are able to manifest all manner of sovereign activities in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions. Suppose a person dreams all manner of transformed things, and when he wakes, all that he saw is gone. Ordinary beings are likewise:
because of the dream of ignorance
, they deludedly give rise to the notion that all dharmas are real entities. All Buddhas, having awakened
(all Buddhas have woken from the dream of ignorance)

, are utterly unattached, and so in all worlds of the ten directions they can, in a single thought, manifest measureless Buddha-works, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing to accomplishment all sentient beings, leading them all to realize and enter the measureless, profound, and wondrous gates of liberation.”

What does the Diamond Sutra teach? The Diamond Sutra teaches the true characteristic of all dharmas—that all dharmas are illusory—leading sentient beings to break delusion and remove attachment and so attain liberation. But sentient beings’ two attachments, to self and to dharmas, are deep-rooted and hard to believe, and so the World-Honored One and Subhūti, in the form of a dialogue, break through doubt layer upon layer, leading Subhūti and we sentient beings to remove doubt and give rise to faith, so that our intrinsic wisdom appears. If one examines it thus, then Buddha and sentient beings are equal and the two attachments both perish—this is indeed the essential technique for leaving illusion and becoming a Buddha. (For a detailed discussion of the true characteristic of all dharmas, see
The True Characteristic of All Dharmas

Zong means the guiding purport; qu means the direction it tends toward. The guiding purport is the method of practice that carries the purport through—how to cultivate in actual practice on the basis of the sutra body; this is what is meant by seeking the purport and returning to its direction. The guiding purport of this sutra is:
detachment from marks
(detachment from the marks of self, person, sentient being, and lifespan, and from the marks of dharma and non-dharma)
. In reliance on the wondrous principle of the true characteristic of all dharmas, one becomes detached from marks and unattached, thereby breaking delusion and removing attachment.
The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Detached from marks, one is without marks; without marks, one is unattached; unattached, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Good man! Those newly learned bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect enlightenment mind should abide in right mindfulness and keep far from all illusions.”
This sutra says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

[The mark of a self] Deludedly clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as truly existing, and taking it as “I” so that thoughts arise—for example, thoughts of gain and loss, favor and opposition, honor and disgrace, and so on. [The mark of a person] Deludedly clinging to the other party, to other people, as truly existing so that thoughts arise—for example, thoughts of like and dislike, right and wrong, superior and inferior, and so on. [The mark of a sentient being] Here “sentient beings” means groups of people—for example, groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and foe, age, sex, workplace, region, ethnicity, skin color, nationality, and so on; the mark of a sentient being is deludedly clinging to these groups as truly existing and giving rise to discriminating thoughts. [The mark of a lifespan] Deludedly clinging to lifespan as truly existing and calculating whether it is long or short. What deluded sentient beings care about most is nothing other than lifespan, and so the mark of a lifespan is set out separately from the mark of a self as an item of its own. [The mark of dharma] Deludedly clinging to all dharmas (including the Dharma of the Way) as truly existing. [The Dharma of the Way] The dharma of cultivating the Way, that is, the dharma for ending birth and death and realizing nirvāṇa. [The mark of non-dharma] Denying all dharmas (including the Dharma of the Way), deludedly clinging to all dharmas as non-existent, and sinking into stubborn emptiness
When the World-Honored One accomplished the Way, his very first words were:
“How wondrous! How wondrous! All sentient beings on the great earth are endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue marks, but because of deluded thoughts and attachment they cannot realize them.”
Therefore, dispelling deluded thoughts and attachment is the way to become a Buddha. How is one to dispel them? By detachment from marks! Hence the fourteenth section of this sutra says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
So-called detachment from marks is simply non-attachment to marks—knowing that marks are illusory, not being deluded by marks, not being turned by marks. This sutra says:
“Not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.” “If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.”

[Attachment to marks] Attachment to marks is taking marks to be real, whereupon desire arises and thoughts arise, and one runs after desires and thoughts. Thereby one creates karma, and thereby one revolves in birth and death. [Not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved] Not clinging to marks as real, and not being moved by them.
In the fifth section, “True Seeing in Accord with Principle,” the Buddha says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”

This says that all marks are illusions, yet sentient beings since beginningless time have taken illusions as real, with deluded thoughts and attachment unceasing, seduced and coerced by them, and so they create karma, receive retribution, and revolve in birth and death, sinking into the sea of suffering. Now, to attain liberation and return to the original source, one must no longer be deluded by illusions, must not be turned by marks—and this requires detachment from marks and the dispelling of deluded thoughts and attachment.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The preceding thought deluded
(attached to marks—turned by marks)
, and one is an ordinary being; the following thought awakened
(detached from marks—thusness, unmoved)
, and one is a Buddha. The preceding thought attached to circumstance
(attached to marks)
, and one is afflicted; the following thought detached from circumstance
(detached from marks)
, and one is bodhi.”
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Seeing illusion, one at once detaches from it, without resorting to skillful means; detached from illusion, one is enlightened, with no gradual stages.”
Therefore one should
“not cling to marks, but abide in thusness, unmoved.”
(The thirty-second section of this sutra)
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“What is called Chan concentration? Outwardly,
detachment from marks
is Chan; inwardly, non-disturbance is concentration. If outwardly one is
attached to marks
, the mind within is disturbed; if outwardly one is
detached from marks

, the mind is not disturbed. The intrinsic nature is of itself pure and of itself concentrated; it is only because one sees circumstances and thinks about circumstances that it is disturbed. If, seeing all circumstances, the mind is not disturbed, this is true concentration.”
Therefore the key to Chan concentration is:
detachment from marks.

To be aware of the present thought and enter the realm of no-thought—this is detachment from marks; this is to do the work of detachment from marks at the very place where thoughts arise and the mind stirs. Inwardly not turning with thoughts, outwardly not drawn by circumstances, amid the vast winds of circumstance one remains one’s own master.
The fourteenth section of this sutra says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

This is the meaning contained in the sutra title, “Vajra Prajñāpāramitā”: becoming a Buddha by detaching from marks through the wondrous wisdom of the vajra. In the thirteenth section, the Buddha says:
“This sutra is named the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā. By this name you should uphold it.”
Vajra prajñā is precisely the great wisdom that, seeing marks, can detach from them.
The eighth section says:
“All Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra.”
The fourteenth section says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
Therefore the way to become a Buddha is precisely what this sutra repeats again and again:
detachment from marks

Detachment from marks requires joining compassion and emptiness: while cultivating the contemplation of emptiness, one also cultivates compassion, and only thus can one be unattached to both emptiness and existence and be detached from marks to the ultimate and thorough degree. If one cultivates only emptiness, then though one is not attached to existence, one becomes attached to emptiness. The sutra says:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

Detachment from all marks means not only detaching from the marks of existence but also detaching from the marks of emptiness; in the end, even the mark of detachment from marks must be detached, until there is nothing left to detach from—only then is it ultimate and perfect, and only then is the Buddha Way accomplished. Hence this sutra says:

“All the various kinds of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought—I cause all of them to enter nirvāṇa without remainder and be delivered to extinction. Yet when innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings have thus been delivered to extinction, in truth there is no sentient being who attains extinction. Why is that? Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has the marks of a self, the marks of a person, the marks of a sentient being, or the marks of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.”
This is joining compassion and emptiness, unattached to both emptiness and existence.
Detachment from marks must first be concretely carried through as non-abiding.

Non-abiding is non-attachment to marks. That is, with respect to the marks of self, person, sentient being, and lifespan, and the marks of dharma and non-dharma, one abides nowhere and attaches to nothing (does not deludedly cling to them as real). The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Detached from marks, one is without marks; without marks, one is unattached; unattached, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”
In this sutra, passages on detachment from marks and non-abiding are found everywhere. For example:
The third section says:
“If a bodhisattva has the marks of a self, the marks of a person, the marks of a sentient being, or the marks of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.”
This says that a bodhisattva must detach from the four marks.
The fourth section says:
“If a bodhisattva gives in charity without abiding in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.”
This says that in giving one must be detached from marks.
The sixth section says:

“When they hear these passages, if even a single thought gives rise to pure faith, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows and sees it, and these sentient beings gain such measureless merit and virtue. Why is that? Because these sentient beings no longer have the marks of a self, the marks of a person, the marks of a sentient being, or the marks of a lifespan; they have no marks of dharma, nor any marks of non-dharma.”
The seventh section says:
“All worthies and sages are distinguished only by the unconditioned dharma.”

The unconditioned dharma is precisely detachment from marks. This passage means: all worthies and sages differ only according to the depth of their detachment from marks, and this is what gives rise to the forty-two stages of attainment. These forty-two stages are: the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. Of these, wondrous enlightenment is Buddhahood. Therefore an ancient worthy said:
“Only exhaust the ordinary sentiments
(one need only cut off all ordinary sentiments)
, and there is no other sage’s understanding.”

[Worthies and sages] Bodhisattva cultivation has fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment, wondrous enlightenment being Buddhahood. Among these, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications are the worthies (called the three worthy stages), while the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment are the sages.
The tenth section says:

“All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or objects of mind; they should give rise to a mind that abides nowhere.”
This speaks of detaching from the marks of the dust-realms: not giving rise to a mind abiding in the dust-realms, and even when a mind arises, not abiding in the dust-realms.
The fourteenth section says:
“A bodhisattva should, apart from all marks, give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
This says: on the bodhi path, from the very beginning, at the moment of giving rise to the aspiration, one must be detached from marks.
In the seventeenth section, Subhūti asks again:
“World-Honored One! When good men and good women give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”
The Buddha replies:

“Good men and good women who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should give rise to such a mind: I should deliver all sentient beings to extinction, and when all sentient beings have been delivered to extinction, not one sentient being has in truth attained extinction.”
Therefore the answer to “How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” is: detached from marks and unattached, delivering sentient beings.
The twenty-third section says:
“With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and one then attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
This says: detached from the four marks, whatever wholesome dharma one cultivates, one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. From this one sees how very important detachment from marks is!

(This passage says that the key to realizing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the absence of the four marks, not the kind of wholesome dharma one cultivates. The wholesome dharma cultivated without the four marks is the unconditioned dharma. Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the universal principle for realizing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; from this one also knows how very crucial it is to be free of the four marks! How very important!)
At the close of this sutra, the World-Honored One says:
“Not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.”

This echoes from afar the World-Honored One’s demonstration at the very beginning of this sutra, when he put on his robe and went begging for food, washed his feet, and sat down on his seat, and it runs through the whole sutra—this is detachment from marks, not turning with circumstances, not drawn by thoughts, thusness unmoved. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“What is called Chan concentration? Outwardly detached from marks is Chan; inwardly non-disturbed is concentration. If outwardly one is attached to marks, the mind within is disturbed; if outwardly one is detached from marks, the mind is not disturbed. The intrinsic nature is of itself pure and of itself concentrated; it is only because one sees circumstances and thinks about circumstances that it is disturbed. If, seeing all circumstances, the mind is not disturbed, this is true concentration.”
Therefore the key to Chan concentration is detachment from marks.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra
volume one
the chapter on “Learning Contemplation” says:
“All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should, with non-attachment as their skillful means, perfect the prajñāpāramitā, because the nature and marks of all dharmas are unattainable.”
“Non-attachment” is non-attachment to marks, that is, detachment from marks.
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.” “Not clinging to marks, one abides in thusness, unmoved.”

This is the core of upholding the Diamond Sutra—detachment from marks. And in the course of learning detachment from marks, one should take “ceasing deluded thoughts and breaking the mark of self” as the essential point and the place to begin.

The guiding purport is the cause, and the benefit is the fruit. This sutra is the dual cultivation of merit and wisdom, and its benefit is: breaking delusion and removing attachment, generating merit and extinguishing transgression, dissolving karma and escaping suffering, and realizing bodhi. Of this the sutra says a very great deal, and it will not be enumerated here; in studying the sutra text one should match them up one by one.

Characteristics of the teaching” refers to the differences in the marks of the Buddha's teaching throughout his lifetime — that is, the features of the various doctrines and their differences. When the Buddha taught sentient beings, he always spoke according to their capacity. Sentient beings' faculties are dull or sharp and their obstructions thick or thin; hence the sutras have the teaching-characteristics of shallow and deep, gradual and sudden, partial and perfect, provisional and definitive, small and great (Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna).

[Partial and perfect] Partial and perfect. “Partial” means leaning to one side; “perfect” means harmonious and unobstructed. [Provisional and definitive] A teaching suited to a particular time is called “provisional”; a teaching that is ultimate and unchanging is called “definitive.”

The teaching-characteristics of this sutra are: the most perfect, the most sudden, the most definitive, a One-Vehicle sutra. “Most perfect” means that this sutra is the most ultimate and of definitive meaning; “most sudden” means that the teaching of this sutra does not pass through the various stages but leaps straight in at once; “most definitive” means that this sutra directly sets forth the true character of all dharmas; “One Vehicle” means that this sutra is the sole teaching that causes people to become Buddhas.

[One Vehicle] Also called the Buddha Vehicle; the only teaching that can cause people to become Buddhas. “Vehicle” means a carriage, used to liken the Buddha's teaching: the teaching can carry people to the other shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called a “vehicle.” [Definitive meaning] Setting forth the principle in a manner altogether perfect, thorough, and ultimate.
Question: Why is the Diamond Sutra said to be the most perfect, most sudden, most definitive One-Vehicle sutra?
Answer: The sutra says:
“All Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, all come forth from this sutra”
(the eighth section);
“The Tathāgata speaks it for those who have set forth on the Mahāyāna, speaks it for those who have set forth on the foremost vehicle”
(the fifteenth section) — showing that this sutra is the most perfect One-Vehicle teaching. The Buddha says:
“Free of all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
This speaks of being free of all marks and directly realizing (without passing through the stages) Buddhahood. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records:
“The Master
(Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan)
constantly urged monks and laypeople: simply uphold the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and directly realize Buddhahood.”
— showing that this sutra is the most sudden. (The fourteenth section.) The sutra constantly uses the formula “
A
is not
A
, and so is called
A”
to demonstrate that all dharmas are illusions, and it also says
“all marks whatsoever are false and vain”
(the fifth section) — all of which speaks of the true character of all dharmas, showing that this sutra is the most definitive.

In annotating sutras and treatises, one usually divides the whole text into paragraphs and sections, which is called textual outlining. Here, the division into major sections is called the major outline; the division of a major section into smaller sections is called the fine outline; and marking the content of each section with concise, essential words is called outline text. On this basis the reader can learn the concise content of the annotation and the thread of its meaning, and can determine the annotator's general view of that sutra or treatise.

The popular edition of the Diamond Sutra divides the whole sutra into thirty-two sections and gives each a heading; tradition holds that these were made by Crown Prince Zhaoming, Xiao Tong (son of Emperor Wu of Liang). This outline is exquisite in intent and its divisions are detailed yet concise, and it is of great help in understanding the text; hence it has been widely transmitted without decline (and the ruins of a sutra platform remain), and this book follows it as well. Since the headings of these thirty-two sections are outline, not part of the sutra text, one should not read them when reciting the sutra.

[The Sutra-Dividing Platform] Located in the Shilian Cave National Forest Park south of Susong County town, Anhui Province. The Sutra-Dividing Platform, also called the Golden-Dividing Stone, is five meters high and elliptical in shape. Carved on it in large characters are the words “Sutra-Dividing Platform,” and beside them is written “Erected on the eleventh day of the sixth month of the first year of Jia Tai of the August Song.” Tradition says that Crown Prince Zhaoming, Xiao Tong, of the Liang divided the Diamond Sutra into thirty-two sections here, and so it is named. The stele was erected in the first year of Jia Tai (
), to commemorate the seven hundredth anniversary of Crown Prince Zhaoming's birth.

In terms of content, this sutra may be divided into two parts, upper and lower. The first through the sixteenth sections are the upper part, and the seventeenth through the thirty-second sections are the lower part. The upper part teaches how to raise the mind, how to save sentient beings, how to subdue delusion, and how to cut off delusion; this breaks the self of a person so as to end fragmentary birth-and-death, but the self of dharmas still remains. Therefore the lower part teaches how to break the self of dharmas and so end transformation birth-and-death. Hence the World-Honored One, at the very beginning of the lower part, says: “There is truly no dharma by which one raises the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Then he breaks the self of dharmas layer by layer, until at the end of the part he says: “How does one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved. Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning; thus should they be contemplated.” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age should keep far from all illusory, transformed, false realms; because of firmly holding to the mind of detachment, the mind that is like an illusion is also to be transcended; detachment itself is an illusion and is also to be transcended; the illusion of transcending detachment is also to be transcended; when one reaches having nothing to transcend, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks rub together, fire comes forth and the sticks are consumed, the ashes fly and the smoke is extinguished. Cultivating illusion by means of illusion is likewise so: when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation.”

[The two selves] The self of a person and the self of dharmas. The self of a person: ordinary beings do not understand the principle that the five aggregates are a false union, and falsely cling to body and mind as “I,” so that there arise the view of self, love of self, pride of self, delusion of self, and so on, forming the obstruction of afflictions. The self of dharmas: ordinary beings do not understand the principle that all dharmas arise dependently and are empty by nature, and falsely cling to all dharmas as truly existent, so that there arise the discriminating mind, the mind of love and hate, the mind of becoming a Buddha, the mind of nirvāṇa, and so on, forming the obstruction of the knowable.

blocks.text: 3. The Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination

inline.s: Traditionally, in annotating sutra texts, the text is divided into three major parts: the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination.

The introduction is the part that narrates the occasion for the arising of this sutra. The first section of this sutra (Section One, “The Occasion of the Assembly”) is the introduction. The introduction is further divided into two parts: the common introduction and the particular introduction.

The common introduction: this is the introductory narrative common to all sutras (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in ...”). For example, the first passage of this sutra (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus.”) is the common introduction. The common introduction is also called the introduction of attestation, because it possesses the six matters of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place, and assembly, attesting that what is said in the sutra is true and credible. These six matters are also called the six accomplishments: the presence of these six conditions accomplishes the Dharma-assembly for expounding the sutra.

The particular introduction: after the common introduction comes the particular introduction, which is the point where the introductions of the various sutras differ from one another. For example, the second passage of this sutra (“At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for food, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged from door to door in order, and returned to his original place. When he had finished eating, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, spread his seat, and sat down.”) is the particular introduction. The particular introduction is also called the introduction of arising, because it explains how this Dharma-assembly came to arise.

The main body is the part in which this sutra is properly spoken. Of the thirty-two sections of the whole sutra, from the second section through to the end of the thirty-first section is the main body.

The dissemination is the part that lists the benefits of upholding this sutra and urges and praises its upholding, recitation, and circulation. In this sutra, the last section (Section Thirty-Two, “Responding and Transforming, Not Real”) is the dissemination.

The occasion of the assembly” refers to this sutra, that is, the cause and origin of the Diamond Dharma-assembly. “Section” corresponds to “chapter.” For example, “Section One, The Occasion of the Assembly” means “Chapter One: The Occasion of the Assembly.”

This section (“Section One, The Occasion of the Assembly”) is the introduction. The introduction is the part that narrates the occasion for the arising of this sutra. The introduction, as said before, is further divided into two parts: the common introduction and the particular introduction.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus.
This is what I personally saw and heard. At that time the Buddha was in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus.

[Thus have I heard] This is what I personally saw and heard. “Thus have I heard” is for the sake of gaining faith: it attests that this sutra was truly spoken by the Buddha and that the recorded text is correct and without error. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, he instructed the Venerable Ānanda: in the future, when compiling the sutras, at the head of every sutra place the phrase “Thus have I heard,” to attest that it was truly spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from the scriptures of the outer paths. [At one time] At that time. This refers to the time when the Buddha spoke this sutra — that is, the time when teacher and disciples were joined in the Way and the capacities of the listeners met the teaching. The Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma reaches through humans and gods, and its compilation and transmission spread throughout the world; because the years, months, and days of the various records cannot be made to agree, the phrase “at one time” is used to mark it. [Teacher and disciples] Teachers and students, masters and followers. [Capacities and teaching meeting] “Capacity” is the faculty of the listeners; “teaching” is the Buddha's bestowal of teaching. Sentient beings' faculties differ, and so the Buddha, according to their capacities, bestows teachings shallow or deep. “Capacities and teaching meeting” means that the faculties of the Dharma-assembly's listeners and the Buddha's teaching respond and accord with each other. [Buddha] An abbreviation of “Buddha”; here it means Śākyamuni Buddha. “Buddha” is a Sanskrit sound, rendered in Chinese as “the Awakened One.” Inwardly awakened, one is free of all deluded thoughts; outwardly awakened, one is unstained by the six dusts.

[The kingdom of Śrāvastī] Its location is in the northwest of present-day India, on the south bank of the Rapti River; its king at that time was King Prasenajit. [The Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden] A grove in the capital of the kingdom of Śrāvastī, where Śākyamuni Buddha spoke this sutra. The trees of this garden belonged to Prince Jeta of Śrāvastī, and the land to the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada; the two together offered it to the Buddha, and so it is called “the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden,” meaning Prince Jeta's grove and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada's garden. The Buddha often expounded the sutras and taught the Dharma there. [Great bhikṣu] “Bhikṣu” is the general term for one who has left home and received the full precepts; males are called “bhikṣu,” females “bhikṣuṇī.” “Great bhikṣu” means a bhikṣu of lofty virtue and advanced years. [Together] In company.

At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for food, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged from door to door in order, and returned to his original place. When he had finished eating, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, spread his seat, and sat down.

At this time the hour for the single midday meal had come, and so the World-Honored One put on his great robe, took up his alms bowl, and leading his disciples with dignified deportment, walked slowly into the capital of the kingdom of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city, without distinguishing poor from rich, noble from lowly, he received alms from door to door in order. When the begging was done, he returned to his dwelling. When the World-Honored One had finished eating, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, spread out his seat, and sat cross-legged in dignified serenity, with right mindfulness unmoved.
The Northern Wei

translation by Bodhiruci reads: “At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for food, put on his robe and took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city, having begged in order, he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and as was his custom spread his seat and sat cross-legged. Straightening his body he remained, with right mindfulness unmoved.”

This passage is the particular introduction. The particular introduction is the point where the introductions of the various sutras differ from one another, and it comes after the common introduction. The particular introduction is also called the introduction of arising, because it explains how this sutra's Dharma-assembly came to arise.

The arising of this sutra's Dharma-assembly is this: through everyday activities (putting on his robe and taking up his bowl, entering the city to beg, and even spreading his seat and sitting down), the World-Honored One taught by his own person, showing that prajñā is everywhere, what awakening is, and what the original scenery is.

[At that time] This time. [The World-Honored One] An honorific title of the Buddha. Because the Buddha possesses ten thousand virtues, is honored by the world, and is supreme in the world, he is called the World-Honored One. [The hour for food] The time for the single midday meal has come. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says: “Shaving off beard and hair and becoming a śramaṇa, one who receives the Dharma of the Way renounces worldly goods and seeks only sufficiency in begging. One meal a day and one night beneath a tree — be careful never to take more! What makes people foolish and benighted is love and desire.”

[Putting on his robe] The three robes and one bowl are the possessions a bhikṣu carries with him. The three robes are the antarvāsa, the uttarāsaṅga, and the saṃghāṭī; all three are called in Sanskrit kaṣāya (“kaṣāya” originally means a dyed robe, because the Dharma-robes worn by renunciant bhikṣus must all be dyed a turbid color). The antarvāsa is rendered in Chinese as the body robe; it is made of five strips (that is, five squares of cloth sewn together in a pattern like a field, hence “field-of-blessings robe”), and is worn for work, sitting, and lying down. The uttarāsaṅga is worn over the antarvāsa, and so is called the upper robe; it is made of seven strips and is put on when performing Dharma affairs and joining the assembly. The saṃghāṭī is rendered in Chinese as the robe for when the assembly gathers, also called the great robe; it is made of nine to twenty-five strips and is worn on solemn occasions. Now, as he was about to enter the city to beg, he deliberately put on the great robe.

[Bowl] An abbreviation of the Sanskrit pātra, the eating vessel of a bhikṣu. [The great city of Śrāvastī] The capital of the kingdom of Śrāvastī; the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden lay five or six li southeast of the city. [Begging for food] A bhikṣu, free of all greedy seeking and subduing his pride, constantly practices begging for food to sustain his physical body and aid his cultivation of the Way. [Begging in order] In begging, a bhikṣu does not cling to flavors, does not slight sentient beings, and does not choose between rich and poor; with an equal mind he begs from house to house in order, not passing seven houses or the appointed time, and even if his bowl is not full he must return. [His original place] The place where he dwelt, the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's Garden. [Finished] Completed.

When the Buddha spoke other sutras, he often arose them by emitting light and displaying auspicious signs. This sutra is the mind-dharma of the Tathāgata's attainment of Buddhahood, yet it is arisen by everyday activities; there is indeed deep meaning in this — it shows that prajñā is nowhere else but in everyday activities. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Ordinary beings are Buddhas; affliction is bodhi. When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the following thought is awake, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought is free of objects, that is bodhi.” This sutra says: “Free of all marks, one is named a Buddha.” The World-Honored One's demonstration is thought-after-thought awakening, thought-after-thought freedom from objects; in putting on his robe and taking up his bowl, entering the city to beg, and even spreading his seat and sitting down, he everywhere displays the wondrous flavor of prajñā — “not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved” — to proclaim the Diamond prajñā-pāramitā, so that the whole assembly may learn and realize in daily life what the original scenery is.

[Not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved] Not holding marks to be real, and so not being moved by them. That is, not clinging to marks and not stirring the mind. [Original scenery] Also called the original face; a Chan-forest expression describing the original state of the self-nature (the state of complete awakening).

There is a story of this kind. A woman went to ask the Buddha: How can I awaken? The Buddha said: What is it that you do? She said: I make my living by drawing water. The Buddha told her: When you draw water, you must be perfectly clear and aware in your mind with regard to every movement (there must be no habitual movement of which you are unaware). The woman earnestly did as the Buddha taught, and awakened.

perfectly clear and aware in your mind with regard to every movement” — this is the wondrous method of being aware and illuminating the present, of bringing practice into life. If one can do this, one will no longer worry about having no time to practice, and will never again be anxious and uneasy, fearing that practice is being delayed. How can practice be brought into life? By never losing awareness and illumination! No matter when or where, never lose awareness and illumination; be perfectly clear about the movements of one's own mind, and do not be turned by objects.

The Buddha means the Awakened. The Buddha is simply the awakened one who has already woken from the dream of ignorance; in daily life he appears the same as ordinary people, but his realm is utterly different — at every moment it is awareness and illumination shining forth.

The World-Honored One shows how to practice in daily life: when conditions come, give; when conditions cease, be still. In giving, never lose awareness and illumination, and at all times be serene and at ease — what is called “not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved.”

It is in this way that the World-Honored One, through daily activities such as putting on his robe, taking up his bowl, begging for food, returning to his original place, eating, putting away robe and bowl, washing his feet, and spreading his seat and sitting down, teaches us that there is no time and no place where practice is impossible, and points out for us who toil in the dust of the world a convenient way to begin.
