Hence in the text below the Elder Subhūti marvels and calls it rare, and says: In acting thus, the Tathāgata truly protects and keeps in mind the bodhisattvas, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas!

Practice is divided into practice on the cushion and practice off the cushion. On the cushion is military drill; off the cushion is actual combat. If one uses it well, there is no time and no place that is not practice. The Sixth Patriarch says: “What is called sitting in meditation? In this Dharma-gate there is no obstruction (not being bound by conditions and objects). Outwardly, with regard to all good and evil objects, not giving rise to thought — this is called sitting; inwardly, seeing the self-nature unmoved — this is called Chan.” A verse says: A day of practice earns a day of merit; a day neglected leaves a day of want. True cultivation lies in daily life — the Buddha Way is found in living itself.

There was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, after a long journey and covered with dust, hurried to the city of Śrāvastī to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. He found the Buddha in the city, begging for food from house to house; every gesture of his hands and body was graceful and beautiful, his six faculties all tamed and protected, serene and still. Bāhiya approached and bowed, imploring the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to speak for him the Dharma of endless benefit and happiness. The Buddha said that he was at that moment going from door to door begging, and it was not suitable to teach the Dharma. But Bāhiya asked again and again, and so the Buddha taught him the Dharma right where he stood: Bāhiya! You should train thus: in the seen there is only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the known, only the known; in the cognized, only the cognized. Bāhiya! When you can make it so that in the seen there is only the seen, in the heard only the heard, in the known only the known, in the cognized only the cognized, then you have reached the state of no clinging and no obstruction. If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no present world and no future world. Having no present and no future, all sorrow, lamentation, and suffering are utterly extinguished. (The original text is in the Udāna of the Theravāda canon, Chapter One, Section Ten.)

[The three times] The past, the present, and the future. Dharmas that have already arisen and ceased are called the “past”; dharmas that have arisen and not ceased are the “present”; dharmas that have not arisen and not come to be are the “future.”

Note: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no present world and no future world. Having no present and no future, all sorrow, lamentation, and suffering are utterly extinguished.” It seems it should read: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no past world and no future world. Having no past and no future, all sorrow, lamentation, and suffering are utterly extinguished.” This may be a copyist's error.

Shanxian” (“Good Manifestation”) is the Chinese translation of the name Subhūti. Subhūti rises from his seat and requests the World-Honored One to teach the Dharma. From this section on, the sutra enters the main body.

At that time the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amid the great assembly. Baring his right shoulder, placing his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms in reverence, he addressed the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata excels in protecting and keeping in mind the bodhisattvas, excels in entrusting and instructing the bodhisattvas. World-Honored One! When good men and good women raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?

At this time the Elder Subhūti, amid the great assembly, rose from his seat. Baring his right shoulder, kneeling on his right knee, joining his palms in reverence, he said to the Buddha: Incomparably wonderful, World-Honored One! You take your own body as the model, and at all times and in all places teach by example — this is truly the best protection, care, and remembrance and the best guidance for all bodhisattvas! World-Honored One! When good men and good women have raised the great mind of attaining Buddhahood and saving sentient beings, how should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?

How should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?” — this is the main theme of this sutra. The upper part of this sutra is precisely the answer to these two questions; at the beginning of the lower part (Section Seventeen, “Ultimately Without Self”), Subhūti raises these two questions again, and the World-Honored One answers them further.
For whom was the Diamond Sutra spoken? From this passage we know that the Buddha spoke this sutra for ordinary beings who have raised the great mind.

[At that time] This time — that is, after the World-Honored One had finished sitting at ease. [Elder] A bhikṣu of advanced years and virtuous reputation. [Subhūti] One of the Buddha's ten great disciples; rendered in Chinese as Kongsheng, Shanxian, or Shanji, and famed among the ten great disciples as “foremost in understanding emptiness.” [Baring the right shoulder] When wearing the kaṣāya, to bare the right shoulder and cover the left. This was originally a ritual of respect in ancient India, and Buddhism adopted it: when a bhikṣu pays homage to the Buddha or inquires after a master or monk, he must bare the right shoulder, meaning that he is ready to serve and to receive orders. [Addressed] To speak from a lower position to a higher. [Rare] Incomparably wonderful! A word of praise. [Tathāgata] One of the Buddha's ten titles. Generally, “World-Honored One” is the general title, used in address; “Buddha” expresses the virtue of the fruit; “Tathāgata” expresses the virtue of the nature.
[The Buddha's ten titles]

The Buddha has ten honorific titles: 1. Tathāgata — the Buddha rides the Way of suchness, comes to accomplish right awakening, and comes into the three realms to bestow transformation; 2. Worthy of Offerings — the Buddha deserves the offerings of humans and gods; 3. One of Perfect and Universal Knowledge — the Buddha truly and universally knows all dharmas; 4. Perfect in Clarity and Conduct — the Buddha is complete in the three clarities of the clarity of past lives, the clarity of the divine eye, and the clarity of the exhaustion of taints, and in the five conducts of the sage's conduct, the brahma conduct, the divine conduct, the infant conduct, and the sick conduct; 5. Well-Gone — the Buddha freely and well departs into nirvāṇa; 6. Knower of the World — the Buddha can understand the affairs and principles of every world; 7. Unsurpassed One — the Buddha is the supreme one; 8. Tamer of Men — the Buddha is the great one who tames and masters all sentient beings, causing them to leave defilement and enter nirvāṇa; 9. Teacher of Gods and Humans — the Buddha is the guide of all gods and humans; 10. World-Honored One — the Buddha is the one honored in common by all the world's people.

[The Tathāgata excels in protecting and keeping in mind the bodhisattvas, excels in entrusting and instructing the bodhisattvas.] “Protecting and keeping in mind” means to care for, look after, and remember with compassion. “Entrusting and instructing” means to entrust and charge, and also means to teach and guide. This sentence is Subhūti's incomparable praise of the World-Honored One for taking his own body as the model and, at all times and in all places, caring for and teaching the bodhisattvas. [Good men and good women] Men and women who cultivate the five precepts and the ten good deeds. [Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] Perfect and unsurpassed wisdom — the Buddha's wisdom. Rendered in Chinese as “unexcelled perfect and universal enlightenment,” also called “unexcelled perfect and universal knowledge.” [Raising the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] Raising the great mind of attaining Buddhahood. “Raising the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” is also abbreviated as “raising the bodhi mind.” Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna's Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

41 says: “When a bodhisattva first raises the mind, taking the unsurpassed Way as his object, ‘I shall become a Buddha’ — this is called the bodhi mind.” [How] How. “How” has several meanings: why, for what reason; how, what to do, in what way. [How should they dwell?] “How should they dwell” means “how should one dwell,” using inverted word order that places “should” after “how” to strengthen the tone. (The answer to “how should they dwell” is in the fourth section: “giving without dwelling in marks.” Not dwelling in marks is emptiness; giving is compassion; the dual practice of compassion and emptiness — this is the bodhisattva path.) [How should they subdue their minds?] How should they subdue their minds? (The answer is in the third section: single-mindedly saving all sentient beings while being free of the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a lifespan. This is the wondrous remedy for affliction — as it is said: better to draw the firewood from beneath the cauldron than to try to stop water from boiling by ladling it out. To single-mindedly save all sentient beings while being free of the four marks is likewise the dual practice of compassion and emptiness.) [Inversion] The rhetorical figure that reverses word order to strengthen the tone, harmonize the rhythm, or vary the sentence pattern; it is often used in classical Chinese, so one should be attentive to this when reading Buddhist sutras.

Day after day the World-Honored One gave this demonstration (not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved), but unfortunately the great assembly did not notice; today it was unexpectedly perceived (its meaning made out) by Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness, who saw with his own eyes the Tathāgata's painstaking heart and could not cease praising it. When the World-Honored One had sat at ease, he at once rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha: Incomparably wonderful, World-Honored One! You take your own body as the model, not grasping at marks and thus unmoved, and at all times and in all places teach by example — this is truly the best protection, care, and remembrance and the best guidance for all bodhisattvas!
But why are the bodhisattvas unable to “not grasp at marks and thus be unmoved”? For this reason Subhūti asked the World-Honored One: How should they dwell, and how should they subdue their minds?

By the Buddha's original vow, he wished only to lay bare the truth (to set out in full the truth of life and the universe) and to have everyone become a Buddha. But sentient beings are thin in virtue and heavy in defilement, weak in will, unable to bear it, and hard to address plainly (just as in the fourteenth section of this sutra the Buddha says: “If again there is a person who hears this sutra and is neither startled, nor frightened, nor afraid, you should know that such a person is very rare.” And again, at the Lotus assembly, Śāriputra three times asked the World-Honored One to reveal the foremost, rare, and hard-to-understand Dharma, and when the World-Honored One began to expound it, five thousand bhikṣus refused to hear and withdrew). He could only use hidden skillful means and accommodate them; hence the word “excels.”

Day after day the World-Honored One gave this demonstration, truly the most skillful protection and remembrance of the bodhisattvas, the most skillful entrusting and instructing. As it is said: not teaching by words but transforming by his own person — the painstaking care of a good craftsman.

In the text of this section, “How should they dwell?” has two readings: the Qianlong Tripitaka and the popular edition adopt “How should they dwell?” while another reading, based on Tang dynasty manuscripts and Ming dynasty block-printed editions, proposes that this sentence should be “Should dwell how?” Which is it, “How should they dwell” or “Should dwell how”? This book, following the Qianlong Tripitaka and the popular edition, adopts “How should they dwell?”

The reason is this: “How should they dwell” in fact means “should dwell how”; it is only that, to strengthen the tone, inverted word order is used, placing “should” after “how.” Inversion is very common in rhetoric, used to strengthen the tone and make the wording vivid. For example, in the

Liezi, “The Moving of the Mountains by the Foolish Old Man”: “How dull you are!” means: your dullness — hui being interchangeable with “wisdom” — is extreme! Wei Zheng's “Expressing My Feelings”: “Ancient trees — the cold birds cry; empty mountains — the night apes wail,” whose meaning is: the cold birds cry on the ancient trees; the night apes wail in the empty mountains. In fact, the four words “thus have I heard” at the very beginning of the sutra are also an inversion. If translated as “I heard it thus,” not only would the force of the wording and the beauty of the style be much diminished — the whole atmosphere would be as different as heaven and earth.
Question: Why is “How should they dwell?” explained as “How should they dwell and abide?”

Answer: Master Kumārajīva's rendering of “how should they dwell” is excellent; the word “dwell” fits the surrounding text perfectly. (For example, the last sentence of the fourth section: “Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught.”) But the meaning of “dwell” here needs to be correctly interpreted. What cultivators care about most is three questions: how to dwell in the mind (to gather the mind so that it is not scattered), how to practice (to correct one's actual conduct of body, speech, and mind), and how to subdue the mind. From the other translations, it appears that in the Sanskrit original Subhūti raised these three questions. For example, in the translation by Master Xuanzang: “World-Honored One! Those who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle — how should they dwell? How should they practice? How should they subdue their minds?” Hence some great masters criticize Master Kumārajīva's translation as “three questions with one missing.”

In fact, combining the two questions into one (merging “how to dwell in the mind” and “how to practice” into “how should they dwell”) was also Master Kumārajīva's painstaking intention. The World-Honored One answered the first two questions together in Section Four, “Wondrous Practice without Dwelling” (how should one dwell in the mind? how should one practice?), and then in the tenth section further clarified the matter of dwelling in the mind and practicing: “All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” And so the Master combined these two questions into one, “how should they dwell” — the wording echoing back and forth, polished and easy on the tongue — and from the surrounding text the reader can readily appreciate that this “dwell” contains both the dwelling of the mind and the practice, that is: how to dwell and abide.

After Master Kumārajīva first translated the Diamond Sutra, five other translations appeared one after another. By rights each later one should surpass the earlier, should it not? Yet history proves that Master Kumārajīva's translation has the greatest power to gather and move people — that is, it accords best with the meaning of the sutra — and it has been widely transmitted without decline.

The Buddha said: Excellent! Excellent! Subhūti, just as you say, the Tathāgata excels in protecting and keeping in mind the bodhisattvas, and excels in entrusting and instructing the bodhisattvas. Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. When good men and good women raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should thus dwell and thus subdue their minds.

The Buddha said: Excellent! Excellent! Subhūti, just as you say, this is truly the Tathāgata's best protection, care, and remembrance and the best guidance for all bodhisattvas! You must listen attentively, and I shall explain for you the method of dwelling in the Way and subduing the mind. When good men and good women have raised the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should thus dwell and thus subdue their minds.

[Excellent] Wonderful! A word of praise. [Listen attentively] To listen with care and attention. [Thus] In this way. Here the two words “thus” point to what follows — “they should thus dwell” refers to the fourth section, and “thus subdue their minds” refers to the third section.

The Buddha said “Excellent” twice in a row to praise Subhūti. The first “Excellent” praises Subhūti for being able to understand the Buddha's demonstration. The Buddha confirms that Subhūti's understanding is without error, saying: Subhūti, just as you say, day after day I give this demonstration, and this is truly the Tathāgata's best protection, care, and remembrance and the best guidance for all bodhisattvas! The second “Excellent” praises Subhūti's wisdom and compassion in being able to request the two questions that leave practitioners unbearably afflicted in their practice and urgently need resolution — how should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?

Then, with regard to the two questions Subhūti requested, the Buddha said: As to the two questions you have raised, you must listen attentively, and I shall explain them in detail for you. When good men and good women have raised the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should thus dwell, and thus subdue their minds.
Indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear it.
Subhūti reverently replied: Yes, World-Honored One! I long greatly and rejoice greatly to hear your teaching on these two questions.
In the

Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sutra, Chapter Thirty-Four, it says: “As the thirsty long for cool water, as the hungry think of fine food, as the sick recall good medicine, as bees crave sweet honey — so too are we: we wish to hear the Dharma of ambrosia!”

[Indeed] “Indeed” is a word of assent. For example, the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “At that time the Buddha told the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati: Now I shall speak for you of the distinguishing marks of the mind-made body. Listen attentively! Listen attentively! Consider it well and keep it in mind. Mahāmati said: Indeed.” “So” here means earnestly hoping to hear the World-Honored One's detailed teaching on the two “thus.” [Indeed, World-Honored One!] Subhūti's reverent reply, expressing a profound wish. [We joyfully wish to hear it] Joyfully wishing to hear that Dharma.

When good men and good women raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should thus dwell, and thus subdue their minds” — this passage has traditionally had two other interpretations; for a better understanding of the sutra's meaning, they are examined and distinguished as follows:
1. The World-Honored One's two “thus” already answer Subhūti's “How should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?” — only Subhūti did not understand.

This interpretation is not sound, because even if Subhūti did not understand the two “thus,” he would not fail to understand the World-Honored One's tone. If the World-Honored One's two “thus” were indeed answering Subhūti's two “how,” and the Elder did not understand, he would have said something like: “We pray the World-Honored One, in great compassion and pity, will expound it separately for all sentient beings” — and not have joyfully followed the World-Honored One's tone, saying, “Indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear it.” Compare the text of the

Lotus Sutra, Chapter Two, “Skillful Means”: “At that time the Buddha told Śāriputra: ... Now listen well, and I shall speak for you. Śāriputra said: Indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear it.”

2. The World-Honored One's two “thus” already answer Subhūti's two questions, and although Subhūti understood, the great assembly had not yet understood, and so he asked on their behalf that the World-Honored One explain in detail.

This interpretation is also not sound. At the very beginning of “Section Fourteen, Free of Marks and Still Extinction”: “At that time Subhūti, having heard this sutra spoken, deeply understood the purport of its meaning, and weeping tears of grief, said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha speaks such a profound sutra; from of old, among the wisdom-eye I have attained, I have never heard such a sutra.” From this passage it appears that Subhūti had not understood before this point.

In fact, the “How should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?” that Subhūti asked is a question at a profound level. Subhūti was already an arhat, his afflictions of view and thought already cut off, and he was foremost in understanding emptiness; the shallow-level “How should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?” he not only understood but had long since put into practice. His question now was raised on the basis of today's insight, gained from the World-Honored One's daily activities such as putting on his robe and taking up his bowl, into the World-Honored One's profound intention and ultimate practice. And this question of Subhūti's finally brought forth the Diamond Sutra — “All Buddhas, and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas, all come forth from this sutra”!

So “Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. When good men and good women raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should thus dwell and thus subdue their minds” means: You must listen attentively, and I shall explain in detail for you the two questions you have raised. When good men and good women have raised the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should thus dwell and thus subdue their minds.

This is like a person asking about a complex matter and the one answering saying, “It is thus.” This is an introductory phrase, used at the beginning of a discourse to call the listener's attention; it means: I shall now explain this matter in detail for you. It does not mean that the words “it is thus” have already answered the question.

Master Xuanzang's translation of this passage reads: “At that time the World-Honored One told the Venerable Subhūti: Excellent! Excellent! Subhūti, it is thus, it is thus. As you say, even the Tathāgata, worthy and perfectly awakened, can with the most excellent gathering gather the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and even the Tathāgata, worthy and perfectly awakened, can with the most excellent entrusting entrust the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Therefore, Subhūti! You should listen attentively and attend most well,
I shall explain it for you in detail

— all those who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle should thus dwell, thus practice, and thus subdue their minds. The Venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: It is thus, it is thus. World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear it.”
Please pay special attention to the phrase “I shall explain it for you in detail.”
[Venerable] A general appellation for a bhikṣu, because a bhikṣu possesses not only the lifespan of the world but also the wisdom-life of the dharmakāya.

So when Subhūti replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One! We joyfully wish to hear it,” he meant: Yes, World-Honored One! I long greatly and rejoice greatly to hear your thorough teaching on these two questions. Hence in the fourteenth section there is: “Subhūti, having heard this sutra spoken, deeply understood the purport of its meaning, and weeping tears of grief, said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha speaks such a profound sutra; from of old, among the wisdom-eye I have attained, I have never heard such a sutra.” It is precisely
The unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma — in hundreds of thousands of kalpas hard to encounter;

In this section Subhūti raised two extremely important questions: How should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds? This is the theme running through the whole text. To make it easier to understand the sutra passages that follow, the answers are set out here first.
Question: How should they dwell?
Answer:
giving without dwelling in marks

. “Subhūti! A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere — that is, give without dwelling in form, give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas. Subhūti! A bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks.” “If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.” (A bodhisattva's practice is the six pāramitās; here the first of the six, giving, stands for all six, and giving without dwelling in marks encompasses the entire six pāramitās.)
Question: How should they subdue their minds?

Answer: By saving all sentient beings without clinging to the mark of saving them. “Thus I save innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved.” “Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.” “Free of all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

blocks.text: 3. The True Doctrine of the Mahāyāna

inline.s: The true doctrine of the Mahāyāna” is the dual practice of compassion and emptiness — seeking the Buddha Way above and transforming sentient beings below; that is, as the text below says: saving all sentient beings (saving all sentient beings to Buddhahood), yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved (in truth there is no such thing as sentient beings attaining salvation and Buddhahood). In studying the Diamond Sutra, one should over and over realize the words “saving all sentient beings, yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved” — this is the true doctrine of the Mahāyāna.
In this section the World-Honored One first says, “they should thus subdue their minds,” echoing the preceding section where he said they should “thus subdue their minds.”

The Buddha told Subhūti: All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus subdue their minds: all the various kinds of sentient beings — whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought — I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without remainder and be saved. Thus I save innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved.

The method by which a bodhisattva subdues his mind is: to universally save sentient beings to Buddhahood (“saving innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings”) while not clinging to the mark of saving them (“yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved”). Compassion and emptiness practiced together: compassionately saving sentient beings without clinging to the mark of saving.
The Buddha told Subhūti: All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus subdue their minds”
— the Buddha said to Subhūti: All great bodhisattvas (all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas) should thus subdue their minds.

[The Buddha told Subhūti] Whenever a passage begins with “the Buddha told Subhūti,” this emphasizes that what is said is of the utmost importance. [Bodhisattva-mahāsattva] Bodhisattvas have upper, middle, and lower stages; to indicate bodhisattvas on the grounds, the term mahāsattva is further used. The Treatise on the Buddha Grounds says: “Here we take the great bodhisattvas on the grounds, and therefore again speak of mahāsattva.” So “bodhisattva-mahāsattva” indicates a bodhisattva on the grounds. Here “all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas” refers to the good men and good women spoken of above who have raised the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this appellation expresses the World-Honored One's boundless expectation of them, that they should take the great bodhisattvas on the grounds as their model and thus subdue their minds. [Bodhisattva on the grounds] From ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva passes through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten grounds are called bodhisattvas on the grounds.

all the various kinds of sentient beings — whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought — I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without remainder and be saved”

— all the various kinds of sentient beings, such as those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, and by transformation, those with form and without form, those with thought, without thought, and neither with thought nor without thought — I shall save them all to Buddhahood.

[Born from eggs] Life that is born after taking form within an eggshell, such as birds. [Born from wombs] Life that is born after taking form within the mother's womb, such as humans. [Born from moisture] Life that takes form relying on moisture, such as insects. [Born by transformation] Life that arises suddenly by the power of karma alone, without relying on anything, such as the gods of the heavens. [With form] Sentient beings in the desire realm and the form realm who possess a physical body. [Without form] Such sentient beings have no physical body but retain the mind of consciousness and dwell in profound and wondrous meditative concentration. [With thought] Among all the heavens, apart from the Heaven of No Thought and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, the rest are heavens with thought. The sentient beings of the heavens with thought have thought and feeling, and so are called with thought. [Without thought] The Heaven of No Thought is the fourth dhyāna heaven of the form realm; the sentient beings of this heaven dwell without mind for five hundred great kalpas. [Neither with thought nor without thought] The Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception is the highest heaven in the three realms; its sentient beings dwell in meditative concentration, and because they have no coarse thought it is called “neither with thought,” and because they still have subtle thought it is also called “not without thought.” [The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who have the two desires of sexual desire and food, including the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below. The form realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who are free of the two desires of sexuality and food but still have a physical body, including the four dhyānas and eighteen heavens. The formless realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who have no physical body but abide with the mind of consciousness in profound and wondrous meditative concentration, including the four empty heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all realms of birth-and-death and transmigration for ordinary beings. [The eighteen heavens] The eighteen heavens of the form realm. The first dhyāna heaven has three heavens: the Heaven of the Multitude of Brahmās, the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā, and the Heaven of Great Brahmā. The second dhyāna heaven also has three: the Heaven of Lesser Light, the Heaven of Boundless Light, and the Heaven of Light-Sound. The third dhyāna heaven also has three: the Heaven of Lesser Purity, the Heaven of Boundless Purity, and the Heaven of Universal Purity. The fourth dhyāna heaven has nine in all: the Heaven of Cloudlessness, the Heaven of Blessed Birth, the Heaven of Vast Fruit, the Heaven of No Thought, the Heaven Without Affliction, the Heaven Without Heat, the Heaven of Good Seeing, the Heaven of Good Manifestation, and the Highest Heaven of the Form Realm.

[Saved] That is, nirvāṇa. “Extinguished” means the extinction of the three delusions of view-and-thought, dust-and-sand, and ignorance; “crossed over” means crossing beyond fragmentary birth-and-death and transformation birth-and-death. [I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without remainder and be saved] I shall save them all to Buddhahood. [Nirvāṇa] The full name is parinirvāṇa, meaning not-arising and not-ceasing. Rendered in Chinese as “perfect stillness,” where “perfect” is the perfection of all the virtues of wisdom, and “stillness” is the still extinction of all delusion and karma. It is also rendered “extinction and crossing over.” This is the true suchness realm, neither arising nor ceasing and beyond time and space, realized by the sages, and it is also the most ideal and most beautiful final home of the myriad sentient beings. [Nirvāṇa without remainder] When a bodhisattva has exhausted the cause of transformation birth-and-death, this is called “nirvāṇa with remainder” (the Hīnayāna realization of the arhat fruit is also called nirvāṇa with remainder); only when the fruit of transformation birth-and-death is exhausted, not a hair of the false marks of arising and ceasing remains, and the Buddha's eternal body is obtained, is it called “nirvāṇa without remainder.”
Thus I save innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved”

— thus saving innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings to Buddhahood, and yet in truth there is no such thing as sentient beings being saved and attaining Buddhahood. This says that a bodhisattva, in saving sentient beings, does not dwell in the mark of saving, and so enters into non-self, and thereby subdues his mind.

Saving innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings” — this is compassion (“compassion” being the mind that uproots the suffering of others); “yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved” — this is not clinging to marks, knowing that the saving of sentient beings is an illusion: this is emptiness. Compassion and emptiness held in balance, practiced together and mutually interfused, runs through the Diamond Sutra from beginning to end. This is because only when compassion and emptiness are mutually fused is there right concentration, and only then can the Buddha-fruit be perfectly accomplished. If one falls into one-sided emptiness (holding that nothing whatsoever exists) or even into neutral indifference (stillness without illumination), one mostly plants the cause of animal rebirth, or falls into the śrāvaka's concentration of extinction, or is reborn in the formless realm. Therefore the World-Honored One in this sutra over and over speaks of giving without dwelling (not dwelling is emptiness, giving is compassion). For a cultivator to dance with the objects is of course muddled; but to become cold and solitary is likewise wrong — one must be very careful!

yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved” — here the World-Honored One warns us that in saving sentient beings we must not cling to the mark of saving. For saving sentient beings means teaching them to be free of marks and to wake from the dream of ignorance; if one is oneself clinging to marks, how can one teach others to be free of marks? It is like saving a drowning person: one wants to save him from the water, not to sink to the bottom of the sea along with him and perish together.

[The concentration of extinction] The concentration in which both mind and mental factors (“mental factors” being the abbreviation of dharmas belonging to the mind, that is, the various psychological phenomena belonging to the mind) are utterly extinguished. That is, the state of mental unification in which the mental activity of the six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness) is entirely extinguished. Although its perception and anxiety are already extinguished, there still remains a subtle mental factor not yet extinguished.

Master Hanshan says: “What Buddhism values is benefiting oneself and benefiting others; only then is one called a bodhisattva. The Sanskrit word bodhisattva means in Chinese ‘a being of the great mind,’ because such a one can enter the realm of sentient beings and can cut off affliction, and so receives this name. If a bodhisattva abandons the world, he has no practice to cultivate; if he abandons sentient beings, he has no instrument for cutting off affliction. Therefore a bodhisattva relies on sentient beings to cut off the afflictions of his own nature — as the stone of another mountain can polish one's jade. Affliction is the various evil habits of greed, anger, self-love, and views of pride (that is, self-love, self-view, and self-pride), which veil the light of the self-nature. Without all the adverse conditions and objects of sentient beings in the world, one cannot grind and polish to cut them off — as the Odes say, ‘cut and file, carve and polish.’” (From the Dream Wandering Collection
Addressed to Yuan Datu)

How should they subdue their minds? Even in saving all sentient beings, not to cling to marks. This says: however high one's attainment and however great one's merit, one must not cling to marks. To cling to marks is not bodhisattva practice, because bodhisattva practice is to turn delusion into awakening, whereas clinging to marks is to enter illusion through illusion, deluded all the more.

When we raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (the mind of attaining Buddhahood), we must make the vow: “all the various kinds of sentient beings ... I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without remainder and be saved,” and moreover “thus I save innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved.” This puts us in a commanding position: we are great bodhisattvas who would save all sentient beings; how could we not be dignified and self-respecting? How could we harm sentient beings? How could we contend with them for fame and profit? How could we oppose them? How could we haggle with them? In this way selfishness and self-interest, fame and gain, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, greed, anger, delusion, and pride, and the rights and wrongs of self and other — all naturally melt away like ice, and the merit one creates is likewise emptied of the three wheels, so that the mind is subdued without needing to be subdued.

[The three wheels emptied] With regard to giving: the giver, the receiver, and the thing given are called the three wheels; if after giving, the marks of these three wheels do not remain in the mind, it is called “the three wheels emptied.”
Why is that? Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.

The World-Honored One said: Why is it that “thus I save innumerable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet in truth there are no sentient beings who are saved”? Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he does not count as a bodhisattva.

Among the four marks, the mark of a self is foremost. Once this mark is set up, the other three marks (the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, the mark of a lifespan) arise along with it. A bodhisattva is a being of the great mind who has raised the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and one who raises the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi must believe in and understand the true character of all dharmas, because the true character of all dharmas is the Buddha Way. To have the four marks is a concrete expression of falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as real, showing that one has not believed in and understood the true character of all dharmas, and therefore one is not a bodhisattva. This principle is set forth in very great detail in the Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma.

All sentient beings without exception possess the nature of awakening, luminous, empty, and still, no different from the Buddha. But because since beginningless kalpas they have never understood, they falsely cling to body and mind (form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) as themselves (the mark of a self), and so give rise to feelings of love and hate, grasping and rejecting. Thus they create karma following feeling, and receive retribution following karma — birth, old age, sickness, and death, and kalpa-long transmigration.

The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversions, like a confused man who mistakes the four directions (for example, taking east for west and south for north), and falsely recognizes the four great elements as the marks of their own body, and the shadowy impressions of the six dusts as the marks of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good men! In the sky there is truly no flower; the diseased one falsely clings. Because of this false clinging, he is not only confused about the self-nature of this empty space, but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false clinging there is the turning about in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

Delusion about the self-nature is precisely this: falsely recognizing this five-aggregate body and mind — which has a name, a form, a sex, an identity, and an age — as oneself, as “I”; and thus one turns about in birth and death.

[The five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formation, and the aggregate of consciousness. These five are produced by accumulation, and so are called the “five aggregates”; they can also cover over people's true nature, causing them to be deluded and inverted and to create all kinds of karma, and so they are also named the “five shadows.” Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called “form-dharmas”; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness belong to mind and are called “mind-dharmas.” These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Of them, the aggregate of form is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) are the mind. [The four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture, fire has warmth, wind has movement. All tangible matter in the world has these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [Shadowy impressions of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six dusts; and since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy impressions of the six dusts — the phantoms of the six dusts.

[Mark] The various marks of things as they appear outwardly and are imagined in the mind. [The mark of a self] Falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as truly existent, and taking them as “I” and giving rise to mind — for example, gain and loss, adverse and favorable, honor and disgrace, and so on. [The mark of a person] Falsely clinging to the other, to other people, as truly existent and giving rise to mind — for example, love and hate, right and wrong, high and low, and so on. [The mark of a sentient being] Here “sentient being” refers to groups of people — for example, groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and foe, age, sex, workplace, region, race, skin color, country, and so on; the mark of a sentient being is falsely clinging to these groups as truly existent and giving rise to a discriminating mind. [The mark of a lifespan] Falsely clinging to lifespan as truly existent and calculating its length. What deluded sentient beings care about most is nothing other than lifespan; therefore the mark of a lifespan is separated out from the mark of a self and established as an item of its own. The Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma was likewise translated by Master Kumārajīva, and in the Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma the Buddha says:

“After the great and adorned Buddha and his great disciples entered nirvāṇa, more and more people came to know that the śramaṇa's Dharma is peaceful and happy, and left home to study the Way; yet they could not know the profound sutras spoken by the Buddha and the unequaled meaning of emptiness, and were mostly deluded by evil māras. At that time those who spoke the Dharma had unsettled minds and spoke impurely, speaking of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan, and not speaking of the emptiness and stillness of all dharmas.” “One who calculates a self holds that there is a lifespan. Because of lifespan, one is dragged about by gain and profit, and is obstructed in the Way.”
To be free of the mark of a lifespan is to accomplish the non-duality of early death and long life.

These four marks are falsely clinging to self, person (the other, other people), sentient being (groups of people), and lifespan as truly existent, and then standing on the ground of “I” to discriminate, calculate, confront, and act. Once the four marks are set up, one cannot understand all dharmas as illusory, and is bound by them and cannot be liberated.

Among the four marks, the mark of a self comes first. Once this mark is set up, the other three marks arise in response. Thereupon selfishness, private advantage, and private desire surge up, and affliction and karmic retribution follow along. To catch the bandits, first catch their ringleader: for a student of Buddhism the first thing to break is the mark of a self, because when there is a mark of a self, there are the marks of a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan. If there is no mark of a self, then there are no marks at all; the very substance is empty and still, and all wisdom naturally appears before one.
In the

Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma, Chapter Three, “Recollection of the Dharma,” the Buddha says: “Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings free of inversion who contemplate things as they truly are, they have right view. If one gives rise to the thought of a self, the thought of a person, or the thought of a sentient being, you should know that such a person walks the wrong path. Śāriputra! The Buddha and his disciples do not speak of a self, do not speak of a person, do not speak of a sentient being, do not speak of a lifespan, do not speak of annihilation or permanence; therefore the Buddha and his disciples are called those of right view. Why is that? Because their contemplation is right and free of inversion.” This shows that one who holds such wrong views as the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan does not even qualify to be a disciple of the Buddha—how much less to be a bodhisattva! In the Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma the World-Honored One sets forth this principle, and the true nature of all dharmas, in exhaustive detail.

[The two views of annihilation and permanence] The “view of annihilation” holds that the self is limited to a single lifetime and that after death everything ceases to be. The “view of permanence” holds that after death the self is not destroyed but is reborn and continues in its present form—for example, one who is born human is human life after life, and one born a dog is a dog life after life. Right view is this: free of annihilation and free of permanence, and taking the Middle Way, the true nature of things.
Question: How are the four marks to be transcended?

Answer: This can be done in two steps. First, do not mistake this body-and-mind of the five aggregates and all conditions for something real and thus cling to them. In the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra of the Mahāyāna the Buddha says: “If practitioners give rise to the clinging to existence or non-existence with regard to objects (if, toward objects, they give rise to the clinging to existence or to non-existence—clinging that things are or that they are not, as when one wrongly holds that an ox has horns and a hare does not), then they are caught in the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan.” Second, once you already have the power to let a thought arise without continuing it, freedom from the four marks is freedom from the four conceptualizations. The marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan are simply the thoughts of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan that surface in your mind; this is why some translations of the Diamond Sutra render the four marks as the four conceptualizations. Kumārajīva’s (350–413) translation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sutra says: “If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.” But the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s (499–569) translation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sutra says: “All bodhisattvas are free of the conceptualization of a self, the conceptualization of a sentient being, the conceptualization of a lifespan, and the conceptualization of a receiver.” Therefore, whenever a thought about a self, a person, a sentient being, or a lifespan surfaces, you must immediately extinguish it (when your skill in contemplating the mind is deep, you can do this), and on no account let it continue and become a conceptualization; you must reach the point where a thought arising is immediately noticed, and once noticed it is gone. The Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma says: “The buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is entirely without conceptualization and without thought.” The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “To stir the mind and move a thought is to depart from the Dharma-substance and to grasp at marks; since beginningless time there has never been a Buddha who grasped at marks.”

“Wondrous practice without dwelling”: “without dwelling” here means knowing that all dharmas are empty, and therefore neither grasping at conditions nor becoming defiled—acting without being attached to the action (free of love and hate, grasping and rejecting); this is called wondrous practice. “Wondrous practice without dwelling” is the giving without dwelling in marks spoken of below. Not dwelling in marks is emptiness; giving is compassion; giving without dwelling in marks is the dual practice of compassion and emptiness. This section answers the question “How should one dwell?”—one dwells (abides) by giving without dwelling in marks, which answers from afar the World-Honored One’s words in Section Two, “one should dwell thus.”

[Without dwelling] Not grasping at marks. That is to say, with regard to the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, a lifespan, dharmas, and non-dharmas, one dwells nowhere (one does not wrongly cling to them as real). The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Free of marks, there is no-mark; with no-mark, there is no dwelling; with no dwelling, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”

[Grasping at marks] Grasping at marks is taking marks as real, so that desire arises and thoughts arise, and one runs after desire and thought. Thus one creates karma, and thus there is birth-and-death and transmigration. Therefore, do not cling to marks as real and be moved by them. This sutra says:
“Not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved.”

Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere—that is, give without dwelling in form, and give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas. Subhūti! A bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks.

This passage comes right after the World-Honored One has finished answering the second question, “How should one subdue the mind?” and immediately answers the first question as well. Subhūti asked, “How should one dwell?” The World-Honored One answers, “Give without dwelling in marks.” That is, a bodhisattva should give free of marks, with the three wheels emptied; this is how one dwells—that is, one dwells (abides) by giving without dwelling in marks.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
—Moreover, Subhūti! Having answered “How should one subdue the mind?” the World-Honored One immediately goes on to answer the question “How should one dwell?” (how should one abide?).
A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere.”

—A bodhisattva should give free of marks, and in giving must not cling to objects and give rise to thoughts, nor be turned by objects. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought is free of objects, that is bodhi.”

Dharma” has several meanings: first, it broadly refers to all things and matters, including thought, speech, and writing, all of which are called “dharmas”; second, law or principle; third, method; fourth, the Dharma of the Way, that is, the principles, methods, and realms of cultivating the Way; fifth, mental objects, the dharmas among the six dusts (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas). Which meaning is intended must be judged from the context. In the sentence “A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere,” “dharmas” broadly refers to all things. [Dwelling nowhere with regard to dharmas] Knowing that all dharmas are empty, and therefore neither grasping at conditions nor becoming defiled.

Giving” means giving to others what one has. There are three kinds of giving: the giving of wealth, relieving the sick, weak, poor, and suffering with material goods; the giving of Dharma, guiding others out of suffering with the right Dharma; and the giving of fearlessness, freeing others from terror and dread.
That is, give without dwelling in form, and give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.”

—This explains the preceding sentence, “A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere.” Concretely, it means giving without dwelling in the dust of form, giving without dwelling in the dust of sound, giving without dwelling in the dust of fragrance, giving without dwelling in the dust of taste, giving without dwelling in the dust of touch, and giving without dwelling in the dust of dharmas.

Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas” are called the six dusts—the dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of fragrance, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, and the dust of dharmas. “Dust” means defilement: it can defile the human mind so that self-nature cannot manifest. They are also called the six objects, that is, the objects grasped at by the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind): the eye sees form, the ear hears sound, the nose smells fragrance, the tongue tastes flavor, the body feels touch, and the mind knows dharmas. “Without dwelling” here means having no love or hate, no grasping or rejecting, toward the objects of the dusts (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas).

The first five dusts (the dusts of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch) include every material object within the reach of the senses, while the dust of dharmas includes every mental object within the reach of the mind. Thus the six words “form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, dharmas” refer to all objects, and the words in Section Ten, “one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas,” mean that no object whatsoever may be clung to. When the Buddha speaks of the six dusts, he always mentions form first and then follows with sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas, because the dust of form (what the eye sees) most easily deludes people and has the greatest influence among the six dusts; therefore he singles it out first as a warning.
When a bodhisattva cultivates the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices,
giving comes first, and giving without dwelling encompasses the remaining five pāramitās. In the

Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter One, “The Prologue,” the Buddha says: “Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving with prajñāpāramitā (that is, giving without dwelling), by the power of wisdom and skillful means he can fulfill the pāramitā of dāna (giving), the pāramitā of śīla (observing precepts), the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience), the pāramitā of vīrya (diligence), the pāramitā of dhyāna (meditative concentration), and the pāramitā of prajñā (wisdom). Śāriputra said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when giving, by the power of wisdom and skillful means fulfills the pāramitā of dāna and on through the pāramitā of prajñā? The Buddha told Śāriputra: Because giver, receiver, and material goods are ungraspable (the three wheels are empty), one can fulfill the pāramitā of dāna. Because guilt and guiltlessness are ungraspable, one fulfills the pāramitā of śīla. Because the mind is unmoved, one fulfills the pāramitā of kṣānti. Because body and mind are diligent without slackening, one fulfills the pāramitā of vīrya. Because one is neither scattered nor dull, one fulfills the pāramitā of dhyāna. Because one knows all dharmas to be ungraspable, one fulfills the pāramitā of prajñā.”
In the

Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter Two, “Learning and Contemplation,” the Buddha says: “All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate prajñāpāramitā can know things as they truly are: if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, taking non-attainment as skillful means, cultivates the pāramitā of giving, and understands that all givers, receivers, and gifts are ungraspable, then such giving, skillful and wise, can fulfill the pāramitās of giving, pure precepts, patient acceptance, diligence, meditative stillness, and prajñā.”

[The six pāramitās] Also called the six pāramitās: the six Dharma-gates by which one may cross from this shore of birth-and-death and affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa’s peace and bliss—namely giving, observing precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and prajñā. Giving can carry one across stinginess and greed; observing precepts can carry one across transgression; patience can carry one across anger; diligence can carry one across slackness; meditative concentration can carry one across distraction; prajñā can carry one across delusion. [The six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices] In brief they are the six pāramitās; in full they are the ten thousand practices, and the six pāramitās include every practice a bodhisattva cultivates.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks.”

—The World-Honored One emphasizes once again: one should give in this way, without dwelling in marks (without giving rise to a discriminating mind toward marks). For giving is meant to use illusion to transcend illusion, not to use illusion to enter further into illusion; it is meant to dissolve the self, not to inflate the self. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “To have a self is itself the fault; to forget one’s own merit is a blessing beyond compare.”
Why is that? If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.

The World-Honored One explains why “a bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks”: because “if a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.” That is, the merit and virtue of giving without dwelling in marks are utterly vast—so vast that the mind cannot even imagine them.

The Four Lessons of Liaofan says: When one does good and the mind does not cling to the good, then whatever one accomplishes is brought to perfection; when the mind clings to the good, then even a lifetime of diligent effort stops at half-good. Suppose, for example, one relieves others with wealth: inwardly one does not see a self, outwardly one does not see a person, and in between one does not see the thing given—this is called the three wheels being empty, this is called the mind of single purity; then a single measure of grain can plant boundless blessings, and a single coin can erase the offenses of a thousand kalpas. But if this mind is not forgotten (if one still clings to the good), then even ten thousand yi of gold will not bring merit to fullness. Long ago a certain woman came to a temple wishing to give but having no wealth; she had only two coins, which she donated, and the abbot himself performed the repentance for her. Later she entered the palace and became rich and noble, and she brought several thousand in gold to the temple to give; the abbot merely had his disciples dedicate the merit. She therefore asked: When I gave two coins before, the master himself performed the repentance for me; now I give several thousand in gold, and the master does not dedicate the merit. Why is this? He said: Before, though the gift was small, the mind of giving was utterly sincere, and nothing short of my own repentance could repay the virtue; now, though the gift is large, the mind of giving is not as earnest as it was then, and having others repent on your behalf is enough.
What follows explains how inconceivable is the merit and virtue of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling in marks.

Subhūti! What do you think? Can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhūti! Can the space in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhūti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are likewise inconceivable. Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught.
Subhūti! What do you think? Can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One.”
—The World-Honored One asks: Subhūti! What do you think—can the vastness of the space stretching away to the east be measured? Subhūti answers: It cannot be measured, World-Honored One!

Can it be measured? No.” Both instances of the character rendered “No” here carry the old reading that means “not so”; in classical Chinese this character is interchangeable with the word for “not so.” Throughout the entire sutra Subhūti answers “No” in more than ten places, and in every case it carries the clear sense of a negative, and so it is read as “not so”; read in the customary way as “it is not,” it also works.
Subhūti! Can the space in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One.”

—The World-Honored One asks: Subhūti! What do you think—can the vastness of the space stretching away along the south, the west, the north, the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest, as well as above and below, be measured? Subhūti answers: It cannot be measured, World-Honored One!
[The four intermediate directions] Southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest are called the four intermediate directions.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are likewise inconceivable.”

—The World-Honored One says: Subhūti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are as vast and boundless as the space of the ten directions (east, south, west, and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below), and cannot be measured.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught.”
—Therefore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply abide by the teaching I have set out above (practicing the six pāramitās without giving rise to a discriminating mind toward marks).

Here it is made clear that what was said above answers the question “How should one dwell?” The “dwell” here means to abide, and it differs in meaning from the “dwell” in “give without dwelling in form, give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.” In that phrase, “dwell” means the mind abiding in objects and thereby giving rise to discrimination and clinging, arousing love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and being turned by objects.
At this point the World-Honored One has answered Subhūti’s two great questions:
Question: How should one subdue the mind? Answer: By delivering all sentient beings without dwelling in marks.

Question: How should one dwell? Answer: “Give without dwelling in marks.” Not dwelling in marks is emptiness; giving is compassion; compassion and emptiness are practiced together, and giving without dwelling in marks encompasses the entire six pāramitās—this is the bodhisattva path.
Question: How do we know that this section answers “How should one dwell?”
Answer: At the end of this section, when summing up this teaching, the World-Honored One says: “Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught (as taught above).”
Question: Why does the World-Honored One not answer the first question first?

Answer: Because the answer to the second question, “How should one subdue the mind?”, is the making of a great vow—to deliver all sentient beings without dwelling in marks—while the answer to “How should one dwell?” is great practice—to give without dwelling in marks. Great practice is built upon the foundation of the great vow, and so the World-Honored One first speaks of the great vow and then of the great practice.
Question: How can one actually give without dwelling in marks?

Answer: This is what Section Ten teaches: “One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”

Seeing reality as it is” is what the passage of this section means by “if you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.” In this section the World-Honored One further clarifies: Why is it that “thus I deliver immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet not a single sentient being is delivered”? Why must there be no mark of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a lifespan? Why is it that “a bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks”? Because: “All that has marks is illusory and false.” And further: “If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.”

[If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata] If, on seeing all marks, you understand (and this is not a verbal understanding) that they are illusory marks, then you see your own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathāgata).
Subhūti! What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of bodily marks?
The World-Honored One asks: Subhūti! What do you think—can sentient beings, dwelling and clinging to their own physical body (bodily marks), see their own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathāgata)?
[Dwelling and clinging to one’s own physical body] Wrongly clinging to the physical body as real and taking it to be oneself.

[Intrinsic nature] Intrinsic nature is also called Buddha-nature, the original face, and suchness. Because intrinsic nature is Buddha, it is called Buddha-nature; because intrinsic nature is the original state of self-nature, it is called the original face, also shortened to “the original”; because intrinsic nature is the original state of self-nature, unchanging and constant, it is called suchness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Intrinsic nature is Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.”
For a detailed discussion of intrinsic nature, see
“Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha”
. [Bodily marks]
This refers to a sentient being’s own physical body.
Older commentaries take

bodily marks” to mean the Buddha’s thirty-two marks. To this, Upāsaka Jiang Weihuang’s Lectures on the Diamond Sutra points out: would such an interpretation not repeat the later passage on the thirty-two marks? Every word and every sentence of the Diamond Sutra has deep meaning; there is certainly no repetition.
The two characters “bodily marks” here should be taken as referring to a sentient being’s physical body.

The Buddha’s meaning in this passage is: You sentient beings—can you, by means of your own bodily marks, see your intrinsic nature? [Would such an interpretation not repeat the later passage on the thirty-two marks]
In the later Section Thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Taught,” the sutra says:

“Subhūti! What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is that? What the Tathāgata speaks of as the thirty-two marks are no-marks, and so they are called the thirty-two marks.”
Of all the principles set out in the preceding passages, the most essential is the repeated clarification that one should not dwell in marks. For example:

“Thus I deliver immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet not a single sentient being is delivered,” “if a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva,” “a bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks”

, and so on. Why, then, should one not dwell in marks? Because only by not dwelling in marks can one realize intrinsic nature. To realize it in part is to be a bodhisattva of the first ground, no longer retreating from the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; to realize it to the fullest is to become a Buddha. And among all marks, what sentient beings care about most and cling to most is their own physical body (bodily marks)—this is the root cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution, and transmigrating. Therefore the World-Honored One here asks in a way meant to awaken them: Can sentient beings, clinging to the physical body, see their intrinsic nature? This is breaking the view of the body.
[Clinging to the physical body is the root cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution, and transmigrating]
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversion, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another, wrongly taking the four elements as the mark of their own body and the shadows cast by the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. The sky truly has no flowers; the sick person wrongly clings to them, and because of that wrong clinging he is not only deluded about the nature of this space but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence comes the turning round in birth-and-death, and so it is called ignorance.”

[Translation: Since beginningless time all sentient beings have had their self-nature deluded and inverted, giving rise to all kinds of inversion and taking the false as real—this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings and takes north for south and east for west: he wrongly takes the flesh formed by the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the mark of his own body, and the deliberating mind of the six faculties as they contact the six dusts (the shadows cast by the six dusts) as the mark of his own mind. It is like a diseased eye falsely seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. In truth there are no flowers in the sky; they are an illusion wrongly clung to by the diseased eye, and because of that wrong clinging one not only wrongly clings to space as real but also believes that the flowers truly arise from there. Because sentient beings are deluded and inverted, they wrongly take the illusory body and mind to be real and cling to them as a self, and so birth-and-death and transmigration never cease; this is what is called ignorance.]
[The view of the body] The wrong view that clings to the body as real.
No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of bodily marks. Why is that? What the Tathāgata speaks of as bodily marks are no bodily marks.

Subhūti answers: No, World-Honored One! One cannot see intrinsic nature by dwelling and clinging to one’s own physical body. Why is that? Because what the Tathāgata speaks of as the physical body (the mark exists) is no physical body (the substance is void); therefore the physical body is illusory, and one must not cling in delusion to the illusory physical body as real and thus see one’s own intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Subhūti: All that has marks is illusory and false.
The World-Honored One further teaches Subhūti: Not only is the physical body (bodily marks) an illusion—all marks whatsoever are also illusions.
[All that has marks is illusory and false] All marks are illusions. In the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
this is set out in detail.
Great Master Guifeng says:

“That all dharmas are like a dream, all the sages say with one voice. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the objects of the dusts are originally empty. The mind of emptiness and stillness is not obscured in its spiritual knowing. This knowing of emptiness and stillness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it come into being because of objects. The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion about it, one wrongly clings to body and mind as a self and gives rise to thoughts of greed and anger. If one meets a good friend who reveals it, one suddenly awakens to the knowing of emptiness and stillness. Knowing is without thought and without form—who then is the mark of a self or the mark of a person? Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies nowhere but here. Therefore, though one undertakes the ten thousand practices in full, one takes no-thought alone as the guiding principle. Once one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought, love and aversion naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses are naturally cut off, and one’s practice naturally advances. Since one understands that all marks are no-marks, there is naturally the cultivation that is no cultivation. When affliction is exhausted, birth-and-death ceases. When birth and extinction are extinguished, still illumination appears before one, and its responsive function is inexhaustible; this is called Buddha.”

(From the Preface to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan.) [Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies nowhere but here] Awakening to all marks as illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must immediately awaken to the fact that one is taking the illusory as real and being turned by illusory marks. Having awakened to this, the deluded thought immediately disappears. The wondrous gate of cultivation is right here!

Here the World-Honored One tells us the ultimate truth: all marks whatsoever are neither truly existent nor entirely nonexistent, but illusory. (They are like things in a dream: not entirely nonexistent, because for the dreamer they truly occur and are truly felt; and yet not truly existent. Hence they are named with such words as illusion, falseness, and emptiness. People everywhere, because they wrongly cling to marks as real, are seduced and driven by them, give rise to delusion and create karma, and suffer transmigration to no purpose.)
All that has marks is illusory and false”—this sentence shows how to contemplate with wisdom; it is the starting point for upholding the Diamond Sutra. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Knowing the illusion, one is immediately free of it, with no need for skillful means; being free of the illusion is itself enlightenment, with no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the final age who cultivate in accordance with this can thereby forever leave all illusions behind.”

This is the crucial point for applying effort in upholding the Diamond Sutra: be free of the illusion! When watching a 3-D film, for instance, if a tiger suddenly lunges at you, you are startled, and then you smile knowingly: it is fake! Watch it a few more times, and you are unmoved. But in a dream, when a tiger hotly pursues you, you flee in panic and suffer unbearably, because you take it as real. This is the difference between awakening and delusion.

Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the truth of the universe and human life: all marks are illusions. On reflection, this is truly astonishing. If so, which of the myriad things in the universe is not an illusion? No wonder the World-Honored One says in Section Fourteen:
“If there is again someone who, hearing this sutra, is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such a person is most rare.”

Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have taken “marks” as real, so that the mind is turned by objects, karma is created, retribution is received, and they turn round in the six realms. Therefore the World-Honored One tells us to be free of marks. To be free of marks means: seeing marks without being deluded and without giving rise to a mind (as a mirror reflects things), not being turned by objects, knowing them to be illusions, free of love and hate, and not grasping at conditions. This is the core of upholding the Diamond Sutra. The Heart Sutra says:

“Because of non-attainment, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has a mind without obstruction. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; far removed from inverted dream-thoughts, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”

Here “prajñāpāramitā” is the wondrous wisdom that clearly knows all marks to be illusory and lets them go—that is, the practice of being free of marks: seeing marks without delusion, and not being turned by objects.

All that has marks is illusory and false”—this is the reason for, and the method of, transcending the four marks (the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan): Why transcend the four marks? Because they are all false. How does one transcend the four marks? By firmly remembering that “all that has marks is illusory and false,” and letting go of the illusion the moment it is seen, with no need for skillful means.

This is like watching a television series: if you are deeply absorbed, then along with the illusory situations your love and hate, grasping and rejecting, joy and anger, sorrow and gladness never cease. This is exactly how it has been since beginningless kalpas: giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution, and transmigrating. But if, while watching, we keep reminding ourselves—This is fake! This is fake!—and even smile faintly, we will grow more and more unmoved, until we have neither the interest nor the patience to watch the whole series of dozens of episodes. So the way to be free of marks (seeing marks without delusion, not being turned by objects) is this: constantly contemplate that “all that has marks is illusory and false,” and make it your own view, your own consciousness, speech, and action—this is to be awakening.
