[A profoundly deep sutra] This says that the theory, method, and realm of this sutra are utterly profound, subtle, and penetrating. [Wisdom-eye] The eye of wisdom, realized by the two vehicles, the wisdom that knows the equal nature and emptiness of all dharmas. [Nature is empty] All things and dharmas are by nature originally empty, with no substantial reality to be obtained.

What was it that made Subhuti so filled with mingled grief and joy and tears of gratitude? His joy was that today he had heard the most perfect, sudden, and true dharma of becoming a Buddha, and so the Elder says below, in deep understanding of its meaning and purport: “Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.” His grief was that since the beginningless kalpa he had had no way to hear the great dharma, and so had sunk down until today. The Elder could not stop rejoicing!
Chen

Paramārtha's translation reads: “At that time the pure-lived Subhuti, because the benefit of the dharma was swift, at once wept aloud.” The Diamond Sutra is a swift dharma; this is the practice of the One Buddha Vehicle: seeing the nature (“if one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata”) and eliminating habit (“they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), detached from all marks, directly realizing Buddhahood (“detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha”).
[A swift dharma] A rapid and sudden dharma.

The theory, realm, and method taught in this sutra are suited not only to beginners (“after the Tathāgata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit,” who can believe, accept, and practice it), but run straight through to the Buddha-fruit: awakening to the unconditioned dharma, without passing through the various stages (without passing through the fifty-two stages), directly realizing Buddhahood. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records: “The Master (the Fifth Patriarch Hongren) constantly urged monks and laypeople alike simply to uphold the Diamond Sutra, and then they would see their own nature and directly realize Buddhahood.” Truly:
The unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous Dharma, in hundreds of thousands of kalpas hard to encounter,

World-Honored One! If again there are people who hear this sutra with pure faith, then the true character is born in them. You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rarest merit. World-Honored One! This true character is no character; therefore the Tathāgata names it the true character.

World-Honored One! If again there are people who hear this sutra with pure faith, then the true character is born in them. You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and rarest merit.”

—Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! If there are still other people who hear this sutra with pure faith, they at once realize the true character (the actual state of affairs in which all things in the universe are illusion). You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme merit.

[If again there are people] If there are still other people. This closely follows the passage above: I, Subhuti, have heard this sutra expounded, deeply understood its meaning and purport, and benefited beyond compare; if there are still other people who hear this sutra, . . . [Faith] The mind that gives rise to belief in the dharma heard, deeply believing without doubt. [Pure faith] Hearing this sutra and deeply believing without doubt, one thereupon sees illusion and at once detaches from it, and amid conditions and objects closely examines (not giving rise to a mind dwelling in form, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere); the clouds of delusion scatter, the light of the nature shows, and the mind attains purity. [True character] The true character is the actual state of affairs in which “all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.” In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter Two, on Buddha-Recitation, the Buddha says: “What is named the true character of all dharmas? All dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.” [Then the true character is born] That is, one realizes in person the actual state of affairs in which all things in the universe are illusion. The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “Within the true character, there truly are no bodhisattvas and no beings. Why? Bodhisattvas and beings are all illusory transformations.” In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
Volume Forty

Chapter on Kaundinya, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are false; wherever they cease, that is named the real, is named the true character, is named the dharma-realm, is named ultimate wisdom, is named the truth of the supreme meaning, is named the emptiness of the supreme meaning.” [Foremost and rarest] Most supreme; here “rare” means supreme.

The work of the Buddhadharma lies entirely in awakening—in the birth of the true character. In the Buddha Treasury Sutra the Buddha says: “The true character of all dharmas, ultimately empty and still—this is the Buddha-way.” The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “The thought before is deluded: one is an ordinary being; the thought after is awakened: one is a Buddha. The thought before clings to conditions: that is affliction; the thought after is detached from conditions: that is bodhi.” This sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain. If one sees all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathāgata.”
World-Honored One! This true character is no character; therefore the Tathāgata names it the true character.”
—Next, Subhuti says: World-Honored One! This true character is without marks (the true character is without marks); therefore the Tathāgata says it is the true character.
This is the emptiness of the supreme meaning—the emptiness of the middle-way true character that is neither empty nor existent, where even the true character is not clung to.
In the Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter One, on the True Character of All Dharmas, the Buddha says: “All dharmas are neither born nor ceasing, without marks and without doing.” This looks at all dharmas from the standpoint of substance. To one within the dream of ignorance, all dharmas have marks; but to one whose eyes are open, there is nothing at all. The Direct Explanation of the True Mind says: “It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky. Or a person without disease says: There are no sky-flowers. The sick person does not believe it. When the eye-disease is gone, the sky-flowers vanish of themselves, and only then does he believe the flowers were not there.” Beings, within the utterly still non-arising, see only arising and ceasing (marks); the Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the non-arising (no marks).
[The true character is without marks] The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

Volume Fourteen says: “If one leaves home and keeps the precepts, does not manage worldly affairs, and constantly contemplates the true character of all dharmas as without marks, then though at first one's faculties are dull, they gradually become sharp. Through various such causes and conditions, this is named the keeping of precepts giving rise to prajñā-pāramitā. Through such things, this is named the perfection of morality giving rise to the six perfections.”
[The perfection of morality] The perfection of keeping the precepts.

World-Honored One! I now hear such a sutra, and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult. But in a future age, in the last five hundred years, if there are beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such a person is foremost and rarest.

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One! I now hear such a profoundly deep sutra, and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult. But if in the fifth five hundred years after the Tathāgata's extinction and thereafter, there are beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such a person is foremost and supreme.

[In a future age, in the last five hundred years] This means the same as “after the Tathāgata's extinction, in the last five hundred years” in the sixth section: the fifth five hundred years after the Tathāgata's extinction and thereafter. [If there are beings] If there are beings. “If” is a conjunction, equivalent to “in case” or “supposing.”

Why? Such a person has no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. Why is this? The mark of a self is no mark; the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are no marks. Why? Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.
This passage of scripture clarifies why “such a person is foremost and rarest.”

Why? Such a person has no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. Why is this? The mark of a self is no mark; the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are no marks.”

—Why is such a person foremost and supreme? Because he no longer has the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life. Why has he no mark of a self, mark of a human, mark of a being, or mark of a life? Because the mark of a self (having marks) is no mark of a self (no substance), and the mark of a self is illusion; the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life (having marks) are no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life (no substance), and the mark of a human, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are illusion.

This says: because such a person believes, understands, receives, and upholds this sutra, and has put “all marks whatsoever are false and vain” into practice in his own thought, speech, and action, these illusory four marks should no longer be present.
Why? Detached from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”
—Why is such a person said to be foremost and supreme? Because, detached from all marks,
one is named a Buddha.
[One is named a Buddha] That is, one is named a Buddha. Here “a” functions like “of,” as in: “Can you serve him?”

From this we know: how does one attain Buddhahood? To be free of all marks—this is the way to Buddhahood. What is called freedom from marks is to see marks without being deluded by them, to be unmoved by circumstances; and to be unmoved by any circumstance whatever is to be a Buddha. The seventh section says: “All the worthy ones and holy ones differ only by the unconditioned Dharma.” That is to say: all the worthy ones and holy ones differ only by the degree of their freedom from marks (their being unmoved by circumstances).

[Freedom from marks] To understand that all marks are illusory, and so to be without love or hate, grasping or rejecting. [Clinging to marks] To take marks as real, and so to have love and hate, grasping and rejecting.

Freedom from all marks” has two great aspects: first, breaking the attachment to a self and cutting off ordinary sentiment; second, breaking the attachment to dharmas and doing away with saintly understanding. In the Lotus Sutra,

Chapter Two, on Skillful Means, the Buddha says: “Shariputra! Since I became a Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions, various parables and illustrations, I have widely set forth the teachings in words, and by countless skillful means have guided beings, causing them to depart from all attachments.” Departing from all attachments is departing from all marks.

The Venerable Subhuti deeply understood the purport of the meaning and realized the most supreme, foremost, and rarest of dharmas: freedom from marks (seeing marks without being deluded by them, not being turned by circumstances). Freedom from marks—this is the unconditioned Dharma. This way of practice differs from the methods of the Three Vehicles that he knew (the shravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle); it is the mind-dharma of the One Buddha Vehicle, the most direct and most perfect and sudden of dharmas, which attains Buddhahood at once without passing through the fifty-two stages.

The practice taught in this sutra is precisely the illusion-like samadhi spoken of by the Buddha in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment: “Knowing illusion, one is at once free of it, without resorting to skillful means; freed of illusion, one is at once awake, and there are no gradual stages.”

What especially calls for attention is this: in the course of departing from illusion, one must use illusion to depart from illusion, and must never, in wanting to depart, instead enter it. For example, giving without dwelling in marks is using illusion to depart from illusion, whereas giving while dwelling in marks is using illusion to enter illusion—seeking to rise, one falls instead.

The crux of departing from illusion is departing from desire, and this must be done first of all. Our Buddha taught people to leave the world, taking the practice of departing from desire as the very first. Hence it is said: “Freedom from desire and stillness is the most excellent.” (The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha)

Freedom from marks—seeing marks without being deluded by them, not being turned by circumstances—is the whole purport of this sutra. The core of practicing the Diamond Sutra is freedom from marks: knowing illusion, one is at once free of it; departing again and again, one reaches the point of nothing more to depart from, and so all illusions are removed. Once all illusions are removed and the dream of ignorance is exhausted, one is named a Buddha. In this sutra the World-Honored One again and again warns us: in the course of departing from illusion, one must certainly use illusion to extinguish illusion, and never use illusion to enter illusion.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and all beings of the final age should depart far from every illusion-like, false, and vain realm. Because of firmly holding to the mind of departure, that mind which is itself like an illusion is also to be departed from; that departure is itself an illusion, and is also to be departed from; departing from the illusion of departure is likewise to be departed from; and when one reaches the point of nothing more to depart from, all illusions are removed.”
Question: How are we to be free of all marks?

Answer: “To be free of all marks is to be named a Buddha”; the corresponding translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sutra reads: “The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are utterly freed of all notions without remainder.” Freedom from marks is therefore freedom from notions. As soon as a notion arises, see through it at once and let it go. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing illusion, one is at once free of it, without resorting to skillful means; freed of illusion, one is at once awake, and there are no gradual stages.” The Buddha Treasury Sutra says: “The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is altogether without notions and without thoughts.”
[The Buddha told Subhuti: So it is, so it is. If again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, know that such people are most rare.]
The Buddha told Subhuti: So it is, so it is!”
—The Buddha said to Subhuti: So it is! So it is!
So it is! So it is!”—with these words the World-Honored One greatly praised Subhuti's experience and understanding set forth above.
If again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, know that such people are most rare.”
—If there are yet others who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, know that such people are most rare.

[If again there are people] Here the World-Honored One, following upon Subhuti's speaking of his own faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding, and of people in the last five hundred years having faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding (being able to have faith, understanding, receiving, and upholding, they surely hear this sutra without being startled, terrified, or afraid), says: if there are yet others . . .

Why is it said that those who “hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid” are most rare? Because this sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” The worlds of all Buddhas have marks, and so the worlds of all Buddhas are all illusions. This is more astonishing by how many times than Copernicus's heliocentric theory in those days! Therefore those who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid are indeed most rare.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Birth and death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike marks of a flower in empty space.” “All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in empty space.” It also says: “Within them, the Buddha-worlds—hundreds, thousands, ten millions, billions, asaṃkhyeyas, inexpressible in number, as many as the sands of the Ganges—are like flowers in empty space, wildly arising and wildly ceasing.” In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,

Chapter Three, on Familiar Practice, the Buddha says: “Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mental consciousness; no ignorance, and no ending of ignorance, and so on up to no old age and death, and no ending of old age and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; no wisdom, and no attainment; no stream-enterer, and no fruit of stream-entry; no once-returner, and no fruit of once-returning; no non-returner, and no fruit of non-returning; no arhat, and no fruit of arhatship; no pratyekabuddha, and no way of the pratyekabuddha; no Buddha, and no way of the Buddha.”

Next the World-Honored One goes on to make clear: why is it that “if again there are people who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, know that such people are most rare”?
[Why is that? Subhuti! The first pāramitā that the Tathāgata speaks of is not the first pāramitā, and so it is called the first pāramitā.]

Why should we know that such people are most rare? Subhuti! The vajra prajñā-pāramitā (the first pāramitā) is likewise an illusion—the Tathāgata says the first pāramitā (a mark that exists), which is not the first pāramitā (its substance being nonexistent), and so it is called the first pāramitā (it is illusion).
[The first pāramitā] This is the Dharma taught in this sutra—the vajra prajñā-pāramitā, also called the mahā-pāramitā. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,

Volume Two, says: “The mahā-pāramitā is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva's prajñā-pāramitā, the honored pāramitā, the first pāramitā, the victorious pāramitā, the wondrous pāramitā, the unsurpassed pāramitā, the unequaled pāramitā, the pāramitā equal to nothing else, the pāramitā like empty space.” [Mahā] Rendered into Chinese as “great.”

In the preceding section the World-Honored One had already spoken of prajñā-pāramitā as an illusion (“The Buddha speaks of prajñā-pāramitā, which is not prajñā-pāramitā, and so is called prajñā-pāramitā”). Not only that, but even the Dharma this sutra itself teaches—the Diamond prajñā-pāramitā—is likewise an illusion.

Next the World-Honored One takes the perfection of patience as an example, showing that the six perfections are also illusions: do not cling to marks, but be free of all marks, and only then can the mind be without obstruction and pass beyond all suffering and distress.
Subhuti! The perfection of patience, which the Tathāgata says is not the perfection of patience, and so is called the perfection of patience.

The World-Honored One also said: Subhuti! The perfection of patience (present as a mark), which the Tathāgata says is not the perfection of patience (empty of self-nature), and so is called the perfection of patience (illusory). This says that the perfection of patience is an illusion, and one must not cling to the mark of the perfection of patience.

[The perfection of patience] is the perfection of patience among the six perfections (giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, prajñā). The old translation of the six perfections is the six pāramitās. “Pāramitā” means arriving at the other shore; in Chinese it is rendered “crossing over” (the same as “ferrying across”), meaning to cross over to the other shore (the shore of nirvāṇa). “Patience” ordinarily means being put to shame or insulted. In fact, in classical Chinese “patience” also carries the meaning of being thwarted and harmed. Master Xuanzang translates the six perfections as: giving, pure precepts, patient endurance, vigor, still reflection, and prajñā. This shows that patience here means peaceful endurance. Therefore, the perfection of patience is: when persons, affairs, and circumstances go against one's intent (vexing and harming), one does not give rise to anger and malice. The heart of patience can guard against the invasion of outer conditions, and is therefore likened to a robe. When the practitioner puts on the robe of patience, he is like a warrior wearing armor, protected from harm.

Therefore, the key to dealing with vexation is not to be turned by conditions but to turn them—to know that vexation is originally an illusion, to give rise to neither anger, hatred, nor rejection, and so the mind is without obstruction, passing beyond all suffering and distress, turning affliction into bodhi, gaining only the benefit and receiving no harm. Remember: Māra is born of the mind, and by the mind is also extinguished. When insulted:

Think of it as expunging karmic retribution. This retribution is self-made and self-received; one should not resent or blame others. Moreover, once it is settled it is settled, and the debt of wrong is wiped clean in a single stroke—a very good thing.

Think of it as a blessing arriving in reverse. Realize that this is a blessing coming against you, and it comes to bring your spiritual practice to completion. Mencius said: “When Heaven is about to lay a great responsibility upon a person, it will first embitter his mind and will, tax his sinews and bones, starve his body, empty his resources, and disorder his undertakings, so as to stir his mind, steady his nature, and augment what he is unable to do.” For the one cultivating the Way, everyone is bringing me to completion; all are my benefactors. Some aid me through favorable conditions, others through conditions adverse yet favorable; all are causing my spiritual work to ripen. I have not even time enough to be grateful—how could I resent? I have only benefactors, no enemies.

Look upon it as an examination question on the path of bodhi. It tests whether one's practice has real power, and through this tempering the practice advances a further storey, so liberation becomes all the more certain. The practitioner faces such an examination at all times and in all places: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” “Do not grasp at marks; abide in the unmoving thusness.”—In the midst of the illusion, did you take it for real? Did your mind stir? How the practice fares can itself be tested thus.

The practice of patience has three levels: first, endure first and then dissolve; second, endure and dissolve at once; third, not even to be aware of it. Here I will give an instance of the practice of patience: “Met with cold glares, yet as if bathed in a spring breeze.”
The Elder Master Guangqin, at

years of age, entered the rear mountain to practice austerities, without food or clothing, passing through thirteen winters and summers. Shortly after he returned to Chengtian Monastery, the incense-offering money set out in the great hall went missing. When the master of the monastery and the keeper of the hall lamp spread the news, the whole monastery was in an uproar. Before he came back, the incense money had never been lost; not long after his return, the incense money the whole monastery relied on for its livelihood vanished without a trace—and what made everyone think at once was that he sat in meditation in the great hall every night. If anyone had laid hands on it, the first to know should have been he; since he showed no reaction, who was the most likely suspect for stealing the incense money? In everyone's mind the answer went without saying. From then on, up and down the monastery, although none spoke it aloud, whenever they met Master Guangqin they greeted him with nothing but cold, hostile looks. The ancients said: “When ten thousand fingers point at a man, he dies though he is not ill.” Under the silent censure of the whole assembly, he let out not a single word of self-justification, and stirred not the least thought of discontent or resentment. So he passed more than a week, with all still glaring at him in anger, yet he remained as if bathed in a spring breeze. Only then did the master of the monastery and the keeper of the hall lamp come forward and unfold the riddle of this case. It turned out the incense money had never been lost—the two masters had only meant by this to test Master Guangqin, to see what sort of skill the thirteen years on the mountain had forged! They had not expected that he should be as if bathed in a spring breeze amid the assembly's anger. With this explanation by the master and the lamp keeper, the whole community was filled with shame—that for this week and more the object of their daily angry glare had been a man of perfect character, a cultivator wholly transcendent of the world. Besides the pang of shame and unease, they felt all the more a pang of admiration and praise. Yet Master Guangqin remained exactly as he had been, unmoved by praise or blame, by gain or loss. (See The Cloud-and-Water Record of the Elder Monk Guangqin.)
Why so? Subhuti! When in the past I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.

The World-Honored One further clarifies: Why must one realize that the perfection of patience is an illusion? Because when in the past I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, at that time I knew all this to be illusion (no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life), and so I endured peacefully without anger.

The World-Honored One is saying: When in former days I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, had I taken the perfection of patience—which is originally an illusion—to be real, then I would have had a mark of a self, a mark of a human, a mark of a being, a mark of a life, and, unable to bear the other's unreasonableness and cruelty, would have given rise to anger and hatred and failed to reach the perfection of patience.

Patience has two kinds: first, the forced endurance that takes the insult to be real; second, the realization that the insult is an illusion—awake eyes watching a dream, and so there is naturally nothing to mind. The latter is the most excellent and lofty. With no self and no human, from where does the insult come? Since the insult does not exist, what need is there to endure? This endurance that does not endure is the great patience. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp

Chapter Twenty-seven records: “Master Sengzhao (one of the four outstanding disciples of Master Kumārajīva), encountering the calamity of the ruler of Qin, on the point of execution recited this verse: The four great elements have no master of their own; the five aggregates are from the outset empty. Setting my head before the bright blade is like cutting the spring breeze (as though the spring wind passed through; “cutting the spring breeze” is an inversion, i.e., the spring breeze cuts).” The Tower Inscription of Master Hanshan at the Five-Peak of Mount Lu records: Master Hanshan, “when tortured in the imperial prison, suddenly entered meditation. The blows of the cane, the needle, and the burn were as if striking wood and stone.” The Collected Works of the Old Man Zibai records: Master Zibai, “when interrogated, though old and frail, passed through every kind of pain and torture, so that all his attendants felt their hearts sink, yet the Master was as a cloud at ease and water at rest, with not a single thing amiss.”

[King Kali] In former days, when the Buddha was practicing on the causal ground, there was a King Kali, of violent, evil, and arrogant nature. At that time the Buddha was practicing meditation outside the city. King Kali led his palace women out to wander and view the sights. The court ladies abandoned the king and came to the Buddha's place, and the Buddha expounded the Dharma for them. When the king saw this he gave rise to an evil mind and asked the Buddha: “Have you attained the fruit of the arhat?” The Buddha said: I have not. “Have you attained the fruit of the anāgāmin?” The Buddha answered: No. The king said: “Then do you, with a body still full of greed and the afflictions, recklessly gaze at women?” The Buddha said: Though I have not yet cut off the bond of greed, within my heart there is truly no attachment. The king then tested him: he cut off the Buddha's ears, yet his countenance changed not at all. The ministers remonstrated with the king, hoping to make him stop, but the king would not listen. He went further to cut off the nose (read “yì”) and the hands, yet the marks of his excellent form remained full and complete without the least change. Then a great rain of sand and stones fell from the sky. The king's heart was filled with terror, and he came to the Buddha, repentant and ashamed, begging for pity. The Buddha said: My heart has neither anger nor greed. The king said: “Great Virtue, how do you know that your heart has no anger and hatred?” The Buddha said: If I had no anger, then let this body be restored as it was. Having made this vow, his body was at once restored. The king was all the more repentant and ashamed, and so entered the gate of the Buddha. [The bond of greed] is one of the five bonds. The affliction of greed and desire binds beings to the births and deaths of the three realms, so that they cannot attain release. The five bonds are: the bond of greed, the bond of anger, the bond of pride, the bond of envy, and the bond of miserliness. “Bond” is another name for the afflictions, because the afflictions can bind and fetter beings, causing them to transmigrate in the three realms.

The World-Honored One uses his own experience to show that only by not clinging to marks can one truly endure; only by not clinging to marks can one fail to give rise to habitual reactions amid conditions. This also confirms that the absence of the four marks is the wondrous method for subduing the mind (see the third section).
The Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra
Volume Twenty-two

Chapter Sixty-eight, on the Six Perfections Absorbing One Another, says: “The Buddha said: When a bodhisattva abides in the perfection of vigor, from the first stirring of the mind of enlightenment even to the sitting at the bodhimandala, if in the midst of these a man or a non-man comes to dismember him joint by joint, the bodhisattva thinks: ‘Who is cutting me? Who is severing me? Who is robbing me?’ And again he thinks: ‘I have gained a great, good benefit. For the sake of beings I take on a body, and beings themselves come to take it.’ At that time the bodhisattva rightly recollects the true character of all dharmas, and holding this merit, shares it with beings and directs it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, not toward the ground of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. This is the bodhisattva abiding in the perfection of vigor, gaining the perfection of patience.”
[Vīrya] is translated in Chinese as “vigor,” one of the six perfections. [Kṣānti] is translated as “patience,” one of the six perfections.

Master Hanshan said: “All beings' implements of birth and death, of suffering, are all brought into being by the existence of a self; the utmost bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, are all reached by the absence of a self. Because the self opposes things, right and wrong arise; when right and wrong arise, love and hate are established; when love and hate are established, joy and anger multiply; the self-nature is befouled and the ground of the mind grows clouded; when the mind is clouded, all evils grow; when all evils grow, all suffering gathers; when all suffering gathers, birth and death lengthen! All of these come of the self—how grave it is! The harm of the self, like a strong city with mighty soldiers, is it easy to break? . . . Therefore, at the moment of a single rising thought test it with patience; at a single step and move, let patience lead; at turning and moving and adjusting the appearance, hold to patience; at joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, examine by patience. Thus the mind dares not stir at random, the body dares not act at random, affairs dare not be done at random, the feelings dare not break forth at random. Hence the old master (Laozi) said: Dare not be first in the world. To dare not—that is another name for patience. Because one dares not be first in the world, patience is the first practice in becoming a Buddha. Thus patience is great and the self is small, so the robe of patience can cover me and can also cover things; the virtue of benefiting oneself and benefiting others goes no further than this. Therefore it is said: The soft and harmonious robe of patience—this is the reason.” (From the Dream Wandering Collection
Addressed to the Meditator Fajin.)

Whether one has a reliable hold on transcending birth and death can be tested from two ends: first, the end of favorable circumstances and success; second, the end of adverse circumstances and affliction—whether in both one has detached from marks: not giving rise to a stirring thought before conditions, not chasing after conditions.
Why so? When in the past I was dismembered limb by limb, if I had had a mark of a self, a mark of a human, a mark of a being, a mark of a life, I should have given rise to anger and hatred.

Why must one be without the four marks? On that day, when I was dismembered limb by limb by King Kali, had I taken this dismembering limb by limb as real (having a mark of self, human, being, life), I would have given rise to anger and hatred.

To know illusion is at once to be free of it; to be free of illusion is at once to be awake. Since there is no self, where is the insult? Without a self, who is there to suffer the insult? This is the method of drawing away the firewood from beneath the cauldron.

The World-Honored One, when formerly dismembered limb by limb, was without the four marks because he had realized in person “all marks whatsoever are false and vain” and “knowing that all dharmas have no self, he attained the patience [of non-arising].” How does one realize this in person? Master Hanshan, in the Dream Wandering Collection

Addressed to the Attendant Qi in the Boat on the Way to Leiyang, gives a most penetrating discourse—in the midst of the dharmas of arising and ceasing, to pass through conditions and test the mind, intimately breaking it through, until one reaches the ground of no doubt and then stops. I transcribe it here:
The Buddhas and patriarchs teach people, amid birth and death, to realize at once the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas
(“The patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas,” for short the non-arising patience, means true wisdom abiding in the true character of the real, which neither arises nor ceases)

, and they always marvel that people, amid the non-arising, falsely see arising and ceasing. This speech is like telling the affairs of a dream to the people in the marketplace; those who hear it are not without being moved to open their eyes
(listeners are never untouched and stirred)

, but they have not yet realized the truth. In sum, what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what is seen. The ancients so valued realization in person because they simply wanted, amid the dharmas of birth and death, to break through intimately—there is nothing else extraordinary about it. I have seen children afraid of ghosts: whenever they walk at night, a thing seems to follow them and they are seized with terror; though the loving mother tells them kindly that there is nothing, they still will not believe, and only after they come to believe themselves without doubt do they stop. Once one reaches the ground of no doubt, even if one frightens him with a false ghost, he will but laugh and let it go.

I once traveled on the frontier, riding by night with some strong fellows. By the side of the road was a rock; all at once the horse caught sight of it and was fiercely startled, almost throwing me to the ground. Then I
(thereupon)
reined in the horse, spurred it on with all my strength, and led it round the rock several dozen times, still drawing it on to look closely
(still leading the horse to look carefully, to be clear that this was a rock and not a monster)

. After a long while, only then did I release it to run on; from that time on, the horse encountered nothing that startled it. Because of this I know that a man traveling the perilous roads of birth and death, passing through conditions and testing the mind, must do it exactly like this and only then be done
(spur the horse around the rock and make it look closely, until it is without doubt and without fear, and only then is it done)
. Therefore the Avataṃsaka uses Sudhana to represent realization
(therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra uses the boy Sudhana's fifty-three pilgrimages to show clearly how to realize in person)
, and the hundred cities he passed through and the many teachers he sought. Even when it came to the mountain of knives and the mass of fire, he also hesitated
(hesitating, wavering)
and waited for encouragement before entering. And once he entered, he indeed gained the cool and great gate of liberation
(realizing in person that the mountain of knives and mass of fire are illusions)
. Is this not what is meant by spurring the horse around the rock and making it look closely?
(Is it not exactly making him “spur the horse around the rock and look closely,” so that he intimately breaks through?)
Viewed in this way, the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other excellence—they are only able to look closely upon the marks of the world
(variant: jian)
(the world)

. Is it not birth and death and misfortune that can be frightened by men? The Buddhas and patriarchs want people to realize the non-arising patience in the midst of them, and moreover plainly say that in the midst of the non-arising they falsely see arising and ceasing
(the Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the non-arising; sentient beings, within the still non-arising, falsely see arising and ceasing)
. Alas! What can this really mean?
(if it were not)
If it were not that, having looked closely, one arrives of oneself at the ground of no doubt, I think that even the gracious Lord's kind admonition would hardly
(perhaps) escape being startled and frightened as well.
I
(I, in these days)
because of spreading the Dharma suffered calamity, offending the holy wrath
(the Master, for spreading the Dharma, was slandered; the emperor's wrath was stirred; he was arrested and thrown into prison, tortured under severe interrogation, his life and death uncertain)
, like a peal of thunder in broad daylight, so that those who heard it stopped up their ears. From my arrest until my release
(banished and sent away from the capital)

, more than two hundred days, I endured every kind of bitter affair beyond words. From beginning to end, as I looked within myself, that one thought of joy in no way diminished from my usual days; those who saw it were all astonished and called it extraordinary. Yet birth and death and misfortune—others were indeed alarmed for me; and when they saw that my joyful thought did not diminish, they were alarmed again. I am not alarmed at what alarms them, and they are alarmed at what does not alarm me—in this there may be a Way!

Attendant Qi, undeterred by a journey of three thousand li, came to the difficulty and questioned me in the dark prison. Soon, by the holy grace, I was exiled to the land of Lingnan, and Qi accompanied me on the boat; I write this to bid farewell. Alas! The perilous road of birth and death is precisely what men fear, and is this not—to hear that my joy did not diminish—like listening to the affairs of a dream?

(At the moment of life and death—this is precisely what men are frightened by; and to hear that my joyful thought did not diminish in the least, is it not just like listening to a man speak of the affairs of a dream?)
Hereafter I shall test you in the field of still extinction; do not take today's words as dream-speech

(in days to come, when you realize the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (in the field of still extinction), you will of yourself verify that what I say is true. [The field of still extinction] is the realm of the realization of the non-arising patience—when delusion is exhausted and the true is revealed, still extinction is present)
, do not take today's words as dream-speech
(From the Dream Wandering Collection
Addressed to the Attendant Qi on the Boat to Leiyang.)

Subhuti! Again I recall that in the past, over five hundred lives, I practiced as the ascetic of patience. In those lives, I had no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.

The World-Honored One continued: Subhuti! Again I recall that in the past I practiced as the ascetic of patience for five hundred lives. In those five hundred lives, I had no mark of a self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life.

[The ascetic of patience] Śākyamuni Buddha, on the causal ground, was the ascetic of patience, cultivating the practice of patience. [In those lives] In those five hundred lives. “Those” means that; “lives” refers to the “five hundred lives” of the preceding sentence. The Tang
Yijing translation reads: “Again I recall that in the past, over five hundred lives, I was an ascetic of patience. At that time I had no such thoughts as these.”

Master Yongjia's Song of Certifying the Way says: “My teacher (Śākyamuni Buddha) was allowed to see Dīpaṃkara Buddha because for many kalpas he had been an ascetic of patience.” This says that the World-Honored One, when practicing on the causal ground, was able to see Dīpaṃkara Buddha and receive the prophecy because for many kalpas he had been an ascetic of patience. From this we see that the single practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice in becoming a Buddha.

Those who study the Diamond Sutra all share one question: how can one be free of the four marks? Where does one begin? The starting point of freeing oneself from the four marks is to cultivate the perfection of patience: whatever is done, one should bear it. At all times and everywhere, bear it, test it, and keep on. At first the self is great and the patience small; then the patience is great and the self small; by vigorous, unflagging effort, persevering, one reaches the absence of the mark of a self. Once the mark of self is extinguished, the other three marks are gone with it. The four marks are illusion, and the perfection of patience is also illusion; yet to use illusion to extinguish illusion, one is only the farther from illusion.

In Master Daozheng's book The Elder Master Guangqin's Practice Examinations, it is written: “On the road of practice there are examinations every day, examinations at all times. In the selection-ground of the Buddha, each person hands in his own report card.” “We may well read the Diamond Sutra early in the morning—‘all marks whatsoever are false and vain,’ ‘do not grasp at marks, abide in the unmoving thusness’—and the scripture is read this way. But suppose someone curses us very fiercely, and the things he curses us with are all unfounded; then we set the Diamond Sutra aside for the moment, take the situation as real, and begin to grieve and to feel wronged. We do not remember in the least: ‘all marks whatsoever are false and vain.’ We begin to run round and round chasing the false marks—not merely grasping at marks, but moreover stirring the mind, and not merely stirring the mind but grieving greatly, without the slightest bit of ‘abiding in the unmoving thusness.’ So having read the scriptures for decades, the moment an applied problem is set, we die on the spot. If others say that our study of Buddhism is all a deception, that we never truly practiced, we hear it and are quite unconvinced. But at the first examination we betray ourselves and show that what the Buddha taught us we have in truth not learned at all. Whatever perfection of patience—set it aside for now, argue a little first, have a good cry first.”
Therefore, Subhuti! The bodhisattva should be free of all marks and raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Subhuti! The bodhisattva should be free of all marks and raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

What was said above—that the first perfection is illusion and the perfection of patience is illusion—means one should cultivate while detached from marks. Now it goes a step further: even at the moment of raising the mind, one should raise it while detached from marks. From this we know that “free of all marks” runs through the whole bodhi path from beginning to end.

[Therefore] A word that carries the previous passage and opens the next. [Free of all marks] Free of the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, the mark of a life, as well as the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas. [Raise the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] Raise the great mind of becoming a Buddha and liberating beings.

One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form; one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling.

One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind without love or hate, without grasping or rejecting. If the mind has a dwelling and attachment, this dwelling and attachment is itself an error.

[If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling] If the mind has a dwelling and attachment, this dwelling and attachment is not (that is, is not a true dwelling). Why? Because if the mind dwells, it is turned by conditions—this is delusion. “If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling” returns again to the question Subhuti asked at the very beginning of this sutra: “How should the mind be abided?” So the answer to “How should the mind be abided?” is: do not abide in marks.

The Collected Annotations on the Diamond Sutra says: “Master Huangbo said: . . . ‘Free of all marks, sentient beings and all Buddhas have no further difference; if only one can be without mind, that is the ultimate.’ ‘If the mind dwells, that dwelling is not a true dwelling’ means the mind of suchness is originally without dwelling. If one does not dwell in the marks of dharmas, one accords with the Way. If one dwells in dharmas, one goes against the right teaching; going against the right teaching, that dwelling is not a true dwelling.”

How does one not dwell in marks? The Sixth Patriarch, in the Platform Sutra, has a passage of extraordinary brilliance: “What is called thoughtlessness? If, on seeing all dharmas, the mind is not stained or attached (without love or hate, grasping or rejecting), that is thoughtlessness. Functioning, it reaches everywhere, yet dwells not anywhere. Only purify the original mind (weakening and weakening the mind of love and hate, grasping and rejecting), so that the six consciousnesses go out through the six gates and, amid the six dusts, are neither stained nor mixed; coming and going freely, in general use without obstruction—this is the prajñā samādhi, self-mastery and liberation, and is called the practice of thoughtlessness. . . . Good and wise friends! One who awakens to the method of thoughtlessness penetrates the ten thousand dharmas; one who awakens to the method of thoughtlessness sees the realm of all Buddhas; one who awakens to the method of thoughtlessness reaches the stage of the Buddha.”

‘so that the six consciousnesses go out through the six gates and, amid the six dusts, are neither stained nor mixed; coming and going freely, in general use without obstruction’ and ‘functioning, it reaches everywhere, yet dwells not anywhere’—this is ‘give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.’

Here the World-Honored One again speaks of the work of guarding and spontaneous flowing: that is, guarding the mind so it does not run after conditions, and letting the mind flow freely so it does not run after conditions. The initial stage is guarding the mind (“one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas”); when the guarding is mature, one sets aside the guarding and does the work of spontaneous flowing, letting the mind flow freely. So the mind, following the desires, never oversteps the rule (“one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”). Take the cure of addiction as a metaphor: the first stage is the guarding stage—to realize deeply the harm of drugs and to keep strictly separated from them; when this is mature, it becomes the stage of spontaneous flowing—though the drug lies at one's side within easy reach, one still will not be tempted.

The addiction of sentient beings since the beginning-less kalpa is to “give rise to a mind toward conditions.” Therefore, in the guarding stage, one should still all the outer conditions and nurture the embryo of the sage. When the guarding is ripe, one should blend one's light with the dust, passing through conditions and testing the mind, realizing the wisdom of non-discrimination, so as to be like one who “passes through a garden of ten thousand blossoms without a single leaf clinging to his body.” A verse says: “Set loose the water-buffalo of Weishan; no one holds the rope by its nose. On the green willows and fragrant grass of the spring breeze bank, at ease it lies up and lies down—free.”

[Blend one's light with the dust] This means to merge with the worldly and not to set oneself apart, yet not to be stained by the evil and turbid. But it must be specially pointed out that the stage of “spontaneous flowing” begins only after the work of “guarding” is mature. [The wisdom of non-discrimination] Also called the mind of non-discrimination; when the bodhisattva, upon the first ground, enters the stage of seeing the Way, he leaves behind all discriminative thinking of feelings—the formless true wisdom. [The stage of seeing the Way] When the bodhisattva first attains the first ground, penetrating a little of the principle of the two non-selves, experiencing suchness, and for the first time seeing the middle Way, it is therefore called the stage of seeing the Way. [The two non-selves] The non-self of persons and the non-self of dharmas. The non-self of persons is realizing that the five aggregates are a false union with no real substance; the non-self of dharmas is realizing that all dharmas are like illusions, with no real substance.
Therefore, the Buddha said, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form when practicing giving. Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way.

Therefore, the Buddha said, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in the six dusts when giving (here form represents the six dusts). Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way.

[The bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form when giving] Using the dust of form to represent the six dusts (citing form, and likewise sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas, and all dharmas), this means the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas when giving—that is, the bodhisattva should give while not dwelling in marks.

Master Xuanzang's Tang translation reads: “Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all bodhisattvas should practice giving without dwelling, and should not practice giving while dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.” [For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way] Example surpasses words; a bodhisattva who truly gives for the benefit of all beings should be free of marks. Moreover, not to give rise to a mind dwelling in form, not to give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, and to give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere—such a Dharma-giving brings beings the greatest and most fundamental benefit. Therefore, in the final section the World-Honored One says: “Subhuti! If a person gives away the seven treasures filling an immeasurable, countless number of worlds; and if a good man or good woman who has raised the bodhi mind holds to this sutra, even a four-line verse, and receives, holds, reads, recites, and expounds it for others, his merit surpasses that. How does one expound it for others? (How does one expound it for others?) Not grasping at marks, abiding in the unmoving thusness.” The Buddha's Forty-Two Chapter Scripture says: “To feed a thousand billion Buddhas of the three times is not so good as feeding one who is without thought, without dwelling, without practice, and without realization.” (“Without thought and without dwelling” is the Sixth Patriarch's teaching in the preceding note; “without practice and without realization” means not producing the thought ‘I am practicing, I have realized.’ This is the one who does not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, and raises a mind that dwells nowhere.)
The Tathāgata says that all marks are not marks. Again he says that all beings are not beings.
The Tathāgata says that all marks (present as marks) are not marks (empty of self-nature). Again he says that all beings (present as marks) are not beings (empty of self-nature).

[All marks are not marks] All marks are illusions. [All beings are not beings] All beings are illusions. This sutra says: “All marks whatsoever are false and vain.” The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “In the real character, there are truly no bodhisattvas and no beings. Why? Boddhisattvas and beings are all illusory transformations.”

Closely following the words above—“Therefore, the Buddha said, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in form when giving. Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all beings, the bodhisattva should give in this way”—the World-Honored One further clarifies that the marks in which one dwells and the beings one benefits are all illusions, saying: “

The Tathāgata says that all marks are not marks. Again he says that all beings are not beings.” This says: all marks and all beings are illusions. This reveals the greatest mystery: the whole universe is an illusion, a great dream! Truly hard to believe. So in what follows the World-Honored One says with great gravity: “Subhuti! The Tathāgata is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker of suchness, the speaker of non-deception, the speaker of non-difference.” In order to teach us beings, the World-Honored One truly poured out his heart and blood!

Subhuti! The Tathāgata is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker of suchness, the speaker of non-deception, the speaker of non-difference. Subhuti! The Dharma the Tathāgata has attained—this Dharma is neither real nor empty.

Subhuti! The Tathāgata is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker of suchness, the speaker of non-deception, the speaker of non-difference. Subhuti! The Dharma of the Way that the Tathāgata has attained is neither really existing nor annihilated, but is an illusion.

[Speaker of truth] “True” means not false. [Speaker of reality] “Real” means not empty. [Speaker of suchness] Words that accord with the true character of things. [Speaker of non-deception] Not words of deceit. [Speaker of non-difference] A thousand words and ten thousand words, always one and the same, and in complete accord with all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three times. [This Dharma is neither real nor empty] The Dharma the Tathāgata has attained is neither really existing nor annihilated, but is an illusion. “Dharma” here refers to the Dharma of the Way, that is, the theory, the realm, and the fruit-ground of cultivating the Way. In the Great Prajñā-Pāramitā Sūtra

Chapter Three, on Familiar Practice, the Buddha says: “There is no Buddha and no Buddha Way.” In the Complete Enlightenment Sutra, the Buddha says: “Good men! These bodhisattvas and the beings of the last age who, practicing this mind, attain success: in this there is no practice and also no attainment (making clear that practice and attainment are both illusion). The perfect enlightenment universally illumines, still and extinction are non-dual; amid it, the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands, ayutas, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are like flowers in the sky, rising and fading in confusion. Not identical, not separate; without bondage, without release. Then one knows that beings have from the outset been Buddha, and birth and death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night.”

Subhuti! If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing. If the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, illumined by the light of the sun, seeing all the various colors.

‘the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving’—this is a conditioned dharma; ‘the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving’—this is the unconditioned dharma.” Compare this with the passage in the fourth section, “the sublime practice of non-dwelling”: “The bodhisattva, with respect to dharmas, should dwell nowhere and practice giving”—and the understanding is the deeper.
Subhuti! If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man who enters the darkness and sees nothing”

—the Buddha tells Subhuti: Subhuti! If the bodhisattva's mind dwells in dharmas, thinking that there are merit, virtue, and fruit-ground to be obtained, and so practices giving, then it is like a man in the darkness who cannot see the direction or the road.
[The mind dwelling in dharmas] Clinging to the mark of dharmas, harboring the mind that there are realms, merits, and fruit-stages to be obtained. [Darkness] Same as “gloom.”

Cultivation is detachment from marks; if the mind dwells in dharmas, that is clinging to marks, and one goes south while driving north. It is like rowing a boat across a lake on a pitch-black night, wanting to reach the far shore: on and on one rows, and the bow has already turned away from the destination without one even knowing it. Giving while dwelling in dharmas may win the praise of others, and one may feel quite good about it; but if love and hate, grasping and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion, and pride—this root of birth and death—do not decrease but increase, then one has entered a wrong path and will surely stir up a host of demonic obstructions: seeking to rise, one falls instead. Moreover, giving while clinging to marks is merit-with-outflows rather than virtue, and though one may enjoy blessings in the next life because of it, by doing evil in reliance on those blessings, in the life after that one falls into evil paths. Hence the Song of Certifying the Way says: “Giving while clinging to marks brings heavenly blessings, like shooting an arrow straight into the sky; when its force is spent, the arrow falls back down, bringing a next life full of disappointment.”

The “dharmas” here, as in the preceding sentence, also mean the dharma of the Way, that is, the theory, method, realm, and fruit-stage of cultivating the Way. The passage above said not to give while dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; here it says one should also not give while dwelling in the mark of dharmas (merit-with-outflows, virtue, fruit-stage). Giving is not to inflate the self but to dissolve the self.
If the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes, illumined by the light of the sun, seeing all the various colors”

—if the bodhisattva's mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving, it is like a man with eyes whose light of wisdom shines brightly, so that the direction and the road are seen perfectly clearly.

[The mind does not dwell in dharmas and so practices giving] To practice giving without seeking and without clinging (the three wheels are empty). “The mind does not dwell in dharmas” is not clinging to the mark of dharmas. [Seeing all the various colors] The “colors” here are the dust of form, meaning all visible realms and objects.

Subhuti! In future ages, if good men and good women can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by Buddha-wisdom, will know such people fully and see such people fully, and they will all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.

Above it was said that the dharma the Tathāgata obtained within this great dream is also illusion. That being so, the bodhisattva's mind should not dwell in the mark of dharmas. But the World-Honored One feared that deluded people might thereby fall into the view of annihilation and dwell in the mark of non-dharmas, and so he added with care: “Subhuti! In future ages, if good men and good women can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathāgata, by Buddha-wisdom, will know such people fully and see such people fully, and they will all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.”

blocks.text: Chapter Fifteen: The Merit of Upholding the Sutra

inline.s: The World-Honored One teaches that this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit.

Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the first portion of the day, and again in the middle portion of the day give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the latter portion of the day also give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus giving their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if again someone hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that person's merit surpasses the former—how much more so one who writes it out, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others.

Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the morning, and again at noon give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the evening again give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus three times a day giving their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if another person hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, the merit he obtains surpasses the former—how much more so if he also writes out the Diamond Sutra, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others: the merit he obtains surpasses the former by a number beyond reckoning!

[First portion of the day] Ancient India divided a day and night into six portions, each portion equal to four hours today. The daytime portions are the first portion of the day, the middle portion of the day, and the latter portion of the day; the nighttime portions are the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. [Kalpa] The extremely long time through which a world passes in formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness is called a kalpa.

Subhuti! In brief, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. The Tathāgata speaks it for those who have aroused the Mahāyāna mind, and speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind.

Subhuti! In brief, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. This is what the Tathāgata speaks for those who have aroused the mind to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna Buddhadharma, and for those who have aroused the mind to receive and uphold the supreme vehicle Buddhadharma.
Here the World-Honored One clearly points out the ones for whom this sutra is intended.

[Mahāyāna] The bodhisattva's dharma-gate, whose aim is to save the world and benefit others, and whose highest fruit is the Buddha-fruit. The Mahāyāna, from an ordinary being's cultivation to Buddhahood, must pass through fifty-two stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of abiding, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. [Supreme vehicle] The highest and unsurpassed teaching, that is, the perfect and sudden teaching, also called the One Buddha Vehicle or the One Vehicle. [Speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind] Speaks it for those who have aroused the mind to receive and uphold the supreme vehicle Buddhadharma.

If someone can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and widely explain it for others, the Tathāgata knows such people fully and sees such people fully, and they all accomplish immeasurable, inexpressible, boundless, inconceivable merit. Such people bear the Tathāgata's anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If someone can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and widely explain it for others, the Tathāgata knows these people fully and foresees these people fully, and they all accomplish immeasurable, inexpressible, boundless, inconceivable merit. Such people are taking up the family inheritance of the Tathāgata's “unsurpassed perfect enlightenment”; they are the Buddha's dharma-heirs.

This sutra is the road to Buddhahood; the cultivator who walks along the road has true benefit and inconceivable merit. The point on which receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting come to rest is this: deeply believing without doubt, and practicing as taught.

Why? Subhuti! Those who delight in the small dharma, clinging to the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life, cannot hear, accept, read, or recite this sutra, nor explain it for others.

Why is it that “such people bear the Tathāgata's anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”? Because those who delight in the small vehicle's Buddhadharma cling to the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life, and so toward this sutra (the Diamond Sutra) they cannot hear, accept, read, or recite it, nor explain it for others; they cannot take up the family inheritance of the Tathāgata's “unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”
From this we know that not clinging to the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life is the key to receiving and upholding the Diamond Sutra.

[Small dharma] The dharma of the small vehicle. The Lotus Sutra says: “Those of dull faculties delight in the small dharma.” “People of dull faculties and small wisdom, who cling to marks and are proud and arrogant, cannot believe this dharma.” (“This dharma” means the One Vehicle Buddhadharma.) [View of a life] That is, the view of a life span. The Buddha Treasury Sutra says: “The Buddha, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does not teach the dharma for people of wrong views and evil ways, nor for those who hold the view of a self, the view of a human, the view of a being, and the view of a life span.” [View of a self] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as a self. [View of a human] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates of others as another. [View of a being] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates of beings as beings. [View of a life] Falsely clinging to the life span of the form body as one's own life span.

The Complete Enlightenment Sutra says: “What is ignorance? Good man! All beings, from beginningless time, have various inversions, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the conditioned shadows of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In the sky there truly are no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them, and because of this false clinging he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this emptiness but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he turns through birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.” [The conditioned shadows of the six dusts] The images that arise in dependence on the six dusts, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six faculties meet the six dusts.

Subhuti! Wherever this sutra may be, all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world should make offerings to it. You should know that such a place is a stupa. All should revere it, bow, and circumambulate it, and scatter flowers and incense there.

Subhuti! Wherever this sutra may be, all the heavenly beings, humans, and asuras of every world should come to make offerings. You should know that such a place (where the Diamond Sutra is) is a stupa and temple of the Buddha. All should revere it, bow, and walk in circumambulation, and scatter various flowers and incense around it.

[Bowing and circumambulating] Bowing and walking in circumambulation (to the right). [Flowers and incense] Flowers and incense. “Flowers” is the same as blossoms, representing the cultivation of the cause; incense represents the true incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. There are rubbed incense, powdered incense, and pellet incense, and so on. “Pellet incense” is made by mixing various incenses into pellets. [The true incense of precepts, concentration, and wisdom] When one's own mind has no wrong, no evil, no jealousy, no greed or anger, no robbery or harm—this is called the incense of precepts. When one sees all good and evil conditions and marks and one's own mind is not disturbed—this is called the incense of concentration. When one's own mind is without obstruction, constantly contemplates the self-nature with wisdom, does not create any evil, and though cultivating all good, does not cling in mind; honoring those above and remembering those below, and taking pity on and succoring the orphaned and poor—this is called the incense of wisdom.
The World-Honored One teaches the immense power of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra: purifying karmic obstructions and realizing the sage-fruit.

Furthermore, Subhuti! If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because of evil karma from former lives that should have led them to fall into evil paths. Because in this present life they are despised by others, their evil karma from former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Not only that, Subhuti! If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because the evil karma created in the past (including this life before receiving and reciting this sutra, and in former lives) would by rights have led them, after death, to fall at once into evil paths. Now, because they receive, uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra, though in this life they are despised by others, the evil karma created in the past is thereby extinguished, and they shall realize the Buddha-fruit.

This teaches that receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra turns heavy karma into light retribution: the heavy karma is falling into evil paths after death, and the light retribution is being despised by others in this life; and the merit obtained is immense:
they shall realize the Buddha-fruit
[They shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] They shall realize the Buddha-fruit.

On the bodhi path, obstructions caused by past evil karma are everywhere, and so it is of the utmost importance for cultivators to repent of karmic obstructions. Yet some karma admits of repentance and some does not. If the offense is extremely heavy and has become fixed karma, repentance is especially difficult. In the scripture, “evil paths” shows that this is heavy karma, and “should have led them to fall” shows that it is fixed karma. Good men and good women who have heavy karma that has become fixed karma, now receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra, are merely despised by others (heavy karma turned into light retribution, fixed karma already transformed), and they will certainly realize the Buddha-fruit. This teaches the immense power of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra: purifying karmic obstructions and realizing the sage-fruit.
From this passage we can also see that those for whom the Diamond Sutra is intended further include good men and good women who, because of evil karma from former lives, should fall into evil paths.

For whom, after all, was the Diamond Sutra spoken? This is an extremely important question. In “Chapter Two, on Good Manifestation's Request,” we see that this sutra was spoken by the World-Honored One in response to the Elder Subhuti's request, for good men and good women who have just aroused the great mind. Moreover, in “Chapter Six, on Right Faith and Rarity,” it says: “After the Tathāgata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit; toward these chapters and verses they can give rise to faith, taking them as true.” In “Chapter Fifteen, on the Merit of Upholding the Sutra,” it says: this is what the Tathāgata speaks for those who have aroused the mind to study the Mahāyāna, and speaks for those who have aroused the mind to study the supreme vehicle. (Scripture: “The Tathāgata speaks it for those who have aroused the Mahāyāna mind, and speaks it for those who have aroused the supreme vehicle mind.”) Here the World-Honored One also says: good men and good women who, because of past evil karma, should fall into evil paths, can also receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, “and because in this present life they are despised by others, their evil karma from former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Therefore we know that the Diamond Sutra is spoken for good men and good women who have just aroused the great mind and for beings above them. The basic condition for receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra is this: keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. Even those good men and good women who, because of past evil karma, should fall into evil paths can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and thereby realize the Buddha-fruit.

Subhuti! I recall that in past ages, countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and served and made offerings to them all, without passing by a single one. If again someone, in a later age of decline, can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—mine does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.

Subhuti! Thinking back over countless kalpas past, before I met Dipankara Buddha I encountered eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and I made offerings to and served them all, without passing by a single one. If someone in a later age of decline can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—my merit does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction of the immense number that reckoning and simile cannot describe.
[Asaṃkhyeya] Rendered in Chinese as “countless,” meaning so many that no number can calculate them. [Nayuta] A numeral, equal to the hundred million of today.

This passage shows that the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra exceeds the merit of making offerings to Buddhas by far, far more. This tells us that even the merit of making offerings to Buddhas is hard to compare with the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra, how much less other merits.

Subhuti! If good men and good women, in a later age of decline, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and I were to set forth fully the merit they obtain, some who heard it would become mad and confused in mind, doubting and disbelieving. Subhuti! You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic reward is also inconceivable.

The World-Honored One said to Subhuti: Subhuti! If good men and good women, in the future age of the Dharma's decline, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and I were to set forth fully the merit they obtain, some who heard it would become deranged and confused in mind, doubting and disbelieving, and even give rise to slander and so create great evil karma; and so I truly have not yet set forth fully the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra! Subhuti! You should know that the grandeur and depth of the meaning of this sutra cannot be imagined by the mind, nor expressed or discussed in words, and that the immensity of the karmic reward of receiving and upholding this sutra likewise cannot be imagined by the mind, nor expressed or discussed in words.

[If I were to set forth fully] If I were to set forth all of it. [Doubting fox] Extremely doubtful. The fox is by nature full of doubt, and so the fox is used as a simile. [Inconceivable] That which cannot be thought or imagined by the mind, nor expressed or discussed in words.

Above, the World-Honored One said that he had not yet set forth fully the merit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra! Then how much merit and blessing has the World-Honored One set forth in the Diamond Sutra? The World-Honored One explains by similes:
1. Compared with giving the seven treasures

Subhuti! What do you think: if a person filled a three-thousand-great-thousand world with the seven treasures and gave them away, . . . and if again someone, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and expounds it for others, his merit surpasses the former.”
(Chapter Eight, on the Birth of All in Accord with the Dharma)

“Subhuti! Suppose all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, and as many Ganges Rivers as those grains of sand: what do you think, are the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers not many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Even the Ganges Rivers alone are countless in number, how much more their grains of sand. Subhuti! I now tell you in truth.
