If there were good men and good women who filled with the seven treasures as many three-thousand-great-thousand worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, and gave them away, would the merit they obtain be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: If good men and good women, within this sutra, receive and uphold even a four-line verse and expound it for others, this merit surpasses the former merit.”
(Chapter Eleven, on the Merit of the Unconditioned Being Supreme)

“Subhuti! If in a three-thousand-great-thousand world, a person took all the kings of Mount Sumeru and heaps of seven treasures such as these and gave them away; and if a person received, upheld, read, and recited even a four-line verse of this Prajñā-Pāramitā Sutra and expounded it for others, the former merit does not come to one hundredth of this, nor to one hundred thousand ten-thousand millionth of this, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.”
(Chapter Twenty-four, on Merit and Wisdom Being Beyond Compare)

“Subhuti! If a person filled measureless asaṃkhyeya worlds with the seven treasures and gave them away; and if good men and good women who have aroused the bodhi mind held to this sutra, even a four-line verse, received, upheld, read, and recited it, and expounded it for others, their merit surpasses the former.”
(Chapter Thirty-two, on Response-Bodies Being Not True)
2. Compared with making offerings to Buddhas

“Subhuti! I recall that in past ages, countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before Dipankara Buddha, I met eight hundred forty million billion nayuta Buddhas, and served and made offerings to them all, without passing by a single one; if again someone, in a later age of decline, can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains—compared with the merit of my offerings to all those Buddhas—does not come to one hundredth of his, nor to one thousand ten-thousand millionth of his, indeed not to any fraction expressible by reckoning or simile.”
(Chapter Sixteen, on Purifying Karmic Obstructions)
3. Compared with giving one's body and life

“Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies and lives as many times as the sands of the Ganges; and if again someone, within this sutra, receives and upholds even a four-line verse and expounds it for others, the latter's merit is far greater.”
(Chapter Thirteen, on Receiving and Upholding in Accord with the Dharma)

“Subhuti! If good men and good women give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges in the first portion of the day, and again in the middle portion of the day give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and in the latter portion of the day also give in charity their bodies as many times as the sands of the Ganges, thus giving their bodies for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; and if again someone hears this sutra and has faith without opposition, that person's merit surpasses the former—how much more so one who writes it out, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and explains it for others.”
(Chapter Fifteen, on the Merit of Upholding the Sutra)
Not only that: the Diamond Sutra can also extinguish karmic obstructions. In this section the World-Honored One says:

“If good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra and are despised by others, this is because of evil karma from former lives that should have led them to fall into evil paths. Because in this present life they are despised by others, their evil karma from former lives is thereby extinguished, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

This says: receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra can extinguish even karma that should lead to the evil paths, and one shall realize the Buddha-fruit; then the lighter karma that obstructs our practice and our daily life can certainly be extinguished as well. The power and benefit of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the Diamond Sutra are truly immense beyond words!

Therefore, to receive, uphold, read, and recite the Diamond Sutra and expound it for others is not only to cultivate wisdom but also to cultivate merit and extinguish karmic obstructions—it is the double cultivation of merit and wisdom!
The first half of this sutra ends here.
The second half of this sutra begins with this section.

No-self is the center of this sutra: breaking the two selves—the self of persons (clinging to a self) and the self of dharmas (clinging to dharmas). The first half of this sutra breaks the self of persons, and the second half breaks the self of dharmas. The scripture of this section says: “in truth there is no dharma by which one arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” “in truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” “in truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva”; hence this section is titled “Ultimate No-Self.”
Then Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

At that time Subhuti again respectfully asked the Buddha: World-Honored One! Good men and good women who have aroused the great mind of becoming a Buddha and liberating beings—how should they abide and uphold it? How should they subdue their minds?

By the end of the preceding chapter, the questions seem already to have been answered, the sutra's name and the merit of receiving, upholding, and transmitting it have been given, and generally speaking the scripture should end here. But what the World-Honored One teaches is the great dharma of becoming a Buddha, of the utmost importance; and though the Elder Subhuti deeply understood its meaning and purport (Chapter Fourteen: “Then, when Subhuti had heard this sutra expounded, he understood its meaning and purport deeply, and with tears of grief and joy he wept.”) and could believe, understand, receive, and uphold it (Chapter Fourteen: “World-Honored One! I now hear such a sutra, and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult”), yet considering that this teaching's meaning and purport are profound and wondrous (in Chapter Fourteen Subhuti said to the Buddha: “Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Buddha has expounded a sutra so profoundly deep. From of old, though I have obtained the wisdom-eye, I had never heard such a sutra”), he hoped the World-Honored One would further clarify: how, through this sutra, does one ultimately reach the other shore? And so he again asked the same questions (how should they abide? how should they subdue their minds?), requesting the World-Honored One's teaching.

The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus give rise to the mind: I should liberate all beings, and when all beings have been liberated, not one being has in fact been liberated.

The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who have aroused the great mind of becoming a Buddha and liberating beings should thus give rise to the mind: I should liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood, and yet when all beings have thus been liberated and brought to Buddhahood, in truth there is no such affair as beings being liberated and attaining Buddhahood.

Cultivation is the cultivation of the mind, which is to say, how one should give rise to the mind. The essence of the two questions “How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” is: how should a cultivator give rise to the mind? Therefore the World-Honored One here uses “should thus give rise to the mind” to answer both questions at once: to vow to liberate all beings while not dwelling in dharmas—that is, even if one liberates all beings and brings them to Buddhahood, one does not cling to the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, nor to the mark of dharmas, nor to the mark of non-dharmas.

Thus should one abide and uphold it; thus should one subdue one's mind: even if one liberates all beings and brings them to Buddhahood, one does not cling to marks in the slightest (“and not one being has in fact been liberated”), how much less in other matters.
This passage of teaching has several layers of meaning:

First, since one is to liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood, one will no longer stand opposed to beings. One will not harm them, will not envy them, will not despise them, will not contend with them for fame and profit. When beings intrude upon one, or even harm one, one will not give rise to anger. In liberating all beings, this stubborn “I” dissolves, and afflictions are naturally subdued.

Second, to liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood is by no means a matter of one lifetime (to the end of this present life); as long as there remains a single moment within the dream of ignorance, one must do one's utmost, and so one naturally abides and upholds it.

Third, to liberate all beings and bring them to Buddhahood is an affair within the dream of ignorance, and of course not one being has in fact been liberated. Yet to be able to give rise to such a mind depends on one's skill in detachment from marks. If one's skill in detachment from marks has reached the point that “when all beings have been liberated, not one being has in fact been liberated,” what need one fear that the work of the Way will not be accomplished? As the saying goes: since one is already in Hanyuan Hall, why ask where Chang'an is.

[Since one is already in Hanyuan Hall, why ask where Chang'an is] Hanyuan Hall was the name of a palace of the Tang dynasty, famous because of the “Rhapsody on Hanyuan Hall” written by Li Hua of the Tang. Chang'an was the capital of the Tang; to be in Hanyuan Hall is naturally to be within the capital.

Why? Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, he is not a bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which one arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva falsely clings to all dharmas as truly existent (having the mark of a self, the mark of a human, the mark of a being, the mark of a life), he is not a bodhisattva. (This sentence repeats the teaching of the third section.) Why is this said? Because even the very matter of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself illusion. (The “dharma” of “in truth there is no dharma” here means the dharma of things and phenomena.)
Question: Why is it said that the very matter of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself illusion?

Answer: Because the “I” that arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is illusion, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is also illusion (see the seventh section: “There is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”).

The question Subhuti raised was: “Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” The World-Honored One answered in the passage above. Going further, the very matter of arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is itself illusion.

Subhuti! What do you think? At the place of Dipankara Buddha, did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning the Buddha has spoken, at the place of Dipankara Buddha the Buddha had no dharma by which to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti! What do you think, was there at the place of Dipankara Buddha such a thing as the Tathāgata attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning the Buddha has spoken, at the place of Dipankara Buddha the Buddha had no such thing as attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Here it is taught that the matter of becoming a Buddha is not existent but is illusion. Because Subhuti himself had not yet had the experience of “attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” he answered on the basis of the Buddha's teaching.

[At the place of Dipankara Buddha the Buddha had no dharma by which to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] The Buddha, on the causal ground, though ascending to the Buddha-way, in truth accomplished nothing: it was accomplishing by accomplishing nothing.

Compare “Chapter Ten, on Adorning the Pure Land”: “The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? In former days, at the place of Dipankara Buddha, did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma? No, World-Honored One! At the place of Dipankara Buddha the Tathāgata in truth obtained no dharma.”

The Tathāgata liberates beings, yet in truth none are liberated; though in truth none are liberated, it is liberating by liberating none. The Tathāgata becomes a Buddha, yet in truth nothing is accomplished; though in truth nothing is accomplished, it is accomplishing by accomplishing nothing.

The two passages above say: one does not see (does not form the thought) that there are beings to be liberated, nor does one see (does not form the thought) that there is a Buddha to be accomplished, because liberating beings and becoming a Buddha are both affairs within the dream of ignorance: using illusion to transcend illusion, one must not cling to them as real.

The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Śākyamuni. But because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Śākyamuni.
The Buddha said: So it is, so it is.”
—The World-Honored One greatly affirmed and praised Subhuti's answer.

Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Śākyamuni.”

—Subhuti! In truth there is no such thing as “the Tathāgata attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Śākyamuni.

[If there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy] The Tathāgata's attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is not truly existent, and so I should not form the thought: I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If I formed the thought that I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I would still be clinging to the mark of “attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”; that is practicing a conditioned dharma, and one has already strayed from the Buddha-way. Dipankara Buddha would of course not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha.
Because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future life you shall become a Buddha, with the name Śākyamuni.”

—Because the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is illusion, and I also do not form the thought that there is truly a dharma by which the Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, therefore Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy.
Why? The Tathāgata means the meaning that all dharmas are thus.
Why is this said? Because “Tathāgata” means realizing that all dharmas are originally thus (originally as they are).

If someone says that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhuti! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi the Tathāgata attained is therein neither real nor empty.

If someone says that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—Subhuti! I tell you in truth, there truly is no such thing as “the Buddha attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” The matter of the Tathāgata's becoming a Buddha is neither existent nor non-existent; it is illusion.

[Neither real nor empty] Neither existent nor non-existent. [The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi the Tathāgata attained is therein neither real nor empty] The matter of becoming a Buddha is neither existent nor non-existent; it is illusion.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma.
Therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are the dharma of the Way of becoming a Buddha.

[Therefore] The tone carries on from the passage above: “the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi the Tathāgata attained is therein neither real nor empty.” [The Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma] Though the Tathāgata's becoming a Buddha is illusion, yet within the dream of ignorance the Tathāgata truly became a Buddha, and so the dharmas the Tathāgata speaks within the dream of ignorance are all the dharma of the Way of becoming a Buddha.

Concerning the scriptural sentence “Therefore the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma,” there have traditionally been two explanations. From the context, “Buddhadharma” here means the dharma of becoming a Buddha; on this point there is no dispute. But as to the meaning of this sentence, because of different punctuation there are two views:
First: “Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma.” (Meaning: therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.)
Second: “Therefore, the Tathāgata says: all dharmas are Buddhadharma.” (Meaning: therefore, the Tathāgata says: all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.)

Those who hold the first view include the Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra, where, under the scriptural sentence “Therefore the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma,” Wang Rixiu comments: “For this reason, the Buddha says that all dharmas are to be used in cultivation and are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.”
Wang Rixiu

That is, the layman Longshu of the Song dynasty, who wrote the Discourse on the Pure Land and edited the Great Amitābha Sutra. When the layman was about to leave the world, he took leave of all his relatives and friends, and urged them on in the work of the Pure Land. Before his death he still lectured and recited with his disciples and bowed to the Buddha as usual, and at death he passed away standing upright.

This book adopts the first view, for the reason that, judging from the essential purport and thread of the sutra's meaning, it should read “Therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are the dharma of becoming a Buddha.” Secondly, “Buddhadharma” here means the dharma of becoming a Buddha. If it were interpreted as “Therefore, the Tathāgata says: all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha,” then the heretical teachings, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, and so on, would also be the dharma of becoming a Buddha—and this assertion (that all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha) especially risks being abused. Must one not be careful? If, out of greed for worldly pleasures, one makes the excuse “eating without eating” or “doing without doing,” that is extremely dangerous. The Song of Certifying the Way says: “Clever emptiness, denying cause and effect, vast and boundless, invites calamity and disaster; abandoning existence and clinging to emptiness is the same disease, like fleeing drowning and throwing oneself into fire.”

Yet, on the other hand, the assertion that “all dharmas are the dharma of becoming a Buddha” is correct when spoken at a deeper level. As the Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says: “All form is Buddha-form, all sound is Buddha-sound.” But one may speak thus only when one has awakened to the corresponding ground. Just as, generally speaking, pouring water will put out a fire, yet if the fire is a blazing inferno, the water poured on is broken down by the high temperature into hydrogen and oxygen: hydrogen can burn of itself and oxygen supports combustion, and the fire blazes the more fiercely. One who has reached this ground finds that “the yellow flowers beyond the window are none of them other than prajñā; the green bamboos before the courtyard are all true suchness.” If one examines it thus, then every matter can be tempered, every moment is practice, everywhere there is benefit, and every place is Buddhadharma.
Subhuti! What is spoken of as all dharmas is not all dharmas; therefore it is called all dharmas.

Subhuti! What is spoken of as all dharmas (having marks) is not all dharmas (no substance); therefore it is called all dharmas (is illusion). This says that all dharmas have marks, have no substance, and are illusion.

Considering that beings might again cling to the Buddhadharma, the World-Honored One added with care: the Buddha says all dharmas are illusion. Since the beginningless kalpa, beings have either clung to existence or clung to nothingness—a habit formed over life after life, extremely stubborn; and so the World-Honored One says again and again in this sutra: not existent, not non-existent, but illusion.
Compare the eighth section: “Subhuti! What is called Buddhadharma is not Buddhadharma; therefore it is called Buddhadharma.”

Subhuti! For example, a human body is tall and great. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! The Tathāgata says a human body is tall and great, which is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body.

Subhuti! For example, a human body is tall and great. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! The Tathāgata says a human body is tall and great (having marks), which is not a great body (no substance); therefore it is called a great body (is illusion).

In the tenth section there is this passage: “Subhuti! Suppose there were a person whose body were like the king of Mount Sumeru: what do you think, is that body great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? The Buddha says it is no body; therefore it is called a great body.” There the World-Honored One had taught the rule of the pure mind (“they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”), and then tossed out this topic of the supreme wondrous reward-body, of such interest to cultivators, to see how well Subhuti had grasped and mastered this rule of the pure mind. Subhuti's first sentence, “Very great,” was like a mirror reflecting an object—this was right. In the second sentence he said at once that this body is illusion, closely guarding the original mind and not dragged by conditions. This shows that the Elder Subhuti has not only understood the rule of the pure mind but applies it well, setting us an example: thought after thought, abiding in the Way. Now the World-Honored One says again: “Subhuti! For example, a human body is tall and great.” So Subhuti says at once: “World-Honored One! The Tathāgata says a human body is tall and great, which is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body.” This is his example of closely guarding the original mind and not being dragged by conditions.

Subhuti! A bodhisattva is also thus. If he says, “I shall liberate immeasurable beings,” then he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without human, without being, without life.

Subhuti! The great body is illusion, and the bodhisattva is also illusion. If a bodhisattva thinks, “I shall liberate immeasurable beings,” he is not a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! Truly speaking, there is no such thing as a bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says there is no such dharma as self, human, being, or life.

[If he says, “I shall liberate immeasurable beings,” then he is not called a bodhisattva] A bodhisattva liberating beings must not cling to marks. “If he says, ‘I shall liberate immeasurable beings’”—this is clinging to marks. Cultivation is meant to turn delusion into awakening, and clinging to marks is delusion; so cultivation that clings to marks cannot succeed—it is what is called boiling sand and expecting rice. Therefore one who practices the six perfections while clinging to marks is not called a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva should say: I shall liberate immeasurable beings, and yet in truth not one being is liberated. [In truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva] There truly is no such thing as “called a bodhisattva.” This says that a bodhisattva is illusion and not truly existent, echoing the passage above, “in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” [The Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without human, without being, without life] This says that there simply is no such thing as self, human, being, or life; they are all illusion.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva says, “I shall adorn the Buddha-land,” he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? The Tathāgata says that what is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self, the Tathāgata names him a true bodhisattva.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva thinks, “I shall adorn the Buddha-land,” he is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this said? Because adorning the Buddha-land is illusion, and to take illusion as real (“I shall adorn the Buddha-land”) is therefore not a bodhisattva. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self (no self of persons, no self of dharmas), such a bodhisattva the Tathāgata names a true bodhisattva. (See “Chapter Ten, on Adorning the Pure Land”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-land? No, World-Honored One! Why? What is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment.”)

Since there is no such thing as self, human, being, or life, a bodhisattva cultivating the six perfections and ten thousand practices to adorn the Buddha-land must likewise not cling to marks. Only one who comprehends the dharma of no-self is truly a bodhisattva.

Above it was said that body and mind are illusion; now it is said that becoming a Buddha is illusion, that self, human, being, and life are illusion, and that a bodhisattva's cultivation adorning the Buddha-land is also illusion. Then who is cultivating? And how does one cultivate?
In the Complete Enlightenment Sutra, Bodhisattva Samantabhadra raised this very question:

“World-Honored One, if those beings know that all is like illusion, and body and mind are also illusion, how can one use illusion to cultivate further illusion? If the nature of all illusions is utterly extinguished, then there is no mind—who is it that cultivates? And why does he again speak of cultivating as illusion? If beings do not cultivate at all, and within birth and death forever dwell in illusion, never knowing the realm of illusion, how can their deluded minds be liberated? May you, for the sake of all beings in the last age, provide the skillful means by which they may practice step by step, so that all beings may forever leave all illusions.”
The World-Honored One taught in reply:

“Good man! All the various illusions of all beings are born from the Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment wondrous mind, just as sky-flowers arise from the sky: though the illusory flowers vanish, the nature of the sky is not destroyed. The illusory mind of beings is in turn extinguished in reliance on illusion; when all illusions are utterly extinguished, the enlightened mind does not move. To speak of enlightenment in reliance on illusion is also called illusion; if one says there is enlightenment, one has not yet left illusion; and to say there is no enlightenment is likewise so. Therefore the extinction of illusion is named the unmoving.”

“Good man, all bodhisattvas and all beings of the final age should depart far from every illusion-like, false, and vain realm; because of firmly holding to the mind of departure, that mind which is itself like an illusion is also to be departed from; that departure is itself an illusion, and is also to be departed from; departing from the illusion of departure is likewise to be departed from; and when one reaches the point of nothing more to depart from, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks are rubbed together, fire comes forth and the wood is consumed, the ash flies and the smoke is extinguished; using illusion to cultivate illusion is just the same—when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation
(it is not that everything becomes nothing; the wondrous enlightened mind shines forth in full).

“Good man! Knowing illusion, one is at once free of it, without resorting to skillful means; freed of illusion, one is at once awake, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and all beings of the final age who practice in accord with this will thus be able forever to depart from all illusions.

“At that time the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again, spoke in verse: Samantabhadra, you should know, all beings without exception have, from beginningless time, illusory ignorance, all established from the Tathagatas' mind of perfect enlightenment. Like a flower in empty space, it depends on space to have its marks; when the flower in space is gone, space itself is never moved. Illusion is born of the various enlightenments; when illusion is gone, enlightenment is complete, for the mind of enlightenment is unmoved. Therefore all bodhisattvas, and all beings of the final age, should constantly depart from illusion, and all illusions will be wholly departed from. As fire comes forth from wood, and when the wood is consumed the fire dies, so enlightenment knows no gradual stages, and skillful means are just the same.”
(for annotation see
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment Explained, a Detailed Commentary

This section uses the five eyes to show that the Buddha's vision is perfectly fused, beholding all things equally, and, amid what appears to be birth and death, seeing only the unborn. Hence its title, One-Vessel Contemplation.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the physical eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the physical eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.
[The physical eye] The physical eye is the eye of an ordinary being of flesh and blood; when it meets darkness or an obstacle, it cannot see.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the divine eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the divine eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the divine eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the divine eye.
[The divine eye] The divine eye is the eye of the gods; near and far, by day and by night, it can see all.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.

[The wisdom eye] The wisdom eye is the eye of the shravaka; it can see through false marks and recognize true emptiness. [True emptiness] The state beyond all marks of form and consciousness—that is, the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Dharma eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Dharma eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Dharma eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Dharma eye.
[The Dharma eye] The Dharma eye is the eye of the bodhisattva; it can thoroughly comprehend every Dharma gate within and beyond the world.
[Subhuti! What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.

[The Buddha eye] The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathagata; having the Buddha eye, one also possesses the four preceding eyes. Nothing is unknown, nothing is unseen; within all dharmas the Buddha eye constantly illumines.

The next passage says that the Tathagata has these five eyes (the physical eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye), knowing all and seeing all, and therefore whatever the Tathagata speaks is true speech seen with his own eyes.

[Subhuti, what do you think? Of all the sand in the Ganges River, would the Buddha say that it is sand? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata says that it is sand. Subhuti! What do you think? If there were as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and the Buddha-worlds were as many as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be many? Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: Within all those lands, the various minds of all the beings—the Tathagata knows them all.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Of all the sand in the Ganges River, would the Buddha say that it is sand? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata says that it is sand. The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? If all the sand in the Ganges River—one grain of sand for one Ganges River—made Buddha-worlds as numerous as the grains of sand of all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be many? Subhuti answered: Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: Within all those lands of yours (that is, within the three thousand great thousand worlds multiplied by the sands of the Ganges and multiplied again by the sands of the Ganges), all the various minds (thoughts) of all beings—the Tathagata knows them all completely.

[Mind] The “mind” here means the deluded mind, that is, thoughts. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions and changes his place; they falsely take the four great elements as the mark of their own bodies, and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own minds.” [The shadowy traces of the six dusts] These are the images that arise in dependence on the six dusts, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six faculties meet the six dusts. [Within all those lands of yours] This refers to “as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and the Buddha-worlds as numerous as the grains of sand of all those Ganges Rivers”; that is, the three thousand great thousand worlds multiplied by the sands of the Ganges and multiplied again by the sands of the Ganges.
[Why is that? The Tathagata says that all minds are not minds, and so they are called minds.]

Why is it that the Tathagata knows all these countless minds completely? Because the Tathagata says that all minds (marks that exist) are not minds (their substance being nonexistent), and so they are called minds (they are illusion).

[All minds] That is, what the passage above calls “the various minds of all beings.” [The Tathagata says that all minds are not minds, and so they are called minds] This says that the minds of all beings are illusions. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,

Chapter Eleven, on the Illusion-Like, says: “Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from an illusion? Are feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness different from an illusion? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One.” Thus we know that body and mind are illusions.

This passage says: Why does the Tathagata know all these countless minds? Because they are the deluded mind of thought-streaming, they are illusions, and illusions have marks (modern science and technology can already measure and record the brain waves produced by thinking), and therefore the Tathagata knows them all.

When an ordinary being gives rise to a thought, the ghosts and spirits all know it—how much more so the Tathagata. In the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang, a bhikshu came from the West, known as the Great-Eared Tripiṭaka, who claimed to have the power of knowing others' minds (the supernatural power of knowing the thoughts of others). Suzong asked National Master Huizhong of Nanyang to test him. The National Master sat for a while and asked: Where is this old monk's mind? He answered: Watching a boat race in Sichuan. After a while the National Master asked again: Where is this old monk's mind? He answered: Watching a monkey show on the Tianjin Bridge. The National Master became utterly still. After a while he asked again: Where is this old monk's mind? The Great-Eared Tripiṭaka could not answer for a very long time, because the National Master's mind had come to rest, still and without marks.
[What is the reason? Subhuti! The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped.]

Why is it said that (these minds) are illusions? Because the past mind, the present mind, and the future mind are all shadowy traces of the six dusts, arising from the dusts and ceasing when the dusts depart (they cannot be grasped); therefore no substance can be spoken of.

The Sutra of the Great Vehicle's Contemplation of the Mind-ground of the Original Birth says: “All mental dharmas of the three times are by nature empty.” The three minds are what dwells; the six dusts are what is dwelt upon; what dwells and what is dwelt upon are both illusions and both cannot be grasped. Therefore one must certainly see through and let go—see through the fact that all marks whatsoever are false and vain, and let go of clinging, discrimination, and false thinking.
[The three times] Past, present, and future.

blocks.text: Universal Transformation of the Dharma Realm, Chapter Nineteen

inline.s: The passage above says that the three minds are illusion; this section says that merit is illusion. “Universal transformation of the Dharma realm” means: if one realizes that merit is an illusion and practices giving without marks, one's giving and transformation pervade the Dharma realm. This is exactly what is said in Section Four, “Wondrous Practice without Dwelling”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! Can the space in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, the merit is likewise inconceivable and immeasurable.”

[Subhuti! What do you think? If someone filled the three thousand great thousand worlds with the seven treasures and used them for giving, would this person, by this causal condition, obtain much merit? So it is, World-Honored One! This person, by this causal condition, obtains very much merit.]

Subhuti! What do you think? If someone took the seven treasures filling the three thousand great thousand worlds and used them for giving, would this person, by this causal condition, obtain much merit? Subhuti answered: So it is, World-Honored One! This person, by this causal condition, obtains very much merit.
[Subhuti! If merit had reality, the Tathagata would not say that much merit is obtained; because merit is without reality, the Tathagata says that much merit is obtained.]

Subhuti! If merit had reality (truly existed), the Tathagata would not say that much merit is obtained; because merit is without reality (it does not truly exist), the Tathagata says that much merit is obtained.

The World-Honored One explains once more: only because merit is illusion is there any “much” to speak of. Compare Section Eight: “Subhuti! What do you think? If a person filled the three thousand great thousand worlds with the seven treasures and used them for giving, would the merit obtained by this person be much? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? Because this merit is not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathagata says that the merit is much.” In Section Eight it is Subhuti who says that only because merit is illusion is there any “much” to speak of; here it is the World-Honored One who says that only because merit is illusion is there any “much” to speak of.

blocks.text: Free of Form, Free of Marks, Chapter Twenty

inline.s: This section says that the Buddha's perfect body of form is illusion, and that the Buddha's thirty-two major marks of a great being and eighty auspicious characteristics are likewise illusion. “Free of form, free of marks” means that the Buddha's perfect body of form, his thirty-two major marks of a great being, and his eighty auspicious characteristics must not be taken as real.

[Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his perfect body of form? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect body of form. Why? The Tathagata says that the perfect body of form is not the perfect body of form, and so it is called the perfect body of form.]

Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his perfect body of form? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect body of form. Why? Because the perfect body of form is an illusion—the Tathagata says that the perfect body of form (a mark that exists) is not the perfect body of form (its substance being nonexistent), and so it is called the perfect body of form (it is illusion).
[The perfect body of form] The perfect body of form.

The perfect body of form has marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and vain; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by it. The sutra says: “If you see that all marks are non-marks, then you see the Tathagata.”

[Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by his perfect marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect marks. Why? The Tathagata says that the perfection of marks is not perfection, and so it is called the perfection of marks.]

Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his perfect marks? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by his perfect marks. Why? Because this very perfection is also an illusion—the Tathagata says that the perfection of marks (a mark that exists) is not perfection (its substance being nonexistent), and so it is called the perfection of marks (it is illusion).

[The perfect marks] The thirty-two major marks of a great being and the eighty auspicious characteristics with which the Buddha's body of form is endowed. Among the supremely excellent features and forms of the Buddha's body of form, those that are prominent and easily seen are thirty-two in number, called the thirty-two major marks of a great being (the thirty-two marks for short); those that are subtle, hidden, and hard to see are eighty in number, called the eighty auspicious characteristics. A wheel-turning sage king also possesses the thirty-two marks, but does not possess the eighty characteristics.

The thirty-two major marks of a great being and the eighty auspicious characteristics” have marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and vain; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by them. The sutra says: “If you see that all marks are non-marks, then you see the Tathagata.”

Compare: Section Five, “The Real Seeing of Suchness”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by his bodily marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by his bodily marks. Why? The bodily marks spoken of by the Tathagata are not bodily marks.” Section Thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Taught”: “Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by the thirty-two marks. Why? The Tathagata says that the thirty-two marks are not marks, and so they are called the thirty-two marks.”

blocks.text: Neither Speaking Nor What Is Spoken, Chapter Twenty-One

inline.s: “Neither speaking nor what is spoken”—one who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and so is called speaking the Dharma.

[Subhuti! Do not say that the Tathagata has this thought: I should speak some Dharma. Do not have this thought! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata speaks a Dharma, he slanders the Buddha, because he cannot understand what I have spoken.]

Subhuti! Do not think that the Tathagata has this thought: I should speak some Dharma. Do not think so! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata has the thought that he speaks the Dharma, that is slandering the Buddha, because this person cannot understand what my speaking of the Dharma really is. (The Buddha speaks while free of marks—speaking yet not speaking.)

The Tathagata's speaking of the Dharma is not speaking from a thought (the Tathagata has no thought of wanting to speak the Dharma, nor any thought of being about to speak or having already spoken the Dharma); rather, it responds to conditions and arises in function, flowing naturally from the self-nature. The Tathagata does not cling to the mark of speaking the Dharma—speaking yet not speaking, as is said: “How does one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, abiding in unmoved suchness.” (See Section Thirty-Two, “Neither Real nor Illusory.”) Moreover, this very matter of the Tathagata's speaking the Dharma is not truly existent; truly there is no dharma called speaking the Dharma. (For “the Tathagata has spoken nothing,” see Section Thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Taught”: “Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathagata spoken any Dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has spoken nothing.”)
[Subhuti! One who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and so is called speaking the Dharma.]
Subhuti! One who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak—this alone is truly speaking the Dharma.

The meaning is that one who clings to the mark of speaking the Dharma (the conditioned Dharma) cannot speak the way of liberation (the unconditioned Dharma), because he himself has not realized and has not upheld the way of liberation. Therefore, at the end of this sutra, the World-Honored One admonishes: “How does one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, abiding in unmoved suchness.” (Section Thirty-Two, “Neither Real nor Illusory.”) At the same time, the self-nature of beings is originally perfect and complete, no different from the Buddhas; in this respect there truly is no dharma to speak, no practice to cultivate, and no fruit to realize. The problem is that the Buddhas are awake and have verified their own nature, while we are still within the dream of delusion and must cultivate and realize before we can awaken. In this respect there is a dharma that must be spoken, a practice that must be cultivated, and a fruit that must be realized. Yet these dharmas, practices, and fruits are all carried on within the dream of ignorance; though it is using illusion to depart from illusion, after all they are illusions, and illusions are not real. The practitioner must never cling to marks. Therefore it is said: no dharma to speak, no practice to cultivate, no fruit to realize.

Master Hanshan says: Beings “only because of beginningless ignorance, which obscures for them the wondrous brightness, give rise to all manner of inversion, false thinking, and discrimination, and create all manner of karma. It is like a waking person who, having nothing to do, suddenly in sleep dreams all manner of dreams; the affairs of joy and sorrow in the dream appear vividly before him, yet when he wakes and looks for them, they cannot be found at all. This is what is called producing something out of nothing—how could it be a real dharma? But the deluded person, being inverted, clings to it as truly existent; this is because his seeing is not thorough. And when the Buddha comes into the world and speaks all manner of dharmas, these are but tools for breaking the dream, and have no root either. Yet students of the Buddha-Dharma again cling to them as dharmas that they truly possess—this is adding a dream within a dream.” (The Dream Wandering Collection
Shown to the Chan Practitioner Tanyan Zong)

The Essential Sayings of the Transmission of the Mind says: “The Buddha has three bodies: the Dharma body speaks the Dharma of the self-nature's empty pervasion, the reward body speaks all pure dharmas, and the transformation body speaks the Dharma of the six perfections and the myriad practices. When the Dharma body speaks the Dharma, it cannot be sought by speech, sound, form, or letters; there is nothing spoken and nothing realized, only the self-nature's empty pervasion. Hence it is said: ‘No dharma to speak—this is called speaking the Dharma.’ The reward body and the transformation body both appear in response to the capacities of beings, and the dharmas they speak also follow the matter and respond to the faculties so as to gather and transform them; none of these are the true Dharma. Hence it is said: the reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they speakers of the Dharma.”

Master Baojing says: “Now the mark of the stillness and extinction of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words; in the ground of actual principle there is originally nothing spoken. This is what is meant by ‘the Way is originally without words, the Dharma is originally without speech.’ As the Diamond Sutra says: if one says that the Tathagata has spoken a Dharma, that is slandering the Buddha. Why then does the Buddha have a Dharma that can be spoken? You should know that the Way is originally without words, and words are borrowed to reveal the Way; the Dharma is originally without speech, and speech is used to reveal the Dharma. If one clings to its being un-speakable, one falls into the outsider's view of cutting off words; if one clings to there being something speakable, one earns the reproach of slandering the Buddha. If one understands that speaking is precisely not speaking, then one may well speak without speaking. Therefore the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for forty-nine years and never spoke a single word. Yet though he never spoke a single word, he spoke horizontally and vertically, speaking ardently and without interval, without end. The wonder of the Buddha-Dharma lies precisely in this.” (A Personal Record of the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra)
[At that time the life-of-wisdom Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Will there be many beings in future ages who, hearing this Dharma, give rise to faith?]
At that time the life-of-wisdom Subhuti reverently said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Many beings in future ages, hearing you speak in this way, will they believe it?
[Life of wisdom] To take wisdom as one's life. Subhuti was foremost in understanding emptiness, taking wisdom as his life, and so he is called the life-of-wisdom Subhuti.

The passage above says: “If a person says that the Tathagata speaks a Dharma, he slanders the Buddha . . . one who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and so is called speaking the Dharma.” Subhuti feared that beings would find this hard to understand, and so asked: in future ages, hearing you speak in this way, will any beings believe it?
[The Buddha said: Subhuti! They are not beings, and yet they are not non-beings. Why? Subhuti! Beings, beings, the Tathagata says are not beings, and so they are called beings.]

The Buddha told Subhūti: Subhūti! They are not sentient beings, and yet they are not entirely non-sentient beings either. Why is that? Subhūti! Because sentient beings are but illusions (these sentient beings, as the Tathāgata declares, are not sentient beings, and so are merely called sentient beings), while their intrinsic nature is the same as the Buddha’s—omniscient and all-capable—and so they are fully able to give rise to faith in this.
[Sentient beings, sentient beings]—through this repetition, spoken in an emphatic tone, it carries forward the passage above: “They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings.”

blocks.text: Section 22: Nothing Attainable in the Dharma

inline.s: The preceding section said that the Tathāgata has no Dharma to teach; this section speaks of how the Tathāgata has no Dharma to attain.
[Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! When the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was there truly nothing attained?]
Subhūti respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! When the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, was it truly a matter of having nothing attained?
[The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhūti! With regard to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have not even the slightest Dharma to attain, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

The Buddha replied: So it is, so it is. Subhūti! Not only do I have nothing attained with respect to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, but I have not even the slightest Dharma to attain. Having completely departed from all marks, this is what is called the supreme, perfect enlightenment.

See Section Seven, “Nothing Attained, Nothing Taught”: “Subhūti! What do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Does the Tathāgata have any Dharma to teach?” Subhūti said: “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, there is no fixed Dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; nor is there any fixed Dharma that the Tathāgata can teach.” And Section Seventeen, “Without an Ultimate Self”: “Subhūti! What do you think? When the Tathāgata was at the abode of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there any Dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?” “No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, when the Buddha was at the abode of Dīpaṃkara, there was no Dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is. Subhūti! There truly is no Dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti! If there were a Dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’ Since there is truly no Dharma by which anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is attained, therefore Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’ Why is that? The Tathāgata is precisely the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. If anyone says that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Subhūti! There truly is no Dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata lies within neither the real nor the unreal.’”

The cultivation that is no cultivation, and the realization that is no realization, hold two levels of meaning: First, why should one cultivate and realize? The purpose is to awaken from the dream of ignorance. Therefore one must cultivate while detached from marks and realize while detached from marks in order to escape illusion; thus, cultivation without cultivating and realization without realizing are the correct path. Second, at the fundamental level, cultivation and realization are both matters within the dream of ignorance—there is no truly existing cultivation or realization—and so it is said that there is no cultivation and no realization. Even so, one must still cultivate and realize in order to awaken from the dream of ignorance, but one must always cultivate while detached from marks and realize while detached from marks.
That the World-Honored One taught no Dharma and attained no anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is truly hard to believe, and so the sutra repeatedly returns to these two matters.

When speaking of how all dharmas are like a dream or an illusion, Great Master Hanshan said: “All Buddhas manifest through the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate through the power of illusion; all two-vehicle practitioners seek stillness through the power of illusion; all externalists are deluded through the power of illusion; all sentient beings pass through birth and death through the power of illusion. Even heavenly palaces and the Pure Land are established through the power of illusion; jade groves and jeweled trees flourish through the power of illusion; iron beds and copper pillars are arrayed through the power of illusion; the boiling cauldron and burning coals rage through the power of illusion; those with scales, shells, and feathers fly and dive through the power of illusion; the creeping, writhing, wriggling creatures rest and move through the power of illusion. That which all Buddhas of the three times have realized and which the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted—all of it never leaves this net of illusion.’ (See Mengyou ji
the instruction to the Chan practitioner Zhenyu’)

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, those bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the final age who, by cultivating and practicing this mind, attain accomplishment—for them there is here neither cultivation nor accomplishment; the perfect enlightenment shines universally, still and extinct, without duality. Within it, the Buddhalands of hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeyas, ineffable as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, rising and vanishing in confusion—neither apart from nor attached to anything, neither bound nor freed. Then for the first time one knows that sentient beings originally are Buddhas, and that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night.”

Great Master Hanshan commented: This re-explains the characteristic of perfect enlightenment universally shining, still and extinct, without duality, in order to reveal the ultimate realization of the one mind. For within the tathāgatagarbha there are originally no marks of delusion or awakening, birth-and-death or coming-and-going. Yet birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are all matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance has been broken, when one looks back upon past events it is but a dream of last night.

blocks.text: Section 23: Purifying the Mind and Practicing Good

inline.s: A pure mind is a mind of purity free of discrimination and attachment. The sutra passage of this section says: “With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, practice all wholesome dharmas, and one then attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” Hence this section is titled: Purifying the Mind and Practicing Good.

[Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal and impartial, with no high or low, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, if one practices all wholesome dharmas, then one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]
Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal and impartial, with no high or low, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

—Moreover, Subhūti! This Dharma (referring to the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi spoken of above) regards all things equally, for having truly realized that these are all illusions, there arise no discriminations of high or low, noble or base, right or wrong, defiled or pure; and so this is called the supreme, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Tang
Xuanzang’s translation: “Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal, and within it there is nothing that is not equal; therefore it is called the supreme, perfect enlightenment.”

This passage says: What is supreme, perfect enlightenment? Supreme, perfect enlightenment is the complete casting away of all discriminations and attachments—this is the Buddha, and this is the Dharma attained by the Buddha.
This Dharma is equal and impartial, with no high or low, and this is called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi”—this carries several meanings:
1. Any sentient being can realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

2. No matter what path is taken, and no matter whether the time be short or long, so long as one fully awakens, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For those who realize it, there is no high or low, no old or new, no shallow or deep.
3. The Dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi regards all things equally.
Why do we discriminate and cling? Because we take illusions to be real! Therefore we cling to marks and grasp at circumstances, and so there is transmigration.

The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “Those who study the Way today, if they do not awaken within their own minds, but instead, beyond the mind, cling to marks and grasp at circumstances, all of this is against the Way. As for the sand of the Ganges, the Buddha says it is sand. When Buddhas and bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas walk over it, the sand is not pleased; when oxen, sheep, insects, and ants trample upon it, the sand is not angered; when precious treasures and sweet fragrances are laid upon it, the sand is not greedy; when excrement and filth are cast upon it, the sand is not repulsed. This mind is the mind of no-mind (not grasping at marks, regarding all things equally). Apart from all marks, sentient beings and Buddhas are no longer different; if only one can be without mind (without discriminating or clinging), that is the ultimate. Those who study the Way, if they do not directly become without mind, though they cultivate for countless kalpas, they will ultimately never accomplish the Way, being bound by the meritorious practices of the three vehicles and unable to gain liberation.”

[Three vehicles] “Vehicle” (yāna) means a means of conveyance; here it is a metaphor for the Dharma-gate that carries sentient beings across birth-and-death to the far shore of nirvāṇa. In accordance with the dull, middling, and sharp faculties of sentient beings, the Buddha spoke three kinds of doctrine: the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle. The three vehicles are: the lesser vehicle, the middling vehicle, and the great vehicle. The lesser vehicle is the śrāvaka vehicle, the middling vehicle is the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the great vehicle is the bodhisattva vehicle.

In this sutra the World-Honored One, with earnest and repeated instruction, simply wants us to awaken from our deluded dreams and cease discriminating and clinging. Love and hate, grasping and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion, and pride are the root of birth-and-death; they must be eradicated before one can put an end to birth-and-death. Therefore one must exert great effort in removing discrimination and clinging from the mind.
The “no-direction verse” of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
If one truly cultivates the Way, he sees not the faults of the world;
If he sees the faults of others, his own faulting is the greater wrong;
Others may be at fault, but I shall not be at fault; my own faulting is itself a fault;
Only do away with this fault-finding mind, and strike down and shatter affliction;
When love and hate no longer touch the heart, stretch out both feet and lie down.

[Love and hate no longer touch the heart] This means that feelings of love and hate no longer arise in the mind. Where sentient beings are deluded, they are deluded by clinging to marks and grasping at circumstances, vainly discriminating.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, because of the accomplishment of enlightenment, you should know that the bodhisattva is not bound by dharmas and does not seek release from dharmas; does not loathe birth-and-death and does not love nirvāṇa; does not revere those who uphold the precepts and does not hate those who break them; does not esteem long practice and does not slight beginners. Why is that? Because all is enlightened. For example, when the light of the eye discerns the scene before it, its illumination being complete, there is no love or hate. Why is that? Because the essence of light is non-dual, and so there is no love or hate.”

Great Master Hanshan commented: This reveals the one mind, still and extinct, equal and non-dual, precisely displaying the characteristic of pure enlightenment. For bondage and liberation, love and hate, and so forth are all dual characteristics; because of the deluded views of ignorance, there are dual characteristics. Now, through universal illumination, all is enlightened, and therefore there is no duality. The light of the eye is the universal illumination of direct perception of the eight consciousnesses; among all the sense faculties the eye is the most manifest, and so it is used as a metaphor for the non-dual essence of perfect enlightenment universally shining.

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, all obstructions are the ultimate enlightenment. Gaining mindfulness and losing mindfulness are no other than liberation. The dharma accomplished and the dharma destroyed are both called nirvāṇa. Wisdom and ignorance are alike prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and by externalists are equally bodhi. Ignorance and true thusness are not different realms. The precepts, samādhi, and wisdom, along with lust, anger, and delusion—all are pure conduct. Sentient beings and lands share the same dharma nature. Hells and heavenly palaces are all the Pure Land. Those with nature and those without nature alike accomplish the Buddha Way. All afflictions are ultimately liberated. The sea of wisdom of the dharma realm, illumining all marks, is like the sky. This is called the Tathāgata’s accordant enlightenment nature.”

Great Master Hanshan commented: This “ultimate” serves to display the equal Buddha-wisdom. The ten pairs—gaining mindfulness and losing mindfulness, and so on—are all matters on the side of delusion and awakening. For the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment does not belong to the paired causality of delusion and awakening; everything is still, extinct, equal, and one. Seen through false views, there are dual characteristics; but if illumined by the sea-wisdom of the dharma realm, it is like the sky, and all marks are utterly ungraspable. (See Great Master Hanshan’s Straight Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment.)
The Song of Realizing the Way says: “In the dream, the six realms are clearly present; after awakening, all is empty—no trichiliocosm.”
With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, if one practices all wholesome dharmas, then one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

—Then how does one realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? The World-Honored One said: With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, by practicing any wholesome dharma, one can realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
With no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan”—that is, realizing that all marks are illusory, with nothing to seek and nothing to cling to.

This says that the key to realizing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the absence of the four marks, not the kind of wholesome dharma one practices. The wholesome dharma practiced without the four marks is the unconditioned dharma. Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the universal principle for realizing anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; from this one also knows how crucial it is to be free of the four marks! How very important!
[Wholesome dharmas] The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra

the third chapter, “The Chapter on Practicing and Responding,” says: “What are wholesome dharmas? They are: the ten courses of wholesome action, the five precepts, the eight-fold observance of full attainment (that is, the eight precepts), the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless concentrations, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four psychic faculties, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.” Because bodhisattvas originally attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through practicing the six perfections, the six perfections are not enumerated in the wholesome dharmas above.
[Subhūti! As for the wholesome dharmas of which I speak, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas, and so they are called wholesome dharmas.]
Subhūti! As for the so-called wholesome dharmas (having marks), the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas (without essence), and so they are called wholesome dharmas (being illusion).

This says that wholesome dharmas are illusory. To prevent sentient beings from again clinging to marks with respect to wholesome dharmas, the World-Honored One earnestly admonished: Wholesome dharmas are illusions, and therefore one must be detached from marks and practice wholesome dharmas with a pure mind.
Those who uphold, read, and recite this sutra and expound it for others—their merit is incomparable, and their wisdom is likewise incomparable; hence it is called “Incomparable Merit and Wisdom.”

[Subhūti! If in the trichiliocosm all the kings of Mount Sumeru, and masses of the seven treasures such as these, were gathered up and someone used them in giving; and if another person upheld, read, and recited this Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, even a four-line verse, and expounded it for others—the merit of the former would not equal one hundredth of the latter, nor one hundred thousand myriad billionth of it, nor could it be reached by reckoning or simile.]

Subhūti! If someone, with the volume of all the kings of Mount Sumeru in the trichiliocosm, were to fill it with the seven treasures and give as a gift; and if another person were to uphold, read, and recite this Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, even a four-line verse, and expound it for others—the merit of the former would not equal one hundredth of the latter, nor one hundred thousand myriad billionth of it, nor even a fraction of that vast number which no reckoning or simile can describe.

After the World-Honored One had spoken of wholesome dharmas as illusion (“Subhūti! As for the wholesome dharmas of which I speak, the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas, and so they are called wholesome dharmas”), he next spoke of the incomparable merit of those who uphold, read, and recite this sutra and expound it for others—lest some fall into the extreme of denying dharmas.
Transforming without transformation’ means that the Tathāgata delivers and transforms sentient beings while detached from marks.

[Subhūti! What do you think? Do not suppose that the Tathāgata conceives the thought, “I shall save sentient beings.” Subhūti! Do not hold such a thought. Why is that? Because in truth there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves. If there were sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves, then the Tathāgata would have a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan.]

Subhūti! What do you think? Do not suppose that the Tathāgata conceives such a thought: “I shall save sentient beings.” Subhūti! Do not think like this. Why is that? Because there is truly no such matter as the Tathāgata saving sentient beings. If the Tathāgata were to think that there is such a matter as the Tathāgata saving sentient beings, then the Tathāgata would have the marks of self, person, sentient being, and lifespan.

[In truth there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves] There is truly no such matter as the Tathāgata saving sentient beings. This says that the Tathāgata’s saving of sentient beings is also an illusion, because “all marks are false and unreal.” When reading the Diamond Sutra, one should note that many passages are expositions of the line “All marks are false and unreal.”

[Subhūti! The Tathāgata, in speaking of a self, says there is no self; yet ordinary people imagine that there is a self. Subhūti! As for ordinary people, the Tathāgata says they are not ordinary people, and so they are called ordinary people.]

Subhūti! The Tathāgata speaks of a self in order to deliver and transform sentient beings, and this “self” spoken of by the Tathāgata is an illusion; yet ordinary people imagine that the “self” truly exists. Subhūti! This “self” is an illusion, and moreover these ordinary people who imagine that “the self truly exists” are also illusions—ordinary people (having marks), as the Tathāgata says, are not ordinary people (without essence), and so they are called ordinary people (being illusion).
[Ordinary people] Sentient beings within the three realms.

blocks.text: Section 26: The Dharmakāya Is Without Marks

inline.s: The dharmakāya is without marks’ means that the dharmakāya is without marks and cannot be seen by them. The Mahāyāna Homogeneous Sutra says: “The Tathāgata’s true dharmakāya is without color, without manifestation, without attachment, invisible, without speech, without abode, without marks, without retribution, without birth, without extinction, without simile.”
[Dharmakāya] One of the Buddha’s three bodies (dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya); it is the body of true thusness realized by all Buddhas.
[Subhūti! What do you think—can one contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti said: So it is! So it is! One can contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.]
Subhūti! What do you think—is one who has the thirty-two marks the Tathāgata? Subhūti replied: So it is, so it is. One can contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.
[Contemplate] The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra (Jingying) says: “To contemplate means to bind the mind in thoughtful examination; this is called contemplation.”

In section thirteen, the question was whether one “sees” the Tathāgata: “Subhūti, what do you think—can one see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is that? The Tathāgata says the thirty-two marks are non-marks, and so they are called the thirty-two marks.” Subhūti answered: “One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.” (Because the thirty-two marks are illusory.)
Here the World-Honored One asks: Can one “contemplate” the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied: So it is, so it is. One can contemplate the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.
This answer is wrong, and so in what follows the World-Honored One corrects it.

[The Buddha said: Subhūti! If one contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a cakravartin (wheel-turning sage king) would be the Tathāgata. Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, one should not contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.]

Subhūti! If one thinks that whoever possesses the thirty-two marks is the Tathāgata, then a cakravartin would be the Tathāgata, for the cakravartin also possesses the thirty-two marks. Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken, one should not think that whoever possesses the thirty-two marks is the Tathāgata.

[Cakravartin sage king] Also called simply a cakravartin, or wheel-turning king, he is the most blessed person in the world, appearing in an age when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, and he governs the four continents. He enjoys four kinds of karmic reward: First, great wealth—treasures, goods, fields, and dwellings are numerous, the greatest in the world; second, a solemn and upright appearance possessing the thirty-two marks; third, a healthy body free of illness, peaceful and happy; fourth, a long lifespan, the greatest in the world. When a cakravartin appears, the world is at peace, the people are happy, and there are no natural calamities or human misfortunes. This results from much cultivation of merit in past lives; but regrettably, without cultivating the wisdom that transcends the world, he becomes merely a blessed great king ruling the world, and cannot cultivate, awaken to the Way, and realize the fruit.
[At that time the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
If one seeks to see me through form, or seeks me through sound,
that person treads a false path and cannot see the Tathāgata.]
At this the World-Honored One spoke in verse: If anyone vainly seeks to see me through form, or seeks me through sound, that person treads a false path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

Both the body of form and sound are illusions; one cannot see the Tathāgata through them. If anyone seeks to see the Tathāgata through the body of form and sound, that path is wrong, and one cannot see the Tathāgata. Then how can one see the Tathāgata? This is what section five says: “If one sees that all marks are not marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.”

Neither annihilation nor extinction’ means that one must not cling to the view of annihilation. Above, the World-Honored One, all the while breaking attachments, repeatedly clarified that dharmas are not truly existing; yet, fearing that sentient beings might fall into the other extreme—thinking that dharmas are wholly nonexistent, even denying that marks exist—he admonishes in this section: “Those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation with regard to dharmas.”

[Subhūti! If you think thus—the Tathāgata, because he does not have the complete marks, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti! Do not think thus—the Tathāgata, because he does not have the complete marks, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.]

Subhūti! If you think thus—the Tathāgata, without needing the complete marks, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (supreme, perfect enlightenment). Subhūti! Do not think thus—the Tathāgata, without needing the complete marks, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[The complete marks] These are the “complete marks” spoken of earlier. The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty minor characteristics, and so he is said to have the complete marks.

The preceding section said that the thirty-two marks are illusory and cannot be used to contemplate the Tathāgata. To prevent his listeners from falling into annihilation, the World-Honored One next admonishes: “Do not think thus—the Tathāgata, because he does not have the complete marks, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

In section twenty there is this passage: “Subhūti! What do you think—can the Tathāgata be seen by the complete marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata should not be seen by the complete marks. Why is that? The Tathāgata says the complete marks are not complete, and so they are called the complete marks.”
Now the World-Honored One tells Subhūti: Do not negate the phenomenal fact that “the Tathāgata must have the complete marks in order to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

[Subhūti! If you think thus—those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi speak of the annihilation of dharmas. Do not think thus! Why is that? Those who give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation with regard to dharmas.]

Subhūti! If you think thus—the Tathāgata, without needing the complete marks, realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—that is, if you negate the phenomenal fact that “the Tathāgata must have the complete marks in order to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,” then you are negating that marks exist, and that is a vain clinging to the view of annihilation.
