True Practice and Real Awakening
Praise of the Diamond Sutra
Doubt severed, faith born; marks cut off, schools transcended; in a flash self and dharmas both forgotten, one understands true emptiness.
Prajñā's flavor, layer upon layer; the four lines, blended and understood; its merit and virtue pass all praise.
[Praise of the Diamond Sutra] That is, the praise of the Diamond Sutra.
Doubt severed, faith born”:

To cut off doubt and deeply believe the wondrous principle that “all dharmas are illusion, and when illusion is exhausted the dream ends”—this is the surpassing use of the Diamond Sutra. Layman Pang says:
“The world prizes rare treasures, I prize a moment's stillness; much gold confuses the mind
(entering illusion)
, in stillness one sees the nature of true suchness
(leaving illusion)

[Layman Pang] Pang Yun, a famous lay Chan practitioner of the Tang dynasty. He awakened upon consulting Mazu in Chan, and was known to the world as Layman Pang and praised as the Vimalakīrti of the East. In the Yuanhe period he traveled north to Xiangyang; loving the customs of the place, he sank his wealth in the river by boat and, with his wife and son, tilled the land himself at the foot of Mount Lumen, often making bamboo ware to maintain their livelihood. At the time of his passing, he sent his daughter Lingzhao out to see how late the day was, and Lingzhao reported back: “The sun is already at its height, but there is an eclipse.” Pang Yun then went out of doors to look, and Lingzhao at once climbed into her father's seat, pressed her palms together, and passed away sitting. Pang Yun laughed and said: “My daughter's blade is swift!” He then postponed his own passing by seven days. Layman Pang's wife went to the field to tell their son, and the son too died standing on his hoe. Not long after, she went about the villages and neighborhoods, took her leave, and retired from the world, and no one ever knew where she ended.
Marks cut off, schools transcended”:
Marks cut off—no mark of self, no mark of a human, no mark of a being, no mark of a life, no mark of dharmas and also no mark of non-dharmas; schools transcended—surpassing all the schools.

[The schools] When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he taught the various doctrines of the great and small, the half and the full, gathering and transforming all capacities and conditions. After the World-Honored One's extinction, the sages and worthies each relied on the teachings to divide into schools for the benefit of those with affinity. The rise of the schools of Chinese Buddhism occurred about the Sui and Tang periods, and there is a saying of thirteen schools, namely: Abhidharma, Satyasiddhi, Vinaya, Three Treatises, Nirvāṇa, Daśabhūmi, Saṃgraha, Pure Land, Chan, Tiantai, Avataṃsaka, Dharma Characteristics, and Esoteric. The Chan school has the saying of five houses and seven schools: the five houses are Linji, Weiyang, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. The seven schools are these five together with the Yangqi and Huanglong branches that split off from the Linji house. [Great and small] The Great Vehicle and the Small Vehicle. [Half and full] The definitive Great Vehicle is the teaching of the full word; the non-definitive Small Vehicle is the teaching of the half word.
In a flash self and dharmas both forgotten, one understands true emptiness”:

In a flash forgetting self and dharmas is in a flash the death of self and dharmas; “forgotten” here is interchangeable with “dead.” That is, there is no longer a self of persons or a self of dharmas.
[True emptiness] The emptiness that is not emptiness: empty yet not empty, that is, marks exist while the essence does not.
Prajñā's flavor, layer upon layer”:
The meaning and import of prajñā are deep and wide, without end.
The four lines, blended and understood—its merit and virtue pass all praise”:

The sutra repeatedly speaks of the inconceivable merit of “receiving and upholding even a four-line verse and expounding it for others.” Therefore, so long as one blends and penetrates any four lines of the sutra (meaning a small portion of it), one's merit and virtue will be without end.

Now the Diamond Sutra takes no-marks as its doctrine, non-dwelling as its essence, and wondrous existence as its function, causing people to awaken to the principle and see the nature, and forever still the deluded mind. What is hoped for in students is that they see the nature of gold within the ore, and smelt it with the fire of wisdom, so that the ore goes and the gold remains—this is called Buddha.
The Great Adept Hanshan has a poem that says:
I see men turning the sutra, understanding by others' words.
The mouth turns, the mind turns not; mind and mouth contradict each other.
When the mind is true, without crookedness, one makes no tangles or coverings.
Only look into yourself; seek no one else to take your place.
When the mind is its own master, one knows there is no within or without.

[Tangles and coverings] Tangles and coverings. Both are other names for affliction: there are ten tangles and five coverings. [The ten tangles] Ten kinds of affliction. A tangle is another name for affliction, because affliction can bind the body and mind of sentient beings so that they cannot escape birth and death and realize nirvāṇa. The ten tangles are: shamelessness, lack of conscience, jealousy, stinginess, remorse, sleep, restlessness, torpor, anger, and concealment. [Concealment] To conceal is to hide. It means hiding the transgressions one has committed, dreading only that others may know, and so being unable to repent and turn to good. [The five coverings] Five kinds of affliction. A covering is another name for affliction, because affliction can cover people's mind-nature so that good dharmas do not arise. The five coverings are: greed and desire, anger and hatred, drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt about the Dharma.
